# THE154 — History, Missions, and Governance

## Course objectives

- 1. Explain the societal and spiritual circumstances that led to the Pentecostal revival of the early 1900s.
- 2. Recount key facts pertaining to the Pentecostal Movement and leading up to the birth of the Assemblies of God.
- 3. Identify central leaders and influencers during defining moments in the Assemblies of God’s history.
- 4. Summarize doctrines, beliefs, and values that define the Assemblies of God and distinguish it from other evangelical and Pentecostal organizations.
- 5. Trace the development of Assemblies of God missions from the beginning to the present and identify factors that have contributed to its remarkable growth and success.
- 6. Outline the histories, missions, and impact of various Assemblies of God programs, ministries, and educational institutions.
- 7. Evaluate the associations that impacted and were impacted by the Assemblies of God over the years.
- 8. Describe key areas of transformation in the Assemblies of God today and explain what must be done to meet the challenges of the future.
- 9. Describe the events that led to the formation of the Statement of Fundamental Truths.
- 10. Explain the structure and organization of the Assemblies of God.
- 11. Identify the Assemblies of God’s historical emphasis on the ministry of the Holy Spirit: baptism and gifts.
- 12. Analyze and apply lessons and biblical principles learned from this course to life and ministry.

## 1

### American Life and the Church in the 1800s

#### 1.1.1 — Explain what is meant by the Second Great Awakening and identify five major shifts that transformed America in the 1800s.

A Great Awakening

After the American Revolution (1775–1783), when the United States gained its independence from Great Britain, the new nation stood on the threshold of major transformation. During the late 1700s and early 1800s, a spiritual revival began to sweep across the land, changing the nation’s historical trajectory and shaping its character as a Christian society. Historians often refer to this time as the Second Great Awakening.

During these same years, America experienced many changes, especially a shift in the population. America doubled in size geographically through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, and people headed west to previously unsettled lands. Continuing immigration from Europe brought in many new cultures with their own languages and customs. These factors would soon lead to an equally transformative change in the churches and religious life of America.

Shifting Religious Methods

Because such a large portion of the population lived in new territories where there were no churches, it became necessary for the church to try new methods to be effective. Changes included the following:

Circuit-Riding Preachers

If the people could not get to the church, the minister would take the “church” to the people. Traveling preachers, also known as circuit riders, were assigned to a “circuit”—a broad territory. These men (and sometimes women) would ride hundreds of miles on horse or mule to visit communities without access to a church or minister. They preached anywhere they were welcome.

The Methodists were leaders in this adaptation, and it proved successful for them. In 1784, there were less than fifteen thousand Methodists in America. By 1839, the Methodist church had become the largest Protestant denomination in America, with around 750,000 Methodist members (Porter 1853, 159–160).

Lay Ministry

As new churches were being established in the growing territories, lay workers often took leadership of meetings when a regular preacher was not available. This opened opportunities for people of varying social standing to exercise their spiritual gifts.

Camp Meetings and Revivals

This era also saw an increasing use of special meetings held in a central location to which people might travel a hundred miles or more to participate—often coming together with people from other denominations, such as Presbyterians, Methodists, and Baptists. Perhaps the most famous camp meeting occurred in August 1801 in Cane Ridge, Kentucky. It was attended by twenty-three thousand people and lasted for a week.

Another change was the use of “revival meetings.” Unlike camp meetings, where people would travel outside their local area, revival meetings were held in a local church, and an outside preacher would come to them for meetings lasting from a few days to several weeks.

Participatory, Persuasive, and Emotional

While the trend in churches in the East had been toward more formal, hierarchical, and less personal services, western frontier services were just the opposite. People were encouraged to participate by singing, testifying, and praying. Sermons were preached in clear and simple language, followed by a persuasive, emotional appeal for repentance or action. These emotional services were often accompanied by manifestations of people’s response to the Holy Spirit, such as dancing, running, singing, weeping uncontrollably, laughing, or shaking.

Charles G. Finney established an effective pattern of preaching for conversion that preachers and evangelists followed for many years. In addition to careful advance preparation and advertising, Finney’s tactics included having an “inquiry room,” or a “mourner’s bench,” where “anxious sinners” under “the conviction of sin” could seek counseling and prayer to make a decision to follow Christ (Finney 1868).

Denominational Shift

Denominations that were quick to adopt and perfect these new methods—the Methodists and Baptists—flourished and spread across the nation. Those denominations that chose not to change with the times remained dominant only in the original colonies. Therefore, the religious makeup of the broader landscape of America changed from predominantly Congregationalist , Anglican (or Episcopalian), and Quaker to predominantly Methodists and Baptists.

Theological Shift

This shift in the relative strength and concentration of the various denominations led to a shift in the religious character of the nation from Calvinism (predestination) to Arminianism (free will). Since the newer churches believed that anyone could be saved, it followed that much effort would be exerted to persuade sinners to repent. A byproduct of this theological shift was increased optimism about the future, as these Christians believed that no one was a lost cause but that every person could be redeemed and transformed.

Societal Shift

These churches, sometimes called evangelical because of their emphasis on salvation through faith in Christ, applied this optimism to their view of society as well. They believed that as Christ transformed and cleaned up individual lives, He would also transform and clean up society. Many Christians became leaders for positive change in human rights issues of the day, including the abolition of slavery and the promotion of education, prison reform, temperance , and women’s rights. The Second Great Awakening was instrumental in reshaping America as a nation in terms of the percentage of Christians, the expansive reach of the church, and its influence on the morals and priorities of the nation.

A Decline into Error and Indifference

Modernism

By the mid to late 1800s, many American scholars began to adopt philosophies that explained the Bible not as a simple document from a single divine source but as a complex text that must be evaluated with a critical and historical approach. This philosophy, which became part of modernism , raised doubts about the historical accuracy of the Bible. This led many to reject the idea that the biblical text was reliable not just as a historical text but as a basis for morality or an understanding of the human condition. Influential writers, such as Immanuel Kant, Friedrich Schleiermacher, Georg Hegel, and Charles Darwin, offered alternative views on the nature of humanity and the basis of reality.

Secularism

The first half of the 1800s in America was a time of progress and great hope for the future as the nation expanded and thrived. This prosperity and progress led to postmillennialism , a belief that society would continue to improve and evolve to a time of perfection that would be followed by Christ’s second coming. This led the church to embrace a social gospel —an emphasis on improving secular society through social change rather than individual conversion.

While this led to many good things, including emphases on helping the poor, education, and the abolition of slavery, the attempt at societal transformation often came at the expense of preaching the good news of salvation through Christ. Much evangelistic work emphasized educating and reforming or “civilizing” non-Christians in America and around the world. This approach brought some success in transforming moral behavior but less success in actual spiritual conversion, leading to forms of cultural Christianity without a personal relationship with Jesus Christ.

Crisis Points

The Civil War of the mid-1800s dealt a serious blow to the idealistic view of humanity’s advancement and ability to save themselves. The postmillennial belief that society would continue to improve and evolve was shattered by the brutality and cost of war that divided the nation. As cultural Christianity proved inefficient in maintaining public morality, national stability faced many crisis points, such as

Rapid urbanization and change in America’s cities

Shifts in industry, leading to modernization of the work force and a growing economic divide between the rich and poor

Financial panic

Civil unrest

Government scandals

Decline of public morality

Increased alcoholism and addiction

Waning impact of the church

The cooling of religious fervor, coupled with the theological heresies introduced by modern thinking and science, led many Christians to recognize the need for change and correction within the churches. This gave rise to a Restorationist Movement, especially fundamentalism and the Holiness Movement, which would profoundly influence Pentecostalism and the formation of the Assemblies of God. Once again, a faithful remnant of believers cried out to God for a fresh move of the Spirit.

**Q:** Why did the growth and westward movement of America’s population cause such a change in religious methods?

**A:** The population was in flux with people moving to the western frontier. To reach people and grow, the church had to move with the people where there were no church buildings and ministers.

**Q:** Name at least three of the new methods that were used effectively during the Second Great Awakening.

**A:** (1) Traveling preachers, camp meetings, and revivals; (2) emotional services that invited involvement; (3) the increasing importance of lay workers and Sunday Schools

**Q:** Why did the Methodists become the predominant denomination in America in the 1800s?

**A:** Denominations that adopted the new ministry methods flourished and grew. The Methodists pioneered and excelled at many of these methods.

**Q:** How might evangelism and outreach to society fit better with an Arminian rather than a Calvinist theological perspective?

**A:** Calvinists believed in predestination, which might lead to a sense of pointlessness in preaching to or attempting to raise the station of those who were predestined to be lost, whereas Arminians believe that each person could be saved no matter how far away from God they seemed.

**Q:** Why might postmillennialism lead to a social gospel?

**A:** People who believe that Christ’s second coming would only happen once society had been perfected might put most of their effort into trying to perfect society and neglect the teaching of personal salvation.

**Q:** Would you describe America today as a Christian nation, a culturally Christian nation, a post-Christian nation, or a non-Christian nation? Explain.

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** What public areas declined when personal Christianity declined?

**A:** Public morality, political integrity, and national stability

**Q:** Given the crisis points and conditions in America prior to great revivals that occurred, what hope does this give you for the future of your community, country, or church?

**A:** Answers will vary.

### Defending the Faith and Preparing the Soil: Restorationism

#### 1.2.1 — Outline how Restorationism led to the birth of different movements.

In reaction to the drift of the church due to modernism, secularism, societal crisis points, and the moral and spiritual decline that followed, a remnant of steadfast believers sought to reform the church from within. Their goal was not to seek some new revelation but rather to restore (thus the term Restorationism) the purer form of Christianity as demonstrated by the early church and seen in the book of Acts and the writings of the apostles.

From this objective sprang several different movements that were foundational to the subsequent Pentecostal revival. At this time, biblical terms and imagery—such as baptism in the Holy Spirit , tongues of fire , Spirit-filled , and tarry —became common in sermons, literature, and songs among these people seeking a renewal of the church.

Fundamentalism—Antidote to Modernism

Christian Fundamentalism, a movement that arose in the late 1800s in reaction to modernism, sought to reaffirm core Christian doctrines as “fundamental” to the faith. These included the historical accuracy and inerrancy of the Bible, the Virgin Birth and bodily resurrection of Jesus, the necessity of the atoning work on the cross, and the imminent and physical return of Christ. The Fundamentalist Movement greatly influenced the Assemblies of God doctrine with regard to its views of Scripture, the person and work of Christ, and the emphasis on Christ’s Second Coming.

Holiness—Antidote to Secularism

The Holiness Movement sprang from the Methodism of the Second Great Awakening. Holiness teaching saw sanctification as a second work of God in believers after salvation. In their understanding, a person was first saved, at which time they are “justified” or made right with God, but after that, there is another work of the Holy Spirit in which they are “sanctified” or cleansed from sin. It was expected that the Holy Spirit would transform individuals who would then transform society.

Major influences of the Holiness Movement on the Assemblies of God include an emphasis on a second experience after salvation, a commitment to holiness in dress and behavior, and the traditions of valuing spiritual experience and earnestly seeking God. Like the Holiness Movement, the Assemblies of God also rejected predestination Calvinism and embraced free will Arminianism.

The Keswick Movement

Whereas Holiness teaching taught that the “second blessing” was for cleansing from the sinful nature and perfecting the soul, one wing of the Holiness Movement, called the “Higher Life” or Keswick Movement (named for the English resort town where yearly Holiness conferences were held), emphasized that the “second blessing” would also include an endowment with the power of the Holy Spirit for service. Some well-known Keswick proponents included ministers D. L. Moody, R. A. Torrey, and Adoniram J. Gordon.

Embracing this theology of sudden empowerment from heaven led many to believe that the power of the Holy Spirit, as experienced by the early church, was also available for them. This led to teaching divine healing and an expectation of miraculous signs and wonders. Such beliefs and practices were considered radical by many within the church communities.

A Shining Example of the Holiness Movement: A. B. Simpson (1843–1919) and the Missionary Training Institute

Although he is not as well-known as other church leaders, few people had more influence on the Pentecostal Movement and the earliest shape of the Assemblies of God than A.B. Simpson did. Born in Canada and called into the ministry at the age of fifteen, Simpson pastored Presbyterian churches in Canada and the United States before encountering Holiness teaching through the book, The Higher Christian Life (1858) by W. E. Boardman. Simpson’s life and ministry changed dramatically.

In addition to being healed of a serious heart ailment, he sought the baptism in the Holy Spirit, believing he would be endued with power by the Spirit for ministry. His heart burned to win souls both in America and abroad. He resigned from the Presbyterian church and started an independent ministry in New York City called the Gospel Tabernacle, where he reached out to the poor and unchurched. In 1897, he formed the Christian and Missionary Alliance (CMA) to promote the deeper Christian life and mobilize consecrated Christians for missions work. Alliance members who would one day contribute to the fledgling Assemblies of God include Daniel W. Kerr, J. Roswell and Alice Reynolds Flower, Carrie Judd Montgomery, Noel Perkin, John W. Welch, Frank M. Boyd, and W. I. Evans.

To further the purposes of the CMA, Simpson started the Missionary Training Institute (MTI) in New York, the first Bible institute of its kind in America. There, he taught the “Fourfold Gospel”: Christ as Savior, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King. As the disciples were trained by Jesus for three years, so Simpson’s Bible Institute model was also a three-year program of intense spiritual development and practical training for Christian service. Students called MTI “Simpson’s Matchbox,” reflecting his longing for them to be set on fire for the Lord’s work.

Since many future Assemblies of God ministers attended Simpson’s school, his teachings would be reflected in Assemblies of God teachings, including the following:

Premillennialism (the belief that Christ would return before the thousand-year period of peace on earth—the Millennium),

Faith healing,

Seeking the gifts of the Spirit,

An emphasis on human responsibility rather than on predestination (Arminianism rather than Calvinism),

A vision for missions, and

The importance of a Bible institute program for ministry training.

From Simpson’s writings and teachings, the Assemblies of God also inherited its ecclesiology and polity (church structure and forms, such as a General Council and presbyters), and many of its early hymns. His writings and teachings influenced a significant portion of our early leaders.

Simpson’s life reminds us that repentance and the prayers of a few—or just one—can move God’s hand and prepare the soil of human hearts for a fresh move of God. In studying the harbingers of the last century’s great Pentecostal revival, we see that today’s stage is set for another. Will you be a part of it?

**Q:** Define what Restorationism was and what it was not.

**A:** It was not a new form of Christianity but an effort to restore or return to a purer form as demonstrated by the Early Church and the apostles.

**Q:** According to the text, what does the Assemblies of God owe to the Fundamentalist Movement?

**A:** The Assemblies of God was greatly influenced in its views of Scripture as inspired and inerrant, the person and work of Christ, and its emphasis on Christ’s second coming.

**Q:** In what way was the Holiness Movement an antidote to secularism?

**A:** The emphasis on a personal relationship with God—holy living and earnestly seeking God—was in direct opposition to the trend toward casual religion in name only.

**Q:** Why were these Christians considered radicals? Compare your beliefs to those of traditional churches of the time. In what ways would you be considered a radical?

**A:** Restorationist Christians were considered radical because in their quest to restore Christianity to its apostolic origins, their dress, actions, and beliefs seemed strange. The Keswick Movement was considered radical because of its belief in the power of the Holy Spirit, including divine healing, gifts of the Spirit, and signs and wonders. Personal answers will vary.

**Q:** What are some of Simpson’s core teachings at his Missionary Training Institute that are reflected in Assemblies of God teachings?

**A:** Premillennialism, faith healing, gifts of the Spirit, free-will Arminianism, missions emphasis, importance of training and education. Prelude: Before the Pentecostal Revival Winds of Revival in America: Topeka, Azusa, and Beyond 2 CHAPTER

#### 1.2.2 — Explain how Fundamentalism provided an antidote to modernism.

In reaction to the drift of the church due to modernism, secularism, societal crisis points, and the moral and spiritual decline that followed, a remnant of steadfast believers sought to reform the church from within. Their goal was not to seek some new revelation but rather to restore (thus the term Restorationism) the purer form of Christianity as demonstrated by the early church and seen in the book of Acts and the writings of the apostles.

From this objective sprang several different movements that were foundational to the subsequent Pentecostal revival. At this time, biblical terms and imagery—such as baptism in the Holy Spirit , tongues of fire , Spirit-filled , and tarry —became common in sermons, literature, and songs among these people seeking a renewal of the church.

Fundamentalism—Antidote to Modernism

Christian Fundamentalism, a movement that arose in the late 1800s in reaction to modernism, sought to reaffirm core Christian doctrines as “fundamental” to the faith. These included the historical accuracy and inerrancy of the Bible, the Virgin Birth and bodily resurrection of Jesus, the necessity of the atoning work on the cross, and the imminent and physical return of Christ. The Fundamentalist Movement greatly influenced the Assemblies of God doctrine with regard to its views of Scripture, the person and work of Christ, and the emphasis on Christ’s Second Coming.

Holiness—Antidote to Secularism

The Holiness Movement sprang from the Methodism of the Second Great Awakening. Holiness teaching saw sanctification as a second work of God in believers after salvation. In their understanding, a person was first saved, at which time they are “justified” or made right with God, but after that, there is another work of the Holy Spirit in which they are “sanctified” or cleansed from sin. It was expected that the Holy Spirit would transform individuals who would then transform society.

Major influences of the Holiness Movement on the Assemblies of God include an emphasis on a second experience after salvation, a commitment to holiness in dress and behavior, and the traditions of valuing spiritual experience and earnestly seeking God. Like the Holiness Movement, the Assemblies of God also rejected predestination Calvinism and embraced free will Arminianism.

The Keswick Movement

Whereas Holiness teaching taught that the “second blessing” was for cleansing from the sinful nature and perfecting the soul, one wing of the Holiness Movement, called the “Higher Life” or Keswick Movement (named for the English resort town where yearly Holiness conferences were held), emphasized that the “second blessing” would also include an endowment with the power of the Holy Spirit for service. Some well-known Keswick proponents included ministers D. L. Moody, R. A. Torrey, and Adoniram J. Gordon.

Embracing this theology of sudden empowerment from heaven led many to believe that the power of the Holy Spirit, as experienced by the early church, was also available for them. This led to teaching divine healing and an expectation of miraculous signs and wonders. Such beliefs and practices were considered radical by many within the church communities.

A Shining Example of the Holiness Movement: A. B. Simpson (1843–1919) and the Missionary Training Institute

Although he is not as well-known as other church leaders, few people had more influence on the Pentecostal Movement and the earliest shape of the Assemblies of God than A.B. Simpson did. Born in Canada and called into the ministry at the age of fifteen, Simpson pastored Presbyterian churches in Canada and the United States before encountering Holiness teaching through the book, The Higher Christian Life (1858) by W. E. Boardman. Simpson’s life and ministry changed dramatically.

In addition to being healed of a serious heart ailment, he sought the baptism in the Holy Spirit, believing he would be endued with power by the Spirit for ministry. His heart burned to win souls both in America and abroad. He resigned from the Presbyterian church and started an independent ministry in New York City called the Gospel Tabernacle, where he reached out to the poor and unchurched. In 1897, he formed the Christian and Missionary Alliance (CMA) to promote the deeper Christian life and mobilize consecrated Christians for missions work. Welch, Frank M. Boyd, and W. I. Evans.

To further the purposes of the CMA, Simpson started the Missionary Training Institute (MTI) in New York, the first Bible institute of its kind in America. There, he taught the “Fourfold Gospel”: Christ as Savior, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King. ## 2

### Charles Fox Parham (1873–1929): Father of Modern-day Pentecostalism

#### 2.1.1 — Describe the process by which Charles Parham became convinced of God's call to ministry.

Charles Parham: Holiness, Healing, and Baptism in the Holy Spirit

Charles Fox Parham (1873-1929) was a Holiness preacher whose early childhood illness caused him to pray for healing. As he began to step out in obedience to a call to preach, he experienced a healing that convinced him that God was real and personally involved in the lives of His people. Despite some continuing physical weakness, he preached A.B. Simpson’s fourfold message of Christ as Savior, Sanctifier, Healer, and Soon Coming King.

However, Parham added an additional tenet of belief that he described as “the baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire, which seals the Bride and bestows the gifts” (Apostolic Faith 1900, 8). This recognition and emphasis was something new at the time, as it identified the “second work of grace” of the Holiness Movement specifically with the baptism in the Holy Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit. In 1898, Parham and his wife, Sarah, opened the Bethel Healing Home in Topeka, Kansas, where people could stay while seeking the Lord for healing. From the home, he also preached, taught, and produced a bimonthly periodical, The Apostolic Faith . Additionally, he worked to increase the social good of the community through feeding programs, finding work for the unemployed, and establishing Christian homes for orphans.

Seeking Evidence

In early 1900, Parham left the Topeka work in the hands of others to visit with ministries he believed showed evidence of the Holy Spirit’s work. These included John Alexander Dowie’s healing ministry in Zion City, Illinois; A. B. Simpson’s ministry in Nyack, New York; and Frank W. Sandford’s Shiloh Ministry in Durham, Maine. Parham was impressed by Sandford’s method of instruction: rather than relying on textbooks that gave the opinions of men, the teachers guided students in studying the Bible directly to establish their theology. He also heard intriguing stories of missionaries overseas being given the gift of xenolalia —speaking in a known human language that one has not learned (for example, speaking Mandarin in China or Russian in Russia). Parham came to believe that this was what was predicted in Joel 2:28–29 and demonstrated in Acts 2. He saw a pattern in the book of Acts that connected tongues with the infilling of the Holy Spirit and concluded that speaking in unknown languages was not only evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit but also would provide supernatural power for one final evangelistic push before the imminent return of Christ.

In October 1900, Parham returned to Topeka and established Bethel Bible College in an elaborate unfinished mansion called Stone’s Folly . He began with forty students, adopting the study method he saw modeled at Sandford’s school. Students were also assigned three-hour shifts in round-the-clock prayer

.

A New Chapter

In late December, before going on a three-day ministry trip, Parham left students with an assignment: study the book of Acts to discover the “biblical evidence” of the “Apostolic baptism” as promised by Jesus in Acts 1:8.

Upon his return, he was excited to learn that they had unanimously concluded that speaking in tongues was the initial physical sign of Holy Spirit baptism, evident in Acts 2 as well as on multiple other occasions (Acts 8:14–20, 9:17, 10:44–48, 19:1–7), whether specifically stated or implied. They determined that other signs, such as visible fire and the sound of a rushing wind, were not reproduced in subsequent outpourings of the Spirit. Parham then encouraged the students to begin to ask God to baptize them for service in the same way He baptized the early believers.

At the prayer meeting on the first day of the new century (January 1, 1901), a student, Agnes Ozman, asked Parham to lay hands on her and pray that she might receive this baptism with the evidence of tongues just as they saw in Acts. Suddenly, God’s Spirit came upon her and she began to speak in a language she did not previously know. Within days, half the students had been filled with the Spirit, and others, including Parham, were fervently seeking.

As Parham continued to cry out to God for his own Spirit baptism, he reported that he heard God’s charge to declare this truth to the world, along with a question: “Are you willing to suffer the persecution, slander, trials, and scandal that will accompany this blessing?” When Parham agreed, he was filled with the Spirit and spoke in tongues. Later, on January 21, 1901, Parham preached the first sermon in modern history focused solely on the baptism in the Holy Spirit as evidenced by speaking in other languages.

Disappointment and New Opportunities

To Parham’s surprise and disappointment, not much came of this initial outpouring beyond criticism and ridicule. Even Holiness leaders were quick to denounce what Parham called the Apostolic Faith Movement .

During this difficult time, Parham wrote his first book, A Voice Crying in the Wilderness , which was the first defense of the young Pentecostal Movement. Hungry believers and leaders across the country and around the world read, learned, and later taught from this influential book.

In the summer of 1905, Parham was invited to hold meetings in Texas. High-profile healings, including the healing of a woman paralyzed in a widely known carriage accident, caught the attention of many. By winter, Parham’s ministry had reached twenty-five thousand people. In Houston, he opened a Bible training school and began teaching on the baptism in the Holy Spirit.

Lucy Farrow (1851–1911), a local Holiness pastor, former slave, and niece of abolitionist Frederick Douglass, served as governess for the Parham family and cook for the school. She became the first African American recorded as being baptized in the Spirit with the evidence of speaking in tongues. Farrow introduced another Holiness preacher, William J. Seymour, to Parham and his teachings. The baton was about to be passed for the next stage of the Pentecostal revival.

**Q:** Read Acts 2 to remind yourself of what Parham’s students were studying and imagine what sort of conclusion you might have reached.

**A:** Answers will vary.

#### 2.1.2 — Identify the unique tenet Parham added to Holiness doctrine and explain its importance in preparing for the Pentecostal Movement.

However, Parham added an additional tenet of belief that he described as “the baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire, which seals the Bride and bestows the gifts” (Apostolic Faith 1900, 8). This recognition and emphasis was something new at the time, as it identified the “second work of grace” of the Holiness Movement specifically with the baptism in the Holy Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit. In 1898, Parham and his wife, Sarah, opened the Bethel Healing Home in Topeka, Kansas, where people could stay while seeking the Lord for healing. From the home, he also preached, taught, and produced a bimonthly periodical, The Apostolic Faith . Additionally, he worked to increase the social good of the community through feeding programs, finding work for the unemployed, and establishing Christian homes for orphans.

Seeking Evidence

In early 1900, Parham left the Topeka work in the hands of others to visit with ministries he believed showed evidence of the Holy Spirit’s work. These included John Alexander Dowie’s healing ministry in Zion City, Illinois; A. B. Simpson’s ministry in Nyack, New York; and Frank W. Sandford’s Shiloh Ministry in Durham, Maine. Parham was impressed by Sandford’s method of instruction: rather than relying on textbooks that gave the opinions of men, the teachers guided students in studying the Bible directly to establish their theology. He also heard intriguing stories of missionaries overseas being given the gift of xenolalia —speaking in a known human language that one has not learned (for example, speaking Mandarin in China or Russian in Russia). Parham came to believe that this was what was predicted in Joel 2:28–29 and demonstrated in Acts 2. He saw a pattern in the book of Acts that connected tongues with the infilling of the Holy Spirit and concluded that speaking in unknown languages was not only evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit but also would provide supernatural power for one final evangelistic push before the imminent return of Christ.

In October 1900, Parham returned to Topeka and established Bethel Bible College in an elaborate unfinished mansion called Stone’s Folly . He began with forty students, adopting the study method he saw modeled at Sandford’s school. Students were also assigned three-hour shifts in round-the-clock prayer

.

A New Chapter

In late December, before going on a three-day ministry trip, Parham left students with an assignment: study the book of Acts to discover the “biblical evidence” of the “Apostolic baptism” as promised by Jesus in Acts 1:8.

Upon his return, he was excited to learn that they had unanimously concluded that speaking in tongues was the initial physical sign of Holy Spirit baptism, evident in Acts 2 as well as on multiple other occasions (Acts 8:14–20, 9:17, 10:44–48, 19:1–7), whether specifically stated or implied. They determined that other signs, such as visible fire and the sound of a rushing wind, were not reproduced in subsequent outpourings of the Spirit. Parham then encouraged the students to begin to ask God to baptize them for service in the same way He baptized the early believers.

At the prayer meeting on the first day of the new century (January 1, 1901), a student, Agnes Ozman, asked Parham to lay hands on her and pray that she might receive this baptism with the evidence of tongues just as they saw in Acts. Suddenly, God’s Spirit came upon her and she began to speak in a language she did not previously know. Within days, half the students had been filled with the Spirit, and others, including Parham, were fervently seeking.

As Parham continued to cry out to God for his own Spirit baptism, he reported that he heard God’s charge to declare this truth to the world, along with a question: “Are you willing to suffer the persecution, slander, trials, and scandal that will accompany this blessing?” When Parham agreed, he was filled with the Spirit and spoke in tongues. Later, on January 21, 1901, Parham preached the first sermon in modern history focused solely on the baptism in the Holy Spirit as evidenced by speaking in other languages.

Disappointment and New Opportunities

To Parham’s surprise and disappointment, not much came of this initial outpouring beyond criticism and ridicule. Even Holiness leaders were quick to denounce what Parham called the Apostolic Faith Movement .

During this difficult time, Parham wrote his first book, A Voice Crying in the Wilderness , which was the first defense of the young Pentecostal Movement. Hungry believers and leaders across the country and around the world read, learned, and later taught from this influential book.

In the summer of 1905, Parham was invited to hold meetings in Texas. High-profile healings, including the healing of a woman paralyzed in a widely known carriage accident, caught the attention of many. By winter, Parham’s ministry had reached twenty-five thousand people. In Houston, he opened a Bible training school and began teaching on the baptism in the Holy Spirit.

Lucy Farrow (1851–1911), a local Holiness pastor, former slave, and niece of abolitionist Frederick Douglass, served as governess for the Parham family and cook for the school. She became the first African American recorded as being baptized in the Spirit with the evidence of speaking in tongues. Farrow introduced another Holiness preacher, William J. Seymour, to Parham and his teachings. The baton was about to be passed for the next stage of the Pentecostal revival.

**Q:** Read Acts 2 to remind yourself of what Parham’s students were studying and imagine what sort of conclusion you might have reached.

**A:** Answers will vary.

### William J. Seymour (1870–1922) and the Azusa Street Revival

#### 2.2.1 — Summarize the difficulties William Seymour overcame and evaluate how they may have affected his ministry.

An Overcoming Spirit

William J. Seymour seemed no more likely than Parham to be a pivotal figure in the history of the church. Although blind in one eye from the smallpox that scarred his face and nearly ended his life, he saw more of the Holy Spirit’s moving than did almost any other person in history. Born to former slaves in Louisiana, Seymour’s early life was marred by racial hostility and grinding poverty.

When his father, who had never fully recovered from malaria he contracted when fighting with the Union army, died in 1891, Seymour was largely responsible for supporting his mother and seven brothers and sisters. In 1896, his mother’s personal possessions were valued at fifty-five cents, and the household property was listed as one old bed and mattress and one old chair.

When Lucy Farrow convinced her young friend to learn about Parham’s new teaching, Jim Crow laws made it illegal for Seymour to learn in the classroom with white students. With grace and dignity, he accepted Parham’s offer to sit and listen in the hallway beside the open door. Before long, although he had not yet been baptized in the Spirit as evidenced by speaking in tongues, Seymour had sufficiently mastered Parham’s teachings to teach them to others. Parham invited Seymour to partner with him in meetings, Parham preaching to Whites and Seymour to African Americans.

Soon, a woman named Julia Hutchinson invited Seymour to pastor a Holiness church in Los Angeles. On March 4, 1906, he preached his first sermon on Acts 2:4, declaring that tongues were the initial physical evidence of Spirit baptism. When he returned for the afternoon service, he found the church doors locked. Believing his teaching to be heresy, Hutchinson’s church turned him away.

Humble Beginnings

Not every church member who heard Seymour preach rejected his message. Edward S. Lee invited Seymour to stay with him and hold Bible studies and prayer meetings there. With no money for fare back to Houston, Seymour agreed. The group soon outgrew Lee’s home and moved the meetings to a larger home a few blocks away, that of Richard and Ruth Asberry at 214 Bonnie Brae Street.

On April 6, the group of seekers called for a ten-day fast with prayer, agreeing to meet together every night to study Acts 2:4 and pray. A few days later, Lee was not feeling well and asked Seymour to pray for him before going to the meeting. Seymour and Farrow, who had just arrived from Houston, laid hands on him and, as they prayed, Lee began to speak in tongues.

When they hurried to the Bonnie Brae gathering and shared this exciting testimony, people started praising the Lord. Many others spoke in tongues at that April 9, 1906 meeting, including Jennie Moore, who later became William Seymour's wife.

News of the Spirit’s outpouring with the gift of tongues traveled quickly, and crowds of all races soon overflowed the house and spilled into the streets. For several nights, Seymour and various speakers preached from the porch to crowds that filled the streets. Some from the church who had locked out Seymour came and were filled with the Spirit—including Julia Hutchins! Seymour himself finally received the baptism on April 12, after tarrying (waiting and praying) with a White brother until 4 a.m.

The Azusa Street Phenomenon

The story of the Azusa Street Revival is one of the best known in modern Pentecostal circles. It is a thrilling account of God’s mighty moving and an important precursor to the birth of the Assemblies of God. Some important lessons for today can be learned from the Azusa Street story:

A. The revival used what was available . The crowds grew so big that the Asberrys’ wooden porch collapsed, making it necessary for the group to move to a larger building. They found a forty- by sixty-foot wooden structure at 312 Azusa Street, and Seymour named it the Apostolic Faith Mission. It had been used as a livery stable, and it both looked and smelled like it.

B. It was intense and long lasting. For the next three years, revival services were held daily at 10 a.m., noon, and 7 p.m. On many days, people never left. Services just blended together in all-day prayer and praise. Within months, attendance grew to between five hundred and seven hundred, although it could soar as high as 1,500 attending in one of the three daily services.

C. It was inclusive and intercultural. The core group of regulars, perhaps two hundred, were truly intercultural. They were reportedly Black (fifty percent), Hispanic (five to ten percent), and White (forty percent), with a smattering of Japanese, Native American, and other races and nationalities. Leadership was shared by Black and White, male and female, rich and poor, young and old. Azusa Street regular attendee and chronicler of the Pentecostal Movement Frank Bartleman exclaimed, “The color line was washed away in the Blood” (McGee 1999).

D . It was expansive. The largest percentage of those in attendance were visitors from beyond Los Angeles. Many Christians who were hungry for more of God came from across the country and around the world in response to Seymour’s paper, The Apostolic Faith, which reported what was happening in Los Angeles. They would return to their homes, neighborhoods, and churches—or go to mission fields overseas—in the power of the Spirit, eager to share what they had experienced, seen, and learned.

E. It was well organized. Some believers have allowed reliance on the Spirit’s leading to undermine their commitment to preparation, planning, and hard work, but the Azusa Street Mission needed to be—and was—a highly organized and efficient operation. From producing the periodical to organizing prayer or witnessing teams, the Azusa Street ministries were well coordinated.

F. It was infectious. The dramatic experiences at the mission, along with the amazing crowds, attracted great attention. It seemed everyone was drawn to what was happening on Azusa Street. While many came to scrutinize, ridicule, and oppose, others came to learn and experience this baptism for themselves. Even those who came to mock were often changed, overcome by the presence and power of God.

G. It was focused on God rather than on a charismatic leader. Such success and approval might have gone to lesser leaders’ heads, causing pride, but Seymour remained humble in spite of being at the center of the church world’s attention. Bartleman described Seymour’s humility as a servant of God: there was no elevated platform for the preacher, and for a long time, no pulpit. Instead, Seymour sat behind two large shoeboxes. He often kept his face hidden in the top box, in prayer, during services, only emerging to speak. One visiting minister from Chicago described Seymour as “the meekest man I ever met” (Synan 2006).

Seymour still considered Parham to be his spiritual father and mentor. For months, he urged Parham to come to Azusa Street. He wanted him to speak at city-wide revival meetings. He also wanted his help in assessing and dealing with some manifestations in the services that Seymour worried seemed more of the flesh than the Spirit. Sadly, when Parham arrived six months after the beginning of the revival and saw the impact of the Azusa Street Revival and its new position as the center of the Pentecostal Movement, his arrival did more harm than good.

Breaking and Shaking

Shocked by the loud and exuberant atmosphere, the manifestations that sounded more like babble than actual languages, and the unprecedented interaction between races, Parham was quick to show his disapproval. He stood up, interrupted the service, and pronounced that these manifestations were not of God but of the devil.

This can be explained in part by Parham’s views of race that were common in the South at that time. Parham was not comfortable with the emotional style of preaching and worship common to many Black churches and evident at Azusa Street. While believing that all people should hear the gospel and receive the baptism in the Holy Spirit, Parham did not believe that it was proper for the races to mix together as was being experienced at Azusa Street.

Additionally, Parham still clung to the idea of xenolalia, the Holy Spirit’s giving of natural languages to aid in evangelism and missions, while the experience of Seymour’s group led them to believe that those filled with the Spirit often spoke in heavenly rather than human languages— glossolalia but not necessarily xenolalia.

Unsurprisingly, Parham’s bold and public denunciation caused an irreparable break between the two men. Seymour never permitted Parham to return. For a time, Parham led his own church nearby, which ended up splitting the church body largely along racial lines.

Although the incredible Azusa Street Revival faded after three years, the larger Pentecostal revival it inspired continued to grow and spread. Seymour remained pastor until his death in 1922. His wife, Jennie, followed him as pastor until her death in 1936.

The contribution of Seymour and the Azusa Street Revival cannot be overestimated. A new diaspora of Spirit-filled believers was launched from Azusa Street to great works of evangelism and missions across America and around the world. Seymour’s emphases on spiritual empowerment, humility, holiness, and unity remain examples for Pentecostals today.

**Q:** How did Seymour’s attitude enable him to be equipped for ministry?

**A:** Despite limitations imposed by racial discrimination, Seymour was a humble and hungry learner and mastered Parham’s teachings enough that he was able to minister.

**Q:** Describe the actions that were a precursor to the outpouring that became the Azusa Street Revival.

**A:** Seeking, fasting, prayer (corporate prayer as well as laying on of hands and praying for each other to be infilled with the Holy Spirit), studying the Word regularly together, and praising the Lord for what He had done.

**Q:** List several of the lessons we can learn from the Azusa Street Revival.

**A:** The revival used what was available. It was intense and long-lasting, inclusive and intercultural, expansive, well-organized, infectious, and focused on God rather than on a charismatic leader.

**Q:** Read 1 Corinthians 1:26–31. How does this apply to many of the people God used to bring about the twentieth century Pentecostal revival? What encouragement does it hold for you?

**A:** Parham was often physically weak. Seymour was poor, blind in one eye, and discriminated against for his race. Lucy Farrow was a poor Black woman and former slave. None were highly esteemed in the world’s eyes, yet God used them.

**Q:** Charles Parham is sometimes called the “Father of Modern-day Pentecostalism.” Give at least two arguments to support or refute this honor.

**A:** Pro: He was the first to articulate the concept of baptism in the Holy Spirit with the initial physical evidence of speaking in tongues; he was the first to teach it; under his teaching, the first instances of speaking in tongues took place, which were understood as being linked to baptism in the Holy Spirit; he was the first to spread this new truth, even attempting a modicum of organization. Con: The Pentecostal Movement and Pentecostalism were a work of God and not of any person; others had spoken in tongues previously. William Seymour and the Azusa Street Revival were more influential in spreading Pentecost.

**Q:** “The Lord has assigned to each his task” (1 Corinthians 3:5). Each person has a part to play in God’s work. It is important to remember that we each build upon the work of others and, if we do our part well, others will build upon ours. Upon whose work did Parham and Seymour build?

**A:** Parham built on the works of Dowie, Simpson, and Sandford; Seymour built on the works of all of those plus Parham, Lucy Farrow, Edward Lee, the Asberrys, and others—even Julia Hutchinson, for she was responsible for inviting Seymour to Los Angeles.

**Q:** Consider: upon whose work are you building?

**A:** Answers will vary. Pentecostal Mission 3 CHAPTER

#### 2.2.2 — Describe the humble beginnings of the Los Angeles Revival and the humility Seymour maintained when the Azusa Street Revival exploded.

An Overcoming Spirit

William J. Seymour seemed no more likely than Parham to be a pivotal figure in the history of the church. Although blind in one eye from the smallpox that scarred his face and nearly ended his life, he saw more of the Holy Spirit’s moving than did almost any other person in history. Born to former slaves in Louisiana, Seymour’s early life was marred by racial hostility and grinding poverty.

When his father, who had never fully recovered from malaria he contracted when fighting with the Union army, died in 1891, Seymour was largely responsible for supporting his mother and seven brothers and sisters. In 1896, his mother’s personal possessions were valued at fifty-five cents, and the household property was listed as one old bed and mattress and one old chair.

When Lucy Farrow convinced her young friend to learn about Parham’s new teaching, Jim Crow laws made it illegal for Seymour to learn in the classroom with white students. With grace and dignity, he accepted Parham’s offer to sit and listen in the hallway beside the open door. Before long, although he had not yet been baptized in the Spirit as evidenced by speaking in tongues, Seymour had sufficiently mastered Parham’s teachings to teach them to others. Parham invited Seymour to partner with him in meetings, Parham preaching to Whites and Seymour to African Americans.

Soon, a woman named Julia Hutchinson invited Seymour to pastor a Holiness church in Los Angeles. On March 4, 1906, he preached his first sermon on Acts 2:4, declaring that tongues were the initial physical evidence of Spirit baptism. When he returned for the afternoon service, he found the church doors locked. Believing his teaching to be heresy, Hutchinson’s church turned him away.

Humble Beginnings

Not every church member who heard Seymour preach rejected his message. Edward S. Lee invited Seymour to stay with him and hold Bible studies and prayer meetings there. With no money for fare back to Houston, Seymour agreed. The group soon outgrew Lee’s home and moved the meetings to a larger home a few blocks away, that of Richard and Ruth Asberry at 214 Bonnie Brae Street.

On April 6, the group of seekers called for a ten-day fast with prayer, agreeing to meet together every night to study Acts 2:4 and pray. A few days later, Lee was not feeling well and asked Seymour to pray for him before going to the meeting. Seymour and Farrow, who had just arrived from Houston, laid hands on him and, as they prayed, Lee began to speak in tongues.

When they hurried to the Bonnie Brae gathering and shared this exciting testimony, people started praising the Lord. Many others spoke in tongues at that April 9, 1906 meeting, including Jennie Moore, who later became William Seymour's wife.

News of the Spirit’s outpouring with the gift of tongues traveled quickly, and crowds of all races soon overflowed the house and spilled into the streets. For several nights, Seymour and various speakers preached from the porch to crowds that filled the streets. Some from the church who had locked out Seymour came and were filled with the Spirit—including Julia Hutchins! Seymour himself finally received the baptism on April 12, after tarrying (waiting and praying) with a White brother until 4 a.m.

The Azusa Street Phenomenon

The story of the Azusa Street Revival is one of the best known in modern Pentecostal circles. It is a thrilling account of God’s mighty moving and an important precursor to the birth of the Assemblies of God. Some important lessons for today can be learned from the Azusa Street story:

A. The revival used what was available . The crowds grew so big that the Asberrys’ wooden porch collapsed, making it necessary for the group to move to a larger building. They found a forty- by sixty-foot wooden structure at 312 Azusa Street, and Seymour named it the Apostolic Faith Mission. It had been used as a livery stable, and it both looked and smelled like it.

B. It was intense and long lasting. For the next three years, revival services were held daily at 10 a.m., noon, and 7 p.m. On many days, people never left. Services just blended together in all-day prayer and praise. Within months, attendance grew to between five hundred and seven hundred, although it could soar as high as 1,500 attending in one of the three daily services.

C. It was inclusive and intercultural. The core group of regulars, perhaps two hundred, were truly intercultural. They were reportedly Black (fifty percent), Hispanic (five to ten percent), and White (forty percent), with a smattering of Japanese, Native American, and other races and nationalities. Leadership was shared by Black and White, male and female, rich and poor, young and old. Azusa Street regular attendee and chronicler of the Pentecostal Movement Frank Bartleman exclaimed, “The color line was washed away in the Blood” (McGee 1999).

D . It was expansive. The largest percentage of those in attendance were visitors from beyond Los Angeles. Many Christians who were hungry for more of God came from across the country and around the world in response to Seymour’s paper, The Apostolic Faith, which reported what was happening in Los Angeles. They would return to their homes, neighborhoods, and churches—or go to mission fields overseas—in the power of the Spirit, eager to share what they had experienced, seen, and learned.

E. It was well organized. Some believers have allowed reliance on the Spirit’s leading to undermine their commitment to preparation, planning, and hard work, but the Azusa Street Mission needed to be—and was—a highly organized and efficient operation. From producing the periodical to organizing prayer or witnessing teams, the Azusa Street ministries were well coordinated.

F. It was infectious. The dramatic experiences at the mission, along with the amazing crowds, attracted great attention. It seemed everyone was drawn to what was happening on Azusa Street. While many came to scrutinize, ridicule, and oppose, others came to learn and experience this baptism for themselves. Even those who came to mock were often changed, overcome by the presence and power of God.

G. It was focused on God rather than on a charismatic leader. Such success and approval might have gone to lesser leaders’ heads, causing pride, but Seymour remained humble in spite of being at the center of the church world’s attention. Bartleman described Seymour’s humility as a servant of God: there was no elevated platform for the preacher, and for a long time, no pulpit. Instead, Seymour sat behind two large shoeboxes. He often kept his face hidden in the top box, in prayer, during services, only emerging to speak. One visiting minister from Chicago described Seymour as “the meekest man I ever met” (Synan 2006).

Seymour still considered Parham to be his spiritual father and mentor. For months, he urged Parham to come to Azusa Street. He wanted him to speak at city-wide revival meetings. He also wanted his help in assessing and dealing with some manifestations in the services that Seymour worried seemed more of the flesh than the Spirit. Sadly, when Parham arrived six months after the beginning of the revival and saw the impact of the Azusa Street Revival and its new position as the center of the Pentecostal Movement, his arrival did more harm than good.

Breaking and Shaking

Shocked by the loud and exuberant atmosphere, the manifestations that sounded more like babble than actual languages, and the unprecedented interaction between races, Parham was quick to show his disapproval. He stood up, interrupted the service, and pronounced that these manifestations were not of God but of the devil.

This can be explained in part by Parham’s views of race that were common in the South at that time. Parham was not comfortable with the emotional style of preaching and worship common to many Black churches and evident at Azusa Street. While believing that all people should hear the gospel and receive the baptism in the Holy Spirit, Parham did not believe that it was proper for the races to mix together as was being experienced at Azusa Street.

Additionally, Parham still clung to the idea of xenolalia, the Holy Spirit’s giving of natural languages to aid in evangelism and missions, while the experience of Seymour’s group led them to believe that those filled with the Spirit often spoke in heavenly rather than human languages— glossolalia but not necessarily xenolalia.

Unsurprisingly, Parham’s bold and public denunciation caused an irreparable break between the two men. Seymour never permitted Parham to return. For a time, Parham led his own church nearby, which ended up splitting the church body largely along racial lines.

Although the incredible Azusa Street Revival faded after three years, the larger Pentecostal revival it inspired continued to grow and spread. Seymour remained pastor until his death in 1922. His wife, Jennie, followed him as pastor until her death in 1936.

The contribution of Seymour and the Azusa Street Revival cannot be overestimated. A new diaspora of Spirit-filled believers was launched from Azusa Street to great works of evangelism and missions across America and around the world. Seymour’s emphases on spiritual empowerment, humility, holiness, and unity remain examples for Pentecostals today.

**Q:** How did Seymour’s attitude enable him to be equipped for ministry?

**A:** Despite limitations imposed by racial discrimination, Seymour was a humble and hungry learner and mastered Parham’s teachings enough that he was able to minister.

**Q:** Describe the actions that were a precursor to the outpouring that became the Azusa Street Revival.

**A:** Seeking, fasting, prayer (corporate prayer as well as laying on of hands and praying for each other to be infilled with the Holy Spirit), studying the Word regularly together, and praising the Lord for what He had done.

**Q:** List several of the lessons we can learn from the Azusa Street Revival.

**A:** The revival used what was available. It was intense and long-lasting, inclusive and intercultural, expansive, well-organized, infectious, and focused on God rather than on a charismatic leader.

**Q:** Read 1 Corinthians 1:26–31. How does this apply to many of the people God used to bring about the twentieth century Pentecostal revival? What encouragement does it hold for you?

**A:** Parham was often physically weak. Seymour was poor, blind in one eye, and discriminated against for his race. Lucy Farrow was a poor Black woman and former slave. None were highly esteemed in the world’s eyes, yet God used them.

**Q:** Charles Parham is sometimes called the “Father of Modern-day Pentecostalism.” Give at least two arguments to support or refute this honor.

**A:** Pro: He was the first to articulate the concept of baptism in the Holy Spirit with the initial physical evidence of speaking in tongues; he was the first to teach it; under his teaching, the first instances of speaking in tongues took place, which were understood as being linked to baptism in the Holy Spirit; he was the first to spread this new truth, even attempting a modicum of organization. Con: The Pentecostal Movement and Pentecostalism were a work of God and not of any person; others had spoken in tongues previously. William Seymour and the Azusa Street Revival were more influential in spreading Pentecost.

**Q:** “The Lord has assigned to each his task” (1 Corinthians 3:5). Each person has a part to play in God’s work. It is important to remember that we each build upon the work of others and, if we do our part well, others will build upon ours. Upon whose work did Parham and Seymour build?

**A:** Parham built on the works of Dowie, Simpson, and Sandford; Seymour built on the works of all of those plus Parham, Lucy Farrow, Edward Lee, the Asberrys, and others—even Julia Hutchinson, for she was responsible for inviting Seymour to Los Angeles.

**Q:** Consider: upon whose work are you building?

**A:** Answers will vary. Pentecostal Mission 3 CHAPTER

Parham was not comfortable with the emotional style of preaching and worship common to many Black churches and evident at Azusa Street. Additionally, Parham still clung to the idea of xenolalia, the Holy Spirit’s giving of natural languages to aid in evangelism and missions, while the experience of Seymour’s group led them to believe that those filled with the Spirit often spoke in heavenly rather than human languages— glossolalia but not necessarily xenolalia.

Unsurprisingly, Parham’s bold and public denunciation caused an irreparable break between the two men. Seymour never permitted Parham to return. For a time, Parham led his own church nearby, which ended up splitting the church body largely along racial lines.

Although the incredible Azusa Street Revival faded after three years, the larger Pentecostal revival it inspired continued to grow and spread. Seymour remained pastor until his death in 1922. His wife, Jennie, followed him as pastor until her death in 1936.

The contribution of Seymour and the Azusa Street Revival cannot be overestimated. A new diaspora of Spirit-filled believers was launched from Azusa Street to great works of evangelism and missions across America and around the world. Seymour’s emphases on spiritual empowerment, humility, holiness, and unity remain examples for Pentecostals today.

**Q:** How did Seymour’s attitude enable him to be equipped for ministry?

**A:** Despite limitations imposed by racial discrimination, Seymour was a humble and hungry learner and mastered Parham’s teachings enough that he was able to minister.

**Q:** Describe the actions that were a precursor to the outpouring that became the Azusa Street Revival.

**A:** Seeking, fasting, prayer (corporate prayer as well as laying on of hands and praying for each other to be infilled with the Holy Spirit), studying the Word regularly together, and praising the Lord for what He had done.

**Q:** List several of the lessons we can learn from the Azusa Street Revival.

**A:** The revival used what was available. It was intense and long-lasting, inclusive and intercultural, expansive, well-organized, infectious, and focused on God rather than on a charismatic leader.

**Q:** Read 1 Corinthians 1:26–31. How does this apply to many of the people God used to bring about the twentieth century Pentecostal revival? What encouragement does it hold for you?

**A:** Parham was often physically weak. Seymour was poor, blind in one eye, and discriminated against for his race. Lucy Farrow was a poor Black woman and former slave. None were highly esteemed in the world’s eyes, yet God used them.

**Q:** Charles Parham is sometimes called the “Father of Modern-day Pentecostalism.” Give at least two arguments to support or refute this honor.

**A:** Pro: He was the first to articulate the concept of baptism in the Holy Spirit with the initial physical evidence of speaking in tongues; he was the first to teach it; under his teaching, the first instances of speaking in tongues took place, which were understood as being linked to baptism in the Holy Spirit; he was the first to spread this new truth, even attempting a modicum of organization. Con: The Pentecostal Movement and Pentecostalism were a work of God and not of any person; others had spoken in tongues previously. William Seymour and the Azusa Street Revival were more influential in spreading Pentecost.

**Q:** “The Lord has assigned to each his task” (1 Corinthians 3:5). Each person has a part to play in God’s work. It is important to remember that we each build upon the work of others and, if we do our part well, others will build upon ours. Upon whose work did Parham and Seymour build?

**A:** Parham built on the works of Dowie, Simpson, and Sandford; Seymour built on the works of all of those plus Parham, Lucy Farrow, Edward Lee, the Asberrys, and others—even Julia Hutchinson, for she was responsible for inviting Seymour to Los Angeles.

**Q:** Consider: upon whose work are you building?

**A:** Answers will vary. Pentecostal Mission 3 CHAPTER

## 3

### The Pentecostal Movement

#### 3.1.1 — Describe how G. B. Cashwell spread the doctrine of the baptism of the Holy Spirit with the evidence of speaking in tongues to the East Coast and the South.

G. B. Cashwell (1862–1916) was a Holiness evangelist from North Carolina. He read reports about the amazing outpouring of the Holy Spirit at the Azusa Street Mission, and he longed to receive this baptism for himself. In November 1906, he borrowed money for a train ticket to Los Angeles. Although he was initially shocked by some of what he saw and heard, he was convinced that it was of God, and he wanted to experience it. However, he was bothered by his reluctance to have Black brothers and sisters lay hands on him in prayer. Retreating to his hotel room, Cashwell repented and “died to many things,” including his racial bigotry.

The next evening, Cashwell returned to Azusa Street as a humble man. He asked William Seymour and several African American brothers to lay their hands on him and pray for him to receive the baptism in the Spirit, which he soon did.

Cashwell spent five weeks learning from and seeking God with the Azusa Street faithful. These brothers and sisters then took up an offering to buy him a new suit and a train ticket home, and sent him to carry this new message of Pentecostal revival to North Carolina. He immediately invited leaders and members of the Holiness groups in the area to a series of meetings where he preached about this new understanding and experience of speaking in tongues. The meetings were widely attended, and the doctrine of tongues as the initial physical evidence of Spirit baptism was well received. Thousands of people received the baptism in the Holy Spirit and spoke in tongues.

Uniquely in the South, entire existing denominations quickly became Pentecostal due to the influence of and demonstration of power in Cashwell’s preaching. Among them were Cashwell’s own denomination, the Pentecostal Holiness Church (PHC), along with the Fire-Baptized Holiness Church, the Free Will Baptist Church, and the Church of God in Cleveland, Tennessee.

The outpouring of the Holy Spirit, accompanied by speaking in tongues, grew in fertile soil prepared by the Holiness movement, which taught believers to expect the supernatural—divine healing, miracles, and visitations of God.

Not everyone responded favorably, however. Sadly, some of the harshest responses came from those within the very groups that had been encouraging to the early Pentecostals, including fundamentalists, many Holiness groups, and even the Christian and Missionary Alliance (CMA).

A. The Christian and Missionary Alliance (CMA) . The Pentecostal revival spread like wildfire through the conventions, meetings, and schools of the CMA in New York and the North. While believing that “there is probably something of God in it somewhere,” founder A. B. Simpson could not accept tongues as the initial physical evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit. The official position became a matter of “do not seek it but do not forbid it.” This quickly quashed the spread of Pentecostalism within the CMA. Those who embraced Pentecostalism withdrew from the fellowship, including future Assemblies of God leaders Alice Reynolds Flower, Frank Boyd, Minnie Draper, William I. Evans, D. W. Kerr, Noel Perkin, W. W. Simpson, A. G. Ward, and J. W. Welch.

B. Holiness Organizations . Other Holiness organizations were even less accepting of the new Pentecostals. The largest of these, the Church of the Nazarene, became fiercely anti-Pentecostal. Their lead was soon followed by other Holiness groups, including the Free Methodist Church, the Wesleyan Methodist Church, and the Salvation Army .

C. Fundamentalist Groups . Perhaps some of the harshest judgments came from well-known fundamentalist writers, theologians, educators, and evangelists. H. A. Ironside called the practice of speaking in tongues “delusion and insanity.” R. A. Torrey denounced it as “emphatically not of God and founded by a sodomite.” G. Campbell Morgan called it “the last vomit of Satan” (Menzies 1971, 72–73).

D. The Broader Church World . Churches that had not been part of the Restorationist movement after the Second Great Awakening mocked and looked down upon the Pentecostals. They considered it just one more church aberration, an urban cult that would soon pass.

Believers who accepted the teaching that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of Holy Spirit baptism were no longer welcome in many of these churches. Therefore, the focus necessarily changed from trying to reform the church from within to creating something outside denominational boundaries— something fresh and new.

**Q:** G.B. Cashwell was unable to receive the fullness of the Holy Spirit before he repented of his bigotry. Search your own heart. Is any sin or wrong attitude keeping you from experiencing everything God has for you?

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** Why might organizations and people God is using reject or fail to recognize God’s working in others?

**A:** They may feel threatened as others start to turn to something new; they may be stuck in the past, when they were at the cutting edge of what God was doing; they may resent something of which they are not at the forefront, and so on.

**Q:** How would you respond to someone who claims to be used by God in a way that is new or foreign to you?

**A:** Answers will vary. 4 Describe the effectiveness of the methods used to spread the Pentecostal Movement. Mass meetings were held in the open air, or held in other unconventional places like warehouses and storefronts. This may have attracted people who would not have normally stepped foot in a church. Gospel bands would go where there was no Pentecostal witness and spend time evangelizing there. When they would leave, some team members would stay behind to disciple the new converts. Printed materials mailed nationwide spread the news of the outpourings of the Holy Spirit and publicized invitations to the meetings. These materials encouraged believers to pray for revival in their own areas, thus expanding the reach of the Movement. 5 Explain how Pentecostal gatherings were a little taste of heaven. Not only were both men and women involved side by side in ministry in the gatherings, but also these gatherings included people of many races and nations. Additionally, the young, old, rich, and poor experienced God ’ s presence. 6 How can you formulate a Pentecostal mindset in your life and ministry? Strive to live a holy life in action and thought, be open to the Holy Spirit ’ s leading and new ways of doing things, be fervent about God, and live a life of faith in all things. 7 Describe a situation in your life or ministry where you saw how the Holy Spirit empowered you for service . Answers will vary. 8 List verses that describe Jesus ’ ministry of healing. Matthew 4:24, 8:16, 10:8, 14:14, 14:35, 14:36, 19:2; Mark 1:34, 2:17, 3:10; Luke 4:38, 4:40, 5:31, 9:2; John 6:2, and others. 9 Have we lost that sense of urgency that our forebears had to the second coming of Christ? Why or why not? Answers will vary. The Call to Organize 4 CHAPTER

### Pentecostal Methods

#### 3.2.1 — List three ways in which Pentecostals took their message directly to the people.

Despite the inevitable mocking, persecution, and strong opposition from the community at large and the organized church, the Pentecostal Movement continued to grow and spread. While the blessing of God was the greatest factor for this growth, early Pentecostals also sought the leading of the Holy Spirit for creative ministry methods that would enable them to share their message with others.

Pentecostals took their message directly to the people . Rather than becoming discouraged when they were not allowed to share their message within established churches, Pentecostals sought avenues outside local churches for ministry.

Mass meetings and conventions

When they were barred from using church buildings and halls, they held open-air meetings, raised tents in fields, and rented storefronts, warehouses, or opera halls in which to hold their services.

Gospel bands

The early Pentecostals assembled small teams known as “ gospel bands .” Groups of five to ten believers would prayerfully select a new town or city without a Pentecostal witness. Upon arrival, they spent time in the community preaching and singing on street corners, praying with anyone who asked, and witnessing to anyone who would listen. These teams often bore the brunt of the persecution and violence suffered by Pentecostals. It was not uncommon for team members to be mocked, threatened, beaten, and driven from town. Still, they persisted, empowered by the Holy Spirit and a passion for souls.

Newsletters, papers, and magazines

Inspiring reports of fresh outpourings of the Holy Spirit spread to every corner of the country and around the globe through a host of periodicals mailed—largely free of charge—from many of the most prominent revivals. Some of the most influential included Charles Parham’s The Apostolic Faith , William Seymour’s The Apostolic Faith , William Durham’s The Pentecostal Testimony , Cashwell’s The Bridegroom’s Messenger , M. M. Pinson’s and E. N. Bell’s Word and Witness , and J. Roswell Flower’s The Christian Evangel . These printed materials publicized meetings and revivals. They also inspired many hungry believers to pray for revival in their own homes or communities. Additionally, they were an important means of connection, union, organization, teaching, and correction.

The Pentecostal Movement Met People’s Needs

When people’s lives are good, they may go to church out of a sense of habit or obligation or for fellowship and entertainment, but when people have problems, they need more from their church and from God. In Pentecostal services, people were encouraged to speak openly about what they needed from God and then joined together to ask God to meet those needs. Whether the needs were physical, financial, emotional, relational, or spiritual, they were encouraged that God could meet those needs. Services often included times of testimony to what God had already done in the lives of others, and these testimonies built the faith of those with similar needs.

Pentecostal Gatherings Were Egalitarian

As prophesied in Joel 2:28 and Acts 2:17, God poured out His Spirit on all people.

Women and Men

In the power of the Spirit, women spoke, prayed, and led as did men. Women were pastors, evangelists, faith healers, publishers, and missionaries. They taught at and ran Bible schools. They launched ministries, founded denominations, and were used by God in all areas of church life, alongside their brothers.

Black and White, Hispanic, and Recent Immigrants

Contrary to common practice in the church world and society at large, Pentecostalism had a distinctively diverse, multiracial, multiethnic following.Racially integrated ministries, churches, and ministry teams were surprisingly common in those earliest days. Pentecostalism bloomed under the leadership of African Americans, Hispanics, Swedes, Italians, and many other ethnically diverse communities. Several of these leaders became missionaries to the land of their birth, taking the Pentecostal message with them.

Young and Old

Although the Pentecostal Movement welcomed people of all ages, it was especially appealing to the young, who, in turn, gave the movement a vibrant, youthful, visionary flavor. J. Roswell Flower was just twenty-six years old when he was chosen as the second-highest leader of the new Assemblies of God. In the gospel bands that were such an effective part of the growth of the Pentecostal Movement, youths outnumbered adults six to one (Goss 1958, 69).

High and Low Station

Although their reputation was that most Pentecostals were uneducated and poor, the reality showed a true balance. The Azusa Street Revival drew wealthy White socialites as well as dirt-poor immigrants of various races and nationalities. Doctors and lawyers tarried around the same altars as migrant farm workers and factory workers. Likewise, some who preached were grade-school dropouts, while others had multiple degrees from prestigious schools. No matter what a person’s station in life, the Pentecostal Movement had a place of service for him or her.

**Q:** Describe the effectiveness of the methods used to spread the Pentecostal Movement.

**Q:** Explain how Pentecostal gatherings were a little taste of heaven.
