### The Pentecostal Mindset

#### 3.3.1 — Summarize what demonstrated the Pentecostals' openness to new things.

Perhaps the key ingredient in the success and growth of the early Pentecostal Movement—other than the Holy Spirit himself—was the Pentecostal people. Here are some important characteristics shared by early Pentecostals that help explain the success of the movement.

Awareness of Holiness

Baptism in the Spirit made Jesus intensely real to believers, leading them to strive to live holy lives of purity in action and thought. Pentecostals wanted to be as close to Jesus as they could and anything that gave even a hint of “worldliness” was rejected lest it distract them from the presence of God in their lives. As Frank Bartleman explained, “A true ‘Pentecost’ will produce a mighty conviction of sin, a turning to God. False manifestations produce only excitement and wonder” (Menzies 1971, 55).

Openness to the New

The Pentecostal Movement was characterized by spontaneity and freshness. They were comfortable with unstructured worship, wanting to maintain an environment that gave free rein to the moving of the Spirit. While they felt strongly about standards of holiness, they were still some of the first Christians to adopt the use of new technology for the gospel, such as radio and, later, television.

Fervency

The belief that Christ was coming soon, combined with the confidence that they carried the power of the Holy Spirit for ministry and service, led to a passion for evangelism and missions almost unrivaled since the first century Christians. This energetic effort to spread the gospel was not often shaken by opposition, hardship, poverty, reproach, physical suffering, or personal danger. Their earnestness and self-sacrifice were both rewarding for themselves and appealing to those who observed their passion.

Faith

Pentecostals lived lives of faith. They trusted God for everything: the big things, such as health, strength, guidance, and provision, and the small things. In the early years, most took no offerings and charged no money for their periodicals or even their schools, instead trusting God to provide what was needed. It was common to go to prayer before going to the doctor. Their faith was rewarded with many displays of divine healing and miraculous provision.

**Q:** How can you formulate a Pentecostal mindset in your life and ministry?

### The Pentecostal Message

#### 3.4.1 — Outline the four core tenets of the Pentecostal message.

Although a message of empowerment through the gifts of the Holy Spirit was the explosive new addition to Pentecostal preaching, they still maintained a balanced focus on the orthodox doctrines of the Christian faith, as well as maintaining the same emphases they had believed and preached as Holiness leaders. Anchored firmly in the authority of God’s Word and centered on Christ, these were the four core beliefs of the Pentecostal Movement right from the start:

Salvation

Pentecostals believed that salvation came only through faith in Christ’s atoning work on the cross and repentance from sin. This conviction led them to feel keenly about their responsibilities of evangelism and missions.

Baptism in the Holy Spirit

Pentecostals believed that, after salvation, Christ empowered believers through the baptism in the Holy Spirit, enabling them to live lives of holiness and entrusting them with the gifts of the Spirit for ministry. The renewal of these gifts was seen as a “ latter rain ” of the Spirit for the empowerment to preach the gospel to the whole world that must precede the coming of the Lord (Matthew 24:14). Just as their conviction regarding salvation led them to feel the responsibility of evangelism, this belief in a “last days outpouring” led them to feel the extreme urgency of evangelism.

Divine Healing

Pentecostals believed that Jesus provided not only for salvation on the cross but also for healing of the body and mind (Isaiah 53:4–5). The conviction that God was not only saving people but meeting their practical needs led them to seek out those who were in need. This proved to be one of the most effective ways of drawing people to hear the gospel and encounter God.

Second Coming

Pentecostals believed that there would be a literal return of Jesus Christ to the earth to judge the living and the dead and establish His kingdom. The very real sense that Jesus was coming soon added urgency to the task of evangelizing at home and overseas. It also imbued the Pentecostals’ work with a sense of importance and value and reminded them that their hope was not in this world but in a world to come.

The Pentecostal message, mindset, and methods were remarkably successful. As the movement grew, there were growing pains that needed to be addressed Disagreements over new teachings and practices brought new challenges. Farsighted, godly leaders within the Movement began to seek God for wisdom so that what God had begun would not only continue but would grow and be ready to meet the needs of coming generations.

**Q:** Describe a situation in your life or ministry where you saw how the Holy Spirit empowered you for service.

**Q:** List verses that describe Jesus’ ministry of healing.

**Q:** Have we lost that sense of urgency that our forebearers had to the second coming of Christ? Why or why not?

#### 3.4.2 — Explain how the tenet of the baptism in the Holy Spirit complements and goes beyond the Holiness tenet of sanctification.

Although a message of empowerment through the gifts of the Holy Spirit was the explosive new addition to Pentecostal preaching, they still maintained a balanced focus on the orthodox doctrines of the Christian faith, as well as maintaining the same emphases they had believed and preached as Holiness leaders. ## 4

### The Need to Organize

#### 4.1.1 — Summarize five problems caused by the independent nature of the Pentecostal Movement that made organizing vital.

After the rapid spread of the Pentecostal Movement that followed the Azusa Street Revival, many Pentecostals suddenly found themselves on their own. Shunned, ridiculed, or persecuted in the church world and society at large, Pentecostals had very few denominational affiliations or fellowships. Many wore this rejection as a badge of honor and evidence that their doctrine was true and their experiences real, as Jesus warned that His believers would be hated as He was (John 15:18–19). They were proud of their independence, as they viewed organizations as necessarily restrictive and authoritarian. They feared that denominations demanded allegiance and obedience that rightly belonged only to God, and they were most fearful of allowing bureaucracy and the rules of people to quench the Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:19). However, independence also brought perils.

Divisions and Potential for Abuse

The early outpourings of the Spirit had developed under the strong leadership of central figures, such as Parham or Seymour. However, the Pentecostal Movement continued to expand beyond the scope of one central leader. This was an important strength, but it could also be a weakness. In the absence of some sort of structure, it also left the Movement disconnected and in danger of forming into small, disjointed groups with little accountability.

Younger ministers were often drawn to older ministers who were more established and experienced. Most of these relationships were good and healthy. But sometimes it could lead to an early form of “celebrity pastors” with less experienced ministers copying the mannerisms and traits of popular preachers and forming small bands attached to particularly charismatic leaders. First Corinthians 1:10–13 warned of the dangers of such divisions based on personalities. Because independent churches and preachers had few avenues for obtaining credentials, the potential for fraud was great. Almost anyone who showed up at a meeting claiming to be a Pentecostal preacher with stories of past meetings and miracles was likely to be invited to speak and, if they did well, to be sent off with an offering. Lacking accountability, sometimes unscrupulous leaders took advantage of vulnerable Christians.

Even the successful local and regional attempts at organization were adding to the confusion and division. At one time, there were three different regional associations of Pentecostals named “Apostolic Faith.” When this became too confusing, one of these changed its name to “Church of God,” unaware of another organization already existing with that name in Cleveland, Tennessee. When that became an issue, they changed their name to “Church of God in Christ,” initially unaware that they were the third association to use that name. It was becoming increasingly difficult to keep up with all of the names, associations, name changes, and distinctions between various groups.

Strange Practices

Because Pentecostals believed that God was restoring miraculous gifts to the church, they were often prone to seek out signs and wonders, even sometimes to the point of fanaticism. One example involved preachers who became known as “snake-handlers.” When the story began to circulate about a preacher who had picked up a rattlesnake that some boys had thrown into his tent meeting and then threw it outside the tent with no fear or danger, some believers saw this as a fulfillment of Jesus’ words in Mark 16:18. They began to teach that Spirit-filled people should intentionally handle venomous serpents or drink poison to prove that the presence and power of God was upon them. Some Pentecostal leaders promoted this practice of handling snakes, and some strongly preached against it, causing confusion among many.

Ineffectiveness of Solitary Missions Endeavors

As noted earlier, Pentecostals believed that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit was both the sign of the end times and the empowerment to win the world to Christ before the end. Therefore, missionary work was a primary focus. However, it was difficult for missionaries to go to the field without a network of support.

The many periodicals published by the Movement often acted as clearinghouses to connect missionaries and donors. The papers would print reports of successes and needs, and readers frequently would send money for the missionaries in care of the periodicals. This often worked well, but it too was subject to abuse and misdirection. Donors worried that there was no way to verify which missionaries and ministries were worthy of donations and which were not. With no organization vetting missionaries, how could a donor know if they remained biblically, theologically, and morally sound? How could they avoid contributing to missions endeavors flush with cash at the expense of deserving missionaries with legitimate and dire needs? Although Pentecostals resisted an organization that would restrict the Spirit’s direction of missionaries, they did want some system of checks and balances on the integrity and effectiveness of missionaries so they could give without hesitation.

Lack of Legal Standing

Because they were not part of a recognized denomination, missionaries often encountered difficulties in purchasing land overseas or securing loans for projects. Meanwhile, on the home front, evangelists or Christian workers who traveled for the ministry were unable to secure valuable clergy rates on trains when they could not point to a recognized organization to demonstrate that they really were legitimate church workers.

Heterodoxy

Baptism in the Holy Spirit almost invariably awakened a burning desire to spread the good news . Many Pentecostals gave up their old lives, leaving their farms and shops to preach, teach, or go to the mission field. Many kept moving because their knowledge was so limited; they would preach all of their sermons or expound on every subject they knew until they needed to find a new audience. Still others were stumped as to how to handle tough questions or challenges to their message. Given the lack of training of so many, it was fairly common for errors to creep into the messages. Unfortunately, no one was checking up on them or had authority to correct error or punish moral failure. This led to the danger of eager, well-meaning Christians who were ignorant of orthodoxy (accepted and true doctrine) leading others astray by the heterodoxy, or error, that they preached.

Problems stemming from the lack of an organized denomination abounded. Still, convincing most leaders of the wisdom of organizing would be a challenge. A popular concern was that any sort of structure would put so much “harness” on the Pentecostal “horse” that it would no longer be able to pull (Menzies 1971, 94). Howard Goss responded to this concern: “From the Book of Acts, as well as from our own experiences, I was led to see that even Spirit-filled people needed some restraint. Just as a good horse still needs a harness to produce worthwhile results, the movement needed a legal form of written cooperative fellowship” (Goss 1977, 272).

**Q:** How did the mannerisms of others influence young preachers?

**A:** Followers would copy certain mannerisms, ways of saying something, or traits of a leader. However, this could lead to followers, especially younger people, idolizing a leader.

**Q:** What abuses or damage have you seen as a result of unaccountable leaders? What did you learn from the incident(s)?

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** How should excesses, peculiarity, and fleshly manifestations be addressed?

**A:** They should be handled in love (1 Corinthians 13).

**Q:** List ways local churches can maintain financial support for missions.

**A:** Encouraging giving to missions, raising a missions budget, and highlighting the work of supported missionaries.

**Q:** In what ways can doctrinal accountability be addressed in your church?

**A:** Instruction and teaching can be provided, and believers should be encouraged to use discernment and correction through the use of Scripture.

### Key Architects

#### 4.2.1 — Identify three key architects of the organizational meeting in Hot Springs, Arkansas, and summarize the unique role of each.

Wise leaders recognized the danger posed by the lack of organization and prayerfully considered ways to correct the situation. They sought to handle these things wisely because of the suspicions of many who had been hurt when rejected by their denominations. Many more believed that organization threatened the Spirit’s moving. The topic of organization needed to be handled with extreme care. Three leaders made the initial call for a gathering in Hot Springs, Arkansas in April 1914 to discuss the matter.

Howard A. Goss

Howard A. Goss (1883-1964) was one of the early initiators and promoters of the 1914 organizational meeting that would lead to the birth of the Assemblies of God. As Goss described it:

As there was no apparent way to gather up the reins of the different cliques which each seemed in danger of galloping off in its own direction, Brother Bell and I worked privately together on some kind of solution. We later found that Brother Opperman saw this need too, as did a few other leaders. We realized that great care was needed at this stage, as we had been strictly taught against any form of organization. Irresponsible brethren, if they heard too much, might immediately use the opportunity to poison the saints against us before we could explain, and call us “compromisers!”—a serious charge in those days. (Goss 1958, 174–175)

Goss, who was pastoring in Hot Springs, Arkansas, volunteered to host the planned organizational meeting. He rented an abandoned theater building, the Grand Opera House, for six months for the use of his church and a training school and offered it for the coming meeting. Leaving his church in the care of another Pentecostal leader, D. C. O. Opperman, Goss traveled to raise awareness and support for the Hot Springs meeting.

D. C. O. Opperman

D. C. O. (Daniel Charles Owen) Opperman (1872–1926) was largely responsible for on-the-ground preparations for the upcoming Hot Springs gathering. Not only did he oversee the physical arrangements, but he also held a short-term worker training school that made the biblical case for organization and order and concluded just before the historic gathering. Opperman had been the principal of schools in Zion City, Illinois, before embracing the Pentecostal Movement. He had then overseen four- to five-week training schools across the country. This experience was extremely valuable as the course of the new fellowship was being set.

E. N. Bell

E. N. (Eudorus Neander) Bell (1866–1923) published the bold call to organize in his paper, Word and Witness (December 20, 1913). Bell wrote and published the invitation, and Goss signed his name in support, as did other influential leaders: D. C. O. Opperman (Houston), M. M. Pinson (Phoenix), and A. P. Collins (Fort Worth). Bell continued to publicize the call in two additional issues of the Word and Witness , skillfully articulating the need and purpose to a national audience. Bell was to play a vital role in the formation and establishment of the Assemblies of God.

### The Call

#### 4.3.1 — Summarize who was and who was not invited to attend the Hot Springs gathering.

Following is the text of the call to organization Bell published in the Word and Witness :

We desire at this time to make this preliminary announcement of this general meeting so that workers far and near, at home and abroad, may sidetrack everything else and be present. Laymen as well as preachers are invited. Especially do we urge all elders, pastors, ministers, evangelists and missionaries to be present. This call is to all the churches of God in Christ, to all Pentecostal or Apostolic Faith Assemblies who desire with united purpose to co-operate in love and peace to push the interests of the kingdom of God everywhere. This is, however, only for saints who believe in the baptism with the Holy Ghost with the signs following, Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6; Mark 16:16–18; 1 Cor. 12:8–11. Neither is this meeting for any captious, contrary, divisive or contentious person. But we leave for the body itself to take up any subjects it desires more than what is herein afterwards mentioned.

Bell articulated five purposes for organizing:

Unity —"We come together that we may set a better understanding of what God would have us teach, so that we may do away with so many divisions, both in doctrines and in the various names under which our Pentecostal people are working and incorporating. Let us come together as in Acts 15, to study the Word, and pray with and for each other with unity our chief aim."

Conservation —"Again we come together that we know how to conserve the work, that we may all build up and not tear down, both in home and foreign lands."

Consider conservation in the sense of a forest conservation agent. Bell meant that it was necessary to be good stewards of God’s work and not allow the Pentecostal Movement to devolve into the error, fanaticism, excess, out-of-control leadership, and disunity that had plagued previous groups that had experienced outpourings of the Holy Spirit.

Missions Oversight —"We come together for another reason, that we may get a better understanding of the needs of each foreign field, and may know how to place our money in such a way that one mission or missionary shall not suffer, while another not any more worthy, lives in luxuries. Also that we may discourage wasting money on those who are running here and there accomplishing nothing, and may concentrate our support on those who mean business for our King."

Legal Standing —“Many of the saints have felt the need of chartering the churches of God in Christ, putting them on a legal basis, and thus obeying the laws of the land, ' as God says. See Romans 13. We confess we have been 'slothful in business' on this point, and because of this many assemblies have already chartered under different names as a local work, in both home and foreign lands. Why not charter under one Bible name—2 Thessalonians 2:14—thus eliminating another phase of division in Pentecostal work? For this purpose also let us come together."

Training —"We may also have a proposition, to lay before the body, for a general Bible Training School with a literary department for our people" ( Word and Witness 1913 ) . E xplain why no business was conducted for the first few days of the Hot Springs meeting.

**Q:** How is the Baptism in the Spirit with speaking in tongues viewed in your church?

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** On the Day of Pentecost, the Spirit was given and received. What signs accompanied this outpouring? What is the significance of these signs?

**A:** The sound of wind and fire (compare Exodus 19:16; 1 Kings 19:11; Ezekiel 1:4, 37:5–14; Isaiah 29:6, 66:15; Luke 3:15–17) and speaking in tongues (Acts 2:17–21; Joel 2:28–32). They were signs that the Lord was with them and He was working.

### Hot Springs Gathering: The Assemblies of God Is Born

#### 4.4.1 — Explain why no business was conducted for the first few days of the Hot Springs meeting.

The Convention

The convention was scheduled for April 2–12, 1914, in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Organizers were pleasantly surprised at the large turnout. Representing twenty states and several foreign countries, more than three hundred people attended, including 128 ministers and missionaries. Especially prevalent were adherents of the Churches of God in Christ; people from the strong missions in the Chicago area; and former members of the Christian and Missionary Alliance. Men and women, young and old, attended.

Because feelings were so strong both for and against organizing, it was essential to take things slowly and carefully. At first, people kept their feelings to themselves but sized each other up. No one was sure who was for and who was against organization, and no one wanted to go first and be judged a “compromiser.”

Therefore, no business was conducted for the first three days, but only prayer, praise, worship, preaching, and fellowship to encourage unity in the Spirit. Bell was the acting chairman, but Mack Pinson preached the opening service, explaining the reason for their meeting, and basing his message on Acts 15, which contained a biblical example of an early church gathering to discuss difficult topics.

Monday, April 6, was the first day of business. The goal of the meetings was clear: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40 KJV). The desire to achieve “Bible order” was the overarching guideline for those in attendance.

Bell, who had been elected chairman, assigned a committee consisting of one representative of each state to study the issues and come up with resolutions and recommendations for incorporation.

The Concerns

Fearing that the official committee would return recommendations for a rigid, authoritarian organization that they believed would quench the Spirit and destroy the autonomy of local churches, a committee opposed to strong central organization met in secret to draft their own resolutions and proposals. This group of eight was led by T. K. Leonard of Findlay, Ohio, and included J. Roswell Flower, both of whom would soon play pivotal roles in the new fellowship.

When word of this informal committee leaked, those on the official committee feared major conflict and disagreement. They were concerned that the covert group intended to oppose and block organization. Therefore, they quietly invited representatives of the group to meet with them, discuss their concerns, and better explain their own intentions.

However, when T. K. Leonard read aloud the resolutions of the smaller group, the tension in the room was replaced with amazement and joy. This “dissenting” group’s proposal—safeguarding local church sovereignty and calling for a cooperative association of like-minded churches—matched their intentions and desires nearly perfectly. In fact, with only a little discussion, they submitted the small group’s document to the entire assembly as endorsed by both groups.

The Consensus

When this resolution was read aloud to the general assembly, it was enthusiastically and unanimously passed. Then Leonard’s group wrote a second proposal, which was also unanimously approved. Whereas the first had carefully protected local church sovereignty, the second proactively established the framework for organization based on voluntary cooperation. These first and second resolutions from Leonard’s small group became the basis of the Preamble (first resolution) and Resolution on Constitution (second resolution) for the Assemblies of God that would be the framework for cooperation and governance until the Constitution itself was adopted in 1927. The resolution established the name “Assemblies of God.” Assembly of God was a common term meaning “church” used by Evangelical congregations in the early 1900s (Menzies 1971, 103).

The group deliberately avoided organizing a denomination but chose instead to have an annual council for conducting business and making decisions. They also avoided formalizing a doctrinal statement, allowing members to come to their own conclusions on some of the most divisive issues of the day.

Preamble and Resolution of Constitution

WHEREAS, God, our Heavenly Father, sent His only begotten Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, into the world, Who purchased and redeemed fallen man with His own Precious blood, and called out of the world and saved a people, of whom He built and established His Church (Assembly of God. Matt. 16:18), upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the Head and Chief Corner-stone (Eph. 2:20), and organized and baptized it with the Holy Spirit, with its government upon His shoulders (Isaiah 9:6–7), and said, “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt. 16:18); and

WHEREAS, He gave the Holy Inspired Scriptures, (Both old and new covenants, Heb. 8:6–13) as the all-sufficient rule for faith and practice, (2 Tim. 3:16), as follows: ‘All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works,’ we therefore shall not add to nor take from it (Rev. 22:18); and

WHEREAS, He commanded that there should be no schism (division, sectarianism) in His Body, the GENERAL ASSEMBLY (Church) of the first born, which are written in heaven, Heb. 12:23; and

WHEREAS, We recognize ourselves as members of said GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF GOD, (which is God’s organism), and do not believe in identifying ourselves as, or establishing ourselves into, a sect, that is a human organization that legislates or forms laws and articles of faith and has jurisdiction over its members and creates unscriptural lines of fellowship and disfellowship and which separates itself from other members of the General Assembly (Church) of the first born, which is contrary to Christ’s prayer in St. John 17, and Paul’s teaching in Eph. 4:1–16, which we so heartily endorse:

THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, FIRST, That we recognize ourselves as a GENERAL COUNCIL of Pentecostal (Spirit Baptized) saints from local Churches of God in Christ, Assemblies of God, and various Apostolic Faith Missions and Churches, and Full Gospel Pentecostal Missions, and Assemblies of like faith in the United States of America, Canada, and Foreign Lands, whose purpose is neither to legislate laws of government, nor usurp authority over said various Assemblies of God, nor deprive them of their Scriptural and local rights and privileges, but to recognize Scriptural methods and order for worship, unity, fellowship, work and business for God, and to disapprove of all unscriptural methods, doctrines and conduct, and approve of all Scriptural truth and conduct, endeavoring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bonds of peace, until we all come into the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and to walk accordingly, as recorded in Eph. 4:17–32, and to consider the five purposes announced in the Convention Call in the February, 1914, issue of ‘WORD AND WITNESS;’

RESOLVED, SECOND, That we recognize all the above said Assemblies of various names, and when speaking of them refer to them by the general Scriptural name ‘Assemblies of God;’ and recommend that they all recognize themselves by the same name, that is, ‘Assembly of God’ and adopt it as soon as practicable for the purpose of being more Scriptural and also legal in transacting business, owning property, and executing missionary work in home and foreign lands, and for general convenience, unity and fellowship.” (Consortium of Pentecostal Archives 1914, 4–5)

The foundational resolution of the Assemblies of God clarified how to use the name correctly. The organization’s official name was “The Assemblies of God.” Each individual church was to be called an “Assembly of God,” as in “First Assembly of God.” Furthermore, the group recognized themselves as a “General Council.”

Additionally, the group decided to do the following:

Incorporate the General Council of the Assemblies of God. They elected a twelve-member Executive Presbytery to conduct business between Council meetings: distribute missionary money, oversee publications, tend to legal matters, and plan annual conferences. E. N. Bell was elected chairman; J. Roswell Flower was elected secretary-treasurer. T. K. Leonard, another executive presbyter, offered his modest printing plant and school in Findlay, Ohio (already presciently named “The Assembly of God”), as a headquarters for the fledgling organization.

Refrain from making an issue of whether Christians should eat meats.

Recognize and encourage a weekly day of prayer.

Recommend Bible and literary schools—two existent schools were recognized, the Nashoba Holiness School in Nashoba, Mississippi, and T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio.

Recognize Bell’s Word and Witness and Flower’s Christian Evangel as official publications of the Assemblies of God (these later merged to become the Pentecostal Evangel , which saw continuous publication until 2014).

Authorize the formation of district councils [sometimes now referred to as "ministry networks"] in harmony with the principles and purposes of the General Council.

Recognize the ministries of elder, evangelist, minister, exhorter, and deacon, as well as the ministries of women.

Discourage divorce and remarriage (Gohr 2014).

The Assemblies of God had been established as a voluntary cooperative of sovereign churches. The leaders selected were given authority to call and plan General Councils, meetings in which the members would come together to make decisions, set the agenda, and confer about doctrine and practice. It would be just seven months before it was determined that the next General Council needed to be held.

**Q:** List ways in which Acts 15 serves as a model for settling disputes between believers.

**A:** a. Provide opportunity to voice concerns b. Appoint trusted, mature believers to facilitate discussion c. Use the Bible as a guide d. Come to a consensus

**Q:** Describe the Pentecostals’ major concern about a rigid church structure.

**A:** Congregations did not want to quench the Spirit or give up their autonomy.

**Q:** Summarize the contributions made by T. K. Leonard to the founding of the Assemblies of God.

**A:** Leonard led the secret small group that wrote the preamble and resolution of the Constitution; he was influential in choosing the name; he offered his facilities to the new fellowship as its headquarters. UNIT 2
