Preamble and Resolution of Constitution

WHEREAS, God, our Heavenly Father, sent His only begotten Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, into the world, Who purchased and redeemed fallen man with His own Precious blood, and called out of the world and saved a people, of whom He built and established His Church (Assembly of God. Matt. 16:18), upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the Head and Chief Corner-stone (Eph. 2:20), and organized and baptized it with the Holy Spirit, with its government upon His shoulders (Isaiah 9:6–7), and said, “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt. 16:18); and

WHEREAS, He gave the Holy Inspired Scriptures, (Both old and new covenants, Heb. 8:6–13) as the all-sufficient rule for faith and practice, (2 Tim. 3:16), as follows: ‘All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works,’ we therefore shall not add to nor take from it (Rev. 22:18); and

WHEREAS, He commanded that there should be no schism (division, sectarianism) in His Body, the GENERAL ASSEMBLY (Church) of the first born, which are written in heaven, Heb. 12:23; and

WHEREAS, We recognize ourselves as members of said GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF GOD, (which is God’s organism), and do not believe in identifying ourselves as, or establishing ourselves into, a sect, that is a human organization that legislates or forms laws and articles of faith and has jurisdiction over its members and creates unscriptural lines of fellowship and disfellowship and which separates itself from other members of the General Assembly (Church) of the first born, which is contrary to Christ’s prayer in St. John 17, and Paul’s teaching in Eph. 4:1–16, which we so heartily endorse:

THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, FIRST, That we recognize ourselves as a GENERAL COUNCIL of Pentecostal (Spirit Baptized) saints from local Churches of God in Christ, Assemblies of God, and various Apostolic Faith Missions and Churches, and Full Gospel Pentecostal Missions, and Assemblies of like faith in the United States of America, Canada, and Foreign Lands, whose purpose is neither to legislate laws of government, nor usurp authority over said various Assemblies of God, nor deprive them of their Scriptural and local rights and privileges, but to recognize Scriptural methods and order for worship, unity, fellowship, work and business for God, and to disapprove of all unscriptural methods, doctrines and conduct, and approve of all Scriptural truth and conduct, endeavoring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bonds of peace, until we all come into the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and to walk accordingly, as recorded in Eph. 4:17–32, and to consider the five purposes announced in the Convention Call in the February, 1914, issue of ‘WORD AND WITNESS;’

RESOLVED, SECOND, That we recognize all the above said Assemblies of various names, and when speaking of them refer to them by the general Scriptural name ‘Assemblies of God;’ and recommend that they all recognize themselves by the same name, that is, ‘Assembly of God’ and adopt it as soon as practicable for the purpose of being more Scriptural and also legal in transacting business, owning property, and executing missionary work in home and foreign lands, and for general convenience, unity and fellowship.” (Consortium of Pentecostal Archives 1914, 4–5)

The foundational resolution of the Assemblies of God clarified how to use the name correctly. The organization’s official name was “The Assemblies of God.” Each individual church was to be called an “Assembly of God,” as in “First Assembly of God.” Furthermore, the group recognized themselves as a “General Council.”

Additionally, the group decided to do the following:

Incorporate the General Council of the Assemblies of God. They elected a twelve-member Executive Presbytery to conduct business between Council meetings: distribute missionary money, oversee publications, tend to legal matters, and plan annual conferences. E. N. Bell was elected chairman; J. Roswell Flower was elected secretary-treasurer. T. K. Leonard, another executive presbyter, offered his modest printing plant and school in Findlay, Ohio (already presciently named “The Assembly of God”), as a headquarters for the fledgling organization.

Refrain from making an issue of whether Christians should eat meats.

Recognize and encourage a weekly day of prayer.

Recommend Bible and literary schools—two existent schools were recognized, the Nashoba Holiness School in Nashoba, Mississippi, and T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio.

Recognize Bell’s Word and Witness and Flower’s Christian Evangel as official publications of the Assemblies of God (these later merged to become the Pentecostal Evangel , which saw continuous publication until 2014).

Authorize the formation of district councils [sometimes now referred to as "ministry networks"] in harmony with the principles and purposes of the General Council.

Recognize the ministries of elder, evangelist, minister, exhorter, and deacon, as well as the ministries of women.

Discourage divorce and remarriage (Gohr 2014).

The Assemblies of God had been established as a voluntary cooperative of sovereign churches. The leaders selected were given authority to call and plan General Councils, meetings in which the members would come together to make decisions, set the agenda, and confer about doctrine and practice. It would be just seven months before it was determined that the next General Council needed to be held.

**Q:** List ways in which Acts 15 serves as a model for settling disputes between believers.

**A:** a. Provide opportunity to voice concerns b. Appoint trusted, mature believers to facilitate discussion c. Use the Bible as a guide d. Come to a consensus

**Q:** Describe the Pentecostals’ major concern about a rigid church structure.

**A:** Congregations did not want to quench the Spirit or give up their autonomy.

**Q:** Summarize the contributions made by T. K. Leonard to the founding of the Assemblies of God.

**A:** Leonard led the secret small group that wrote the preamble and resolution of the Constitution; he was influential in choosing the name; he offered his facilities to the new fellowship as its headquarters. UNIT 2

## 5

### Four Core Beliefs

#### 5.1.1 — List the four core doctrines of the Assemblies of God and one Bible verse supporting each doctrine.

Baptism in the Holy Spirit as evidenced by speaking in tongues was what set Pentecostals apart from other Christians in the Holiness and Reformist traditions. When the call to organize the Assemblies of God was published in 1914, this was the only doctrinal test set forth to distinguish who was and who was not welcome to participate. Still, the early Pentecostals were careful not to focus on baptism in the Holy Spirit to the exclusion of other key doctrines and at the expense of balance. Drawing from the creed of A. B. Simpson’s Christian and Missionary Alliance (CMA), Pentecostals generally focused on four roles of Jesus Christ: Christ as Savior, Christ as baptizer in the Holy Spirit (the CMA had described this role as “Christ as Sanctifier”), Christ as the divine healer, and Christ as soon-coming King. Before long, these would be crystalized as the four core doctrines of the Assemblies of God :

Salvation (Luke 24:47; John 3:3; Romans 10:13–15; Ephesians 2:8; Titus 2:11, 3:5–7),

Baptism in the Holy Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:4,8; 1 Corinthians 12:1–31; Acts 8:12–17, 10:44–46, 11:14–16, 15:7–9),

Divine healing (Isaiah 53:4–5; Matthew 8:16–17; James 5:14–16), and

The second coming of Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Romans 8:23; Titus 2:13; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52).

These four doctrines united Assemblies of God preachers, believers, and churches. But the seeds of discord would soon grow, even in some of these key areas.

### Sanctification: A Finished Work

#### 5.2.1 — Contrast the Assemblies of God's views of the timing of sanctification and what it accomplished with the Wesleyan view of sanctification as the second blessing.

The teaching of the Holiness Movement brought an understanding that there was more for the believer after salvation. But how they understood that was varied.

Some held to the Wesleyan view of sanctification: that at the initial moment of salvation, the believer was “justified,” and his guilt of sin was removed. However, the heart remained full of sin, and there was a “second work” of grace that freed him from the power of sin. They understood this second work to be the baptism in the Holy Spirit. Because of this, many Holiness believers were not open to the Pentecostal revival, as they considered themselves to have already been baptized in the Spirit. On the other hand, those in the Keswick wing, as well as adherents of the Christian and Missionary Alliance, were more open to the Pentecostal revival. They believed that baptism in the Holy Spirit was an experience separate from sanctification, the purpose of which was to empower believers for ministry. They believed in a three-step process of being saved, sanctified, and filled with the Spirit.

At a Pentecostal conference in Chicago in 1910, a third way of understanding sanctification was brought to the forefront in a sermon by William H. Durham (1873-1912). Durham received the baptism in the Holy Spirit at Azusa Street in 1906 and soon found the North Avenue Mission he pastored in Chicago rivaling the influence of the Los Angeles church in spreading the Pentecostal message and experience.

In his conference sermon, Durham preached that the idea that it takes two separate works of God to fully provide salvation – one to save ( justification ) and one to cleanse (sanctification) was not biblical. He taught that God dealt with all the nature of sin at conversion. He referred to this teaching as “the finished work of Calvary” – that after salvation, a man did not need a second work of salvation for sanctification but only to receive and walk in the Spirit, holding fast to faith and continually growing in Christ. In this view, holiness came through growth and maturity in faith rather than an instantaneous work of God.

While this made sense for Pentecostals from a Keswick or CMA background to accept, those with a Wesleyan Holiness background, including Charles Parham and William Seymour, felt that this compromised the importance of holiness. The growing controversy caused quite a rift, and both sides were unnecessarily harsh and condemning of their opponents, causing the first doctrinal split in the young Pentecostal Movement.

When the founders of the Assemblies of God met to organize in Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914, most of those gathered agreed with Durham’s “finished work” doctrine of sanctification. However, they did not make the matter a binding issue of faith, and all were welcome and accepted. Even so, the title of Mack Pinson’s sermon that opened the convention, “The Finished Work of Christ,” effectively set the doctrinal course for the Assemblies of God. This theory set the Assemblies of God apart from some other Pentecostal groups, especially in southern fellowships such as The Church of God in Cleveland, Tennessee, the Pentecostal Holiness Church, and the Church of God in Christ, which held fast to the second work of sanctification teaching.

**Q:** Explain the different understandings of holiness among various groups.

**A:** Some saw holiness as a second act of grace following salvation and equated this with the baptism in the Holy Spirit. Others believed baptism in the Spirit was a separate experience following salvation that empowered believers for ministry.

**Q:** Describe your experience of being baptized in the Holy Spirit. How has this impacted your life and spiritual formation?

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** Define holiness.

**A:** Holiness means to be set apart, pure, clean, sanctified.

**Q:** Why is holiness important to one’s profession of faith?

**A:** To be holy is to reflect God and Christ.

### God: The Trinity

#### 5.3.1 — Explain four problems with Oneness theology that turned the tide in favor of traditional views of the Trinity.

The first doctrinal issue seemed somewhat obscure, with everyday believers remaining rather unclear on the difference between the two views of sanctification or how it impacted their daily walk with Christ. The Jesus Only dispute, the “ New Issue ,” as it came to be known, was different. It threatened to rip the Fellowship apart and align it with historically heretical teaching.

Even while the Assemblies of God was organizing in Hot Springs, Arkansas, an old heresy masquerading as a new revelation was surfacing in California. At first glance, it seemed harmless enough. Although in the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20) Jesus instructed His followers to baptize new disciples “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” Acts 2:38 records the apostles urging the crowd: “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ.” Therefore, some ministers baptized converts according to the Matthew 28:19 formula, while others preferred using that in Acts 2:38. At an international Pentecostal camp meeting near Los Angeles in 1913, one man woke up the camp early one morning claiming to have had a revelation from God about the power in the name of Jesus and the importance of baptizing in the name of Jesus only which, according to Acts 2:38 would be followed by the promise of God’s blessing: “You will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

Following the formational meeting of the Assemblies of God, two prominent ministers in California, Frank Ewart, and Glenn Cook, were rebaptized in the name of Jesus only. They committed themselves to promulgating this new revelation by every means possible believing that this was the way the apostles did it. Several factors contributed to the rapid spread of this “Apostolic Pentecostalism.”

It was touted as a new revelation. In those early days of the revival, Pentecostals yearned for and highly valued new revelations from God, so this was extremely appealing to many.

It was viewed as a further restoration of apostolic faith. The Holiness Movement had been a restorationist reform aimed at returning to the practices of the apostles at the birth of the church. Therefore, many were open to what they believed was a furthering of this purpose.

Pentecostals already gave a central position to Jesus. Their core beliefs as built upon those of the CMA focused on Jesus as Savior, baptizer, healer, and coming King.

Greater blessings were promised to those who followed the pattern of baptism in Jesus’ name.

For these reasons, many people in the Assemblies of God eagerly embraced the new teaching. As the teaching spread to the Midwest in the spring of 1915, editors E. N. Bell and J. R. Flower published articles in the denominational publications standing against it. Therefore, the Fellowship was stunned when it was learned that Bell was rebaptized in Jesus’ name at a July camp meeting in Tennessee. Many followed Bell, one of the most beloved and influential leaders, in rebaptism in Jesus’ name. Soon rumors swirled that all of the AG leadership had followed suit, and the young church was thrown into confusion and turmoil.

Although many, like Bell, who embraced the rebaptism formula, considered it to be just an effort to follow the leading of the New Testament apostles, it soon developed into an entire doctrine that the Christ of the New Testament was Jehovah of the Old Testament. The terms “Father, Son, and Holy Ghost” were all titles of the same person – Jesus. Frank Ewart began teaching that the apostles were baptized “in the name of Jesus” because Jesus was the name of the “Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.”

AG Secretary Flower was one of those who recognized this teaching as a dangerous denial of orthodox trinitarian teachings about God and stood firmly against it. He called for the third General Council to be convened in October to deal with the New Issue. Bypassing Chairman A. P. Collins, who seemed eager to avoid conflict, and Assistant Chairman D. C. O. Opperman, who favored the Oneness position— neither of whom were in attendance when the council convened—Flower and newly elected chairman J. W. Welch presided over the great debate. Both sides were allowed to voice their arguments fully, but because the founding of the Assemblies of God had provided no mechanism whereby doctrinal disputes could be settled with final authority, the issue was not fully resolved at the 1915 Council. Instead, a resolution was passed that called for neutrality, liberality, and respect for the rights of conscience of all (Burgess et al. 1988, 645). The resolution highlighted four points on which the new theology differed from biblical teaching and articulated “careful safeguards for distinguishing properly the persons within the Trinity” (Menzies 1971, 116).

In spite of these efforts, the conflict intensified. Oneness advocates became more aggressive in pressuring others, some even teaching that those who had not been baptized in the name of Jesus could not be saved. Despite the greater pressure, the tide started to turn in favor of the Trinitarians as the problems with Oneness theology became clearer. These problems included the following:

At its beginning, the Assemblies of God’s ministers had agreed not to preach any new revelations until they could be reviewed, debated, and established by the Fellowship. Oneness preachers refused to wait for the next General Council.

It made the name of Jesus a sort of talisman or magic word that brought power and blessings. They revered the Name so highly that they often refrained from writing it.

Oneness proponents had begun to teach that one must be baptized (or rebaptized) in the name of Jesus only and speak in tongues to be saved.

It relied on revelation over the Bible. When pressed regarding Scripture’s teaching on the Trinity, Oneness preachers would often dismiss it by saying that the new teaching could not be proven from the Bible but must be understood through revelation, a position many Pentecostals felt to be a dangerous precedent that challenged the final authority of Scripture.

When Chairman Welch called for the next General Council in 1916, he wrote, “This will be the most vital and important council which has ever been held since the first council at Hot Springs, Ark.” (Welch 1916, 1). A team that included Bell, who had publicly denounced non-Trinitarian views and distanced himself from the Oneness movement, was tasked in advance with drafting a statement of fundamental truths that the entire body might debate, shape, and approve to restore unity.

Executive Presbyter D. W. Kerr led the team assigned with drafting this doctrinal statement and was largely responsible for its content and wording. As an experienced and well-educated pastor in Ohio, he spent much time in prayer and study in the time before the 1916 Council.

Some of those in attendance at the 1916 General Council felt that they should not adopt such a statement of truths. They argued that the Preamble adopted in 1914 stated that “the holy inspired Scriptures are the all-sufficient rule for faith and doctrine” and that the Assemblies of God should not adopt a man-made creed.

Nevertheless, each doctrinal statement presented by Kerr’s committee was discussed and voted on separately. The most controversial – and, by far, the longest and most detailed – was the statement on the nature of Christ which strongly affirmed the historic Christian teaching on the Trinity. In the end, the document was approved and adopted. Those who could not agree with this statement of truths were removed from the membership roll. Of the 585 ministers affiliated with the Assemblies of God, 156 were lost, including founding fathers D. C. O. Opperman, and Howard Goss.

**Q:** Define the doctrine of the Trinity. Why is this important to our faith?

**A:** One God in three Persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Matthew 28:19; Galatians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 12:4–6; 2 Corinthians 13:14; 1 Peter 1:1–2. Doctrine unifies believers.

**Q:** What litmus test should be applied for verifying personal revelation?

**A:** The Scriptures

### Sixteen Fundamental Truths

#### 5.4.1 — Restate in your own words the Sixteen Fundamental Truths of the Assemblies of God.

The Oneness–Trinitarian controversy made it clear that the Assemblies of God needed to articulate and codify the doctrines that distinguished it as a body from others. Although there were originally seventeen doctrinal statements approved at the 1916 General Council, the doctrines were soon streamlined and combined to form the Statement of Sixteen Fundamental Truths. All affiliated ministers and churches were expected to agree with these doctrines. A condensed version of the text is given below.

Assemblies of God Fundamental Truths (Condensed)

These are nonnegotiable tenets of faith that all Assemblies of God churches adhere to. This list is derived from the official Statement of Fundamental Truths.

1. WE BELIEVE…The Scriptures are inspired by God and declare His design and plan for mankind.

2. WE BELIEVE…There is only One True God—revealed in three persons…Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (commonly known as the Trinity).

3. WE BELIEVE…In the Deity of the Lord Jesus Christ, as God’s son Jesus was both human and divine.

4. WE BELIEVE…Though originally good, man willingly fell to sin, ushering evil and death, both physical and spiritual, into the world.

5. WE BELIEVE…Every person can have restored fellowship with God through salvation (trusting Christ, through faith and repentance, to be our personal Savior).

6. WE BELIEVE…and practice two ordinances—(1) water baptism by immersion after repenting of one’s sins and receiving Christ’s gift of salvation, and (2) holy communion (the Lord’s Supper) as a symbolic remembrance of Christ’s suffering and death for our salvation.

7. WE BELIEVE…The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a special experience following salvation that empowers believers for witnessing and effective service, just as it did in New Testament times.

8. WE BELIEVE…The initial physical evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit is speaking in tongues, as experienced on the Day of Pentecost and referenced throughout Acts and the Epistles.

9. WE BELIEVE…Sanctification initially occurs at salvation and is not only a declaration that a believer is holy, but also a progressive lifelong process of separating from evil as believers continually draw closer to God and become more Christlike.

10. WE BELIEVE…The Church has a mission to seek and save all who are lost in sin. We believe ‘the Church’ is the Body of Christ and consists of the people who, throughout time, have accepted God’s offer of redemption (regardless of religious denomination) through the sacrificial death of His son Jesus Christ.

11. WE BELIEVE…A divinely called and scripturally ordained leadership ministry serves the Church. The Bible teaches that each of us under leadership must commit ourselves to reach others for Christ, to worship Him with other believers, to build up or edify the body of believers—the Church and to meet human need with ministries of love and compassion.

12. WE BELIEVE…Divine healing of the sick is a privilege for Christians today and is provided for in Christ’s atonement (His sacrificial death on the cross for our sins).

13. WE BELIEVE…in the Blessed Hope—when Jesus raptures His Church prior to His return to Earth (the second coming). At this future moment in time, all believers who have died will rise from their graves and will meet the Lord in the air, and Christians who are alive will be caught up with them to be with the Lord forever.

14. WE BELIEVE…in the millennial reign of Christ when Jesus returns with His saints at His second coming and begins His benevolent rule over earth for one thousand years. This millennial reign will bring the salvation of national Israel and the establishment of universal peace.

15. WE BELIEVE…A final judgment will take place for those who have rejected Christ. They will be judged for their sin and consigned to eternal punishment in a punishing lake of fire.

16. WE BELIEVE…and look forward to the perfect New Heaven and a New Earth that Christ is preparing for all people, of all time, who have accepted Him. We will live and dwell with Him there forever following His millennial reign on Earth. ‘And so shall we forever be with the Lord!’ (General Council 2021b).

Notice that statements 5, 7, 12, and 13 are the four cardinal truths of the Assemblies of God; statements 2 and 3 are particularly relevant to the Oneness–Trinitarian conflict that led to the drafting of the statement; statement 9 addresses the sanctification issue described earlier; and statement 8 deals with the doctrinal disagreement discussed in the next section.

**Q:** Summarize why it was important that the Assemblies of God have articulated statements describing its fundamental truths

**A:** Having these statements helped to clarify, not just to those inside the Assemblies of God but also to others outside of it, what we believe and why. They helped to prevent controversies and heresies.

### Tongues: The Initial Physical Evidence

#### 5.5.1 — Give a synopsis of D. W. Kerr's decisive case for speaking in tongues as the initial physical evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit.

The young Fellowship had one more doctrinal issue on which to come to an agreement. The teaching of speaking in tongues as the initial physical evidence was not as fractious as the other two controversies, but the discussion was of special importance in clarifying what became the key distinctive doctrine of the Assemblies of God.

Early Pentecostals had almost uniformly accepted the conclusion Charles Parham reached at the Bible school in Topeka in 1900 – that speaking in tongues was the first outwardly visible evidence that a person had been filled with the Spirit.

But in 1917, healing evangelist F. F. Bosworth, a man who had been a delegate to the organizational meeting of the Assemblies of God and later an Executive Presbyter, began to question whether speaking in tongues was indeed the only acceptable first manifestation of being filled with the Spirit. He did not in any way reject speaking in tongues but believed it to be one of many gifts that Spirit-filled people received from God. Bosworth’s conclusion that any gift of the Spirit was sufficient evidence of Spirit baptism would not have disqualified him from fellowship in the Assemblies of God at that point, but Bosworth was a powerful speaker and a persuasive man. He moved three well-known and influential leaders of the Assemblies of God to his position: founding Father Mack Pinson and previous General Superintendent A.P. Collins, as well as future General Superintendent William T. Gaston.

Although the Fellowship’s leaders did not wish for another contentious General Council so soon after the last one, confusion and requests for clarification made it necessary for the matter to be discussed at the next General Council in 1917. There it became necessary for Assemblies of God ministers to endorse the Statement of Fundamental Truths, which stated that tongues were the initial physical evidence of the infilling of the Holy Spirit. Bosworth turned in his credentials in July of 1918. However, he was given, along with others, the opportunity to address the issue at the next General Council held in September of that year in the new headquarters city of Springfield, Missouri.

While many other leaders defended the orthodox Pentecostal view of the initial physical evidence as demonstrated in the book of Acts, it was the persuasive wisdom of D. W. Kerr that won the argument.

Kerr not only marshaled all the truths presented by his brethren but also drove home again and again that it is the Word of God, not the experiences of famous men, that is the touchstone for the Pentecostal belief concerning the immediate, outward evidence of the Baptism. The Scriptural record had not been twisted by Pentecostals; no isolated case had been set forth as the sole basis for their belief; but in every case in which the results of the experience in Acts are recorded, each recipient spoke in tongues. (Brumback 1961, 128)

Afterward, delegates unanimously approved a resolution that stated:

RESOLVED, That this Council considers it a serious disagreement with the Fundamentals for any minister among us to teach contrary to our distinctive testimony that the baptism of the Holy Spirit is regularly accompanied by the initial physical sign of speaking in other tongues as the Spirit of God gives the utterance, and that we consider it inconsistent and unscriptural for any minister to hold credentials with us who thus attacks as error our distinctive testimony. (General Council Minutes 1918, 8)

Bosworth encouraged others to stay within the Assemblies of God and he maintained a good relationship with the broader Pentecostal movement throughout his long ministry. The conciliatory Christian spirit evidenced at the meeting kept the Assemblies of God from splintering while reaffirming its most distinctive doctrine, which Pinson, Gaston, and Collins embraced once again. In addition, it demonstrated remarkable maturity in dealing with complex and emotional issues in a godly and biblical manner, relying on God’s Word rather than on human experience or feeling.

For the next century, the fundamental doctrines of the Assemblies of God remained remarkably unchallenged and unchanged.

**Q:** Clarify: what is the Assemblies of God’s key distinctive doctrine?

**A:** Its key distinctive doctrine is that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit. The Pattern and Practice of Assemblies of God Missions 6 CHAPTER

## 6

### In the Beginning

#### 6.1.1 — Cite at least three facts that demonstrate the Assemblies of God's early passion for missions.

A passion for missions has been in the DNA of the Assemblies of God from the very beginning. The desire for missionary oversight to ensure an expansive and effective missionary work was one of the five basic reasons given in the call to organize the AG in Hot Springs, Arkansas, in April 1914. Their early theology of missions was based largely on the words of Jesus in three passages (McGee 1986, 166):

Matthew 24:14, “ This gospel of the kingdom will be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come,” which reflected their understanding that missionary outreach to the entire world must precede the second coming of Christ.

Acts 1:8, “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth,” which indicated the power by which this overwhelming task would be completed.

Mark 16:15, 17–18, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation…And these signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up snakes with their hands; and when they drink deadly poison, it will not hurt them at all; they will place their hands on sick people, and they will get well,” which revealed the confirming signs they expected would accompany their missionary endeavors.

Given its rejected status within the broader church world, as well as its humble beginnings and small size, the commitment to the greatest evangelism the world has ever seen was a rather ambitious resolution. However, the people of the Assemblies of God believed wholeheartedly in the Holy Spirit’s power and were ready to commit themselves to live and die in service to God through the Great Commission. The Assemblies of God considered itself a missionary fellowship, underscoring its passion for and focus on winning the lost. Therefore, the first department created by the AG was the Missionary Department in 1919.

In keeping with the AG’s promise not to override the autonomy of local churches and workers, our earliest missionaries largely answered only to God, themselves, and the church or churches that supported them financially. This led to great successes but also to failures, excesses, and missed opportunities. Throughout the twentieth century, Assemblies of God World Missions learned and grew, refining its missionary practices and clarifying its theology.

### Establishing a Theology of Missions

#### 6.2.1 — List six principles the 1921 General Council outlined as New Testament methods for missionary endeavors.

At the 1915 General Council, this continuing emphasis on missions was again reflected in the minutes. The Fellowship agreed to do everything in its power to promote evangelization of the lost in accordance with New Testament missionary methods . What this meant was more fully fleshed out at the 1921 General Council when the delegates agreed upon six principles for fulfilling this resolution:

1. Cooperative Faith (1 Corinthians 3:5–11)

“The missionaries, the Foreign Missions Committee, and the home constituency shall look to God together to supply the needs of the work,” read the minutes of the 1921 General Council (Consortium of Pentecostal Archives 1921, 61). Everyone was responsible for the missionary task; each had a role to play. In time, this cooperation would extend beyond just the members and parts of the Assemblies of God. The Movement, the Missionary Department, and the missionaries on the field would work cooperatively with other Pentecostals, with other mission organizations, and with local believers in foreign lands to accomplish more than could be done alone. This remains one of the three key emphases of Assemblies of God missions.

2. Unreached People (Matthew 24:14; Romans 15:20)

Assemblies of God missionaries would follow the apostle Paul’s example, deliberately choosing to go where the name of Jesus had not yet been preached. From the earliest days of the Assemblies of God, missionaries eagerly volunteered to take the gospel to the most remote and often dangerous spots on earth. To this end, from 1948 to 1951, the Missions Department successively owned and operated two repurposed military war planes, the Ambassador and Ambassador II, to fly missionaries and their equipment to fields that would otherwise have taken missionaries weeks or even months to reach by boat (Warner 1985, 3).The Ambassador and Ambassador II were purchased largely with funds from Speed the Light, the youth program that raises funds for transportation and communication equipment to help missionaries “speed the light” of the gospel around the world.

The second principle of the 1921 General Council only formalized what was already the goal and practice. Deliberately seeking out neglected regions where the gospel had not yet been preached remains one of the three key emphases of AG missions.

3. Indigenous Churches (Acts 14:21–23)

The common practice of many mission organizations was paternalistic—a top-down control of the work by Western missionaries. However, thanks to the efforts of pivotal people such as Alice Luce, Noel Perkin, and Melvin Hodges (see Lesson 6.3), from the beginning, the Assemblies of God recognized the value of partnering with locals. Rather than forcing local converts to adopt Western practices and culture, the indigenous church principle called for discipling native leaders and working to quickly make them able to succeed independent of missionary assistance. The goal was to establish self-governing, self-supporting, and self-propagating native churches.

The commitment to planting indigenous churches would become perhaps the defining strategy of effective Assemblies of God missions that endures to this day. Today, this is reflected in the fourfold strategy of the Assemblies of God World Missions Department: (1) reach (evangelize), (2) plant (start churches), (3) train (disciple and educate local leaders, including by founding Bible schools and colleges to equip indigenous believers to reach, plant, and train others), and (4) serve (implement compassion ministries to reach people who might otherwise never encounter the church or the love of God) (AGWM 2020, 6). Churches are the perfect focal point from which to launch relief, compassion, and outreach efforts.

4. Broad Support and Central Distribution

Acts 4:34–35 would be the model of missionary support and its distribution. All believers and churches were encouraged to give sacrificially to the work, laying their contributions “at the feet” of duly appointed leaders who would then distribute it fairly and honestly. At first, the Missionary Department primarily worked to account for donated funds and as a liaison, publicizing needs, opportunities, and testimonies of God’s working while accepting contributions from churches and individuals at home and transmitting them safely to the intended missionaries on the field. While this is still an important part of the World Missions Department’s portfolio, their responsibilities and focus have expanded greatly over the years.

When Noel Perkin assumed leadership of the Missionary Department in 1927, he was handed an envelope box with yellow duplicate receipts for more than $300,000 worth of donations. Perkin, who had been a banker before becoming a missionary, was the right man to set up a practical and efficient accounting system with each missionary and donor having his or her own account (McGee 2004, 212).

5. Equipping of Foreign Nationals (2 Timothy 2:2)

You have heard the saying, “Give a man a fish, and you’ll feed him for a day; teach a man to fish, and you’ll feed him for a lifetime.” This is the basic principle behind the fifth principle adopted by the AG at the 1921 General Council. The common practice at that time was for missionaries to raise funds to pay the salaries of their indigenous coworkers, but the Assemblies of God resisted this trend. “The native workers should receive a call from God for the work, just as do the missionaries who go from the home base” (Consortium of Pentecostal Archives 1921, 63).

The wisdom of this has been proven repeatedly. In 1966, when a change in Burma’s government led to the expulsion of all missionaries, denominations that had directly paid Burmese workers saw their work vanish practically overnight when the funding and oversight stopped, but the Assemblies of God left behind a vibrant native church that was able to thrive and grow even without overseas help (Hurst 2008, 48–52).

6. Standards of Training and Testing (Acts 6:1–7; 13:2–3)

In the beginning, few missionaries had been trained for service beyond their initial call of God. Bible schools at that time were geared toward training pastors and Christian workers but had little to offer future missionaries in what to expect and how to be effective (McGee 1986, 168). This sixth principle empowered the Foreign Missions Committee to work to ensure that only well-prepared, well-vetted candidates who were physically and spiritually healthy would reach the field. The committee was charged with defining proper standards for the training and testing of missionary candidates.

Pentecostals who formed the Assemblies of God valued the Spirit’s leading and zealously guarded against any structure or authority they feared might come between individuals and the Spirit’s leading. Still, order, planning, and coordination were also needed to be effective. The early Foreign Missions Committee and the Missions Department tried to carefully balance individual freedom and the ability to follow the Spirit’s leading with oversight—primarily in the areas of training and testing. This would ensure that money and resources would be given to missionaries who would be effective, rather than investing in people who were not committed or informed about the cost or those who would be unable to handle the stresses of missionary life.

By 1959, the annual School of Missions (now Missionary Renewal) had been established to provide missionaries with continual training, education, encouragement, and fellowship before going to the field or when on furlough (McGee 1986, 168). The emphasis on training and education continued under the leadership of the man elected to succeed Perkin, J. Philip Hogan. During his tenure (1959–1989), important international ministries were launched to assist in this effort, including the Brazilian Extension School of Theology, the Christian Training Network, and the International Correspondence Institute.

**Q:** How might local churches work cooperatively to build the Kingdom of Christ?

**A:** Answers may include: by partnering with others of like faith and strategic planning to reach the unreached.

**Q:** Explain how your church can support missionary endeavors.

**A:** Follow the Acts 4:34–35 model. Answers may also include having missionary speakers, missions' conventions, regular offerings for missionaries, supporting missionary programs, etc.

**Q:** Describe the impact your church has on the local community. How can that be expanded worldwide?

**A:** Answers will vary. Might include: By proclaiming the gospel of Christ, with the empowerment of the Holy Spirit and confirming signs; helping with local church plants and helping with overseas church plants; providing funds for local ministries and overseas ministries.

### Shapers and Champions of AG Missions

#### 6.3.1 — Explain the influence of one key individual regarding the indigenous church principle.

The Indigenous Church Principle

The 1921 General Council set the pattern for Assemblies of God missions that still define missionary practice today. Although paternalistic missionary practices were commonplace at the time the Assemblies of God followed a different path. This was due, in large part, to the influence of three people.

Alice E. Luce—The Prompter . Alice was a pioneer missionary (the first AG missionary to Mexico). She had eagerly read Roland Allen’s book Missionary Methods: St. Paul’s or Ours? (1912) and embraced its principles of New Testament missionary practices, especially the indigenous church principles.

In the months preceding the important 1921 General Council, Luce wrote a series of three articles for the Pentecostal Evangel promoting the indigenous church principles and New Testament missionary practices. She articulated the importance of establishing churches that were self-supporting, self-governing, and self-propagating. She advocated for training local believers who were empowered by the Holy Spirit and sufficient in Him to sustain and advance work independently of Western funds and governance.

She explained that leadership in newly planted works should be based on spiritual wisdom and experience rather than on race or nationality. She argued that the goal of AG missionaries should be to win and train indigenous leaders who would plant multiplying indigenous churches to reach their nations and the world.

She emphasized our Pentecostal convictions, declaring that both locals and missionaries must be empowered by the Holy Spirit. She also noted that such Spirit-empowered ministry would be accompanied by manifestations of the Spirit’s power—miracles, deliverances, signs and wonders, and spiritual gifts. Her teaching brought the principles of New Testament missionary practices to the forefront at a key moment when the Assemblies of God was making important decisions regarding its missionary practice.

Noel Perkin—the Promoter . Noel Perkin led the Missionary Department from 1927 through 1959. The Lord used his background in banking and missions, along with his kind and friendly personality, to make the changes needed to set the Assemblies of God on a strong foundation biblically and in practice. He promoted indigenous church principles, encouraging all missionaries to read Roland Allen’s book and apply its principles.

Melvin Hodges—the Professor . Melvin Hodges was a missionary in Latin America who applied indigenous church principles with great success. He understood that the church multiplied its effectiveness and honored God’s plan for redeeming mankind when it trained and empowered national workers. He stressed that churches needed to be indigenous from the beginning. Hodges warned that it was far better to build on a foundation of indigeneity than to attempt correcting the situation after straying from indigenous church principles.

In 1953, the Division of Foreign Missions asked Hodges to share the indigenous church principles that had led to such phenomenal growth in Central America. He wrote The Indigenous Church , the first missionary theology written from a Pentecostal perspective. The widely read book was used in missionary training both inside and outside the Assemblies of God.

Prior to Hodges, the Assemblies of God was, in large part, considered a fringe movement with little, if anything, to offer the broader Christian world. Hodges’ writings opened the door for the Assemblies of God to be viewed as a legitimate member of the broader Christian and missions communities.

The Cost of the Commission

AG Missionary Ivan Voronaev was killed in the Siberian Gulag on November 5, 1937. He left behind hundreds of newly planted and united churches in the Soviet Union, which have since multiplied into the thousands.

In the fall of 1964, Assemblies of God missionary J. W. Tucker was bludgeoned to death by Congolese rebels. His body was thrown into a river to be consumed by crocodiles. God used Tucker’s death to open the door for the gospel among the Mangbetu tribe of the Republic of The Congo.

In October of 1969, Mark and Gladys Bliss tragically lost all three of their children in an automobile crash in Iran. Mark and Gladys refused to give in to despair or stop believing in God’s goodness. Mark sang a hymn about the love of God at the funeral of his three children. Today, the underground church in Iran is growing faster than any other church in the world.

In recent years, an AGWM missionary was detained in North Africa, and his family was forced to evacuate. He was eventually released, but his local partners remain imprisoned. This family is now heading to another restricted-access Islamic country to make Jesus known.

Heroes at Home

As was made clear at the General Council of 1921, the Assemblies of God was to be a cooperative missionary fellowship. Not all can go, but every believer and every church shares responsibility for reaching the world with the full gospel. Every person has some part to play, whether by giving money, praying, encouraging, or other avenues of support. Many missionaries testify to times when they were keenly aware of the prayer support back home during critical moments. Countless weary and homesick workers overseas have been encouraged by a letter, news from home, or a gift. Here are just some of the Assemblies of God programs developed over the years to allow those on the home front to help fulfill the Great Commission.

Women’s Missionary Council (1925). Etta Calhoun (1870–1940) had learned much about leadership, public speaking, and organizing women for action in her role as a temperance leader. She was first exposed to the message of Pentecost when Charles Parham visited her Texas town, where she received the baptism and led her pastor and church to do the same. In 1925, Calhoun organized a women’s intercessory prayer group to pray for missionaries. She encouraged the women to consider practical ways in which they could offer support. When Calhoun learned that the children at Lillian Trasher’s orphanage needed clothing, Calhoun’s group sewed three hundred sets of clothing to supply the need. Soon Calhoun was traveling and speaking to women in other AG churches and districts, encouraging them to start similar women’s groups. First the Texico (Texas and New Mexico) District and then the General Council quickly recognized the grassroots groups as extensions of AG ministries. In 1951, the Women’s Missionary Council (now Women’s Ministries) became an official national department. One missionary emphasis has continued to be collecting money to furnish missions institutions with indoor equipment (Oberg 2017a).

Speed the Light (1944). The youth missions ministry of the AG was founded in 1944 by National Youth Ministries director Ralph Harris to give young people a chance to help “speed the light” to a world in darkness. Speed the Light (STL) is a student-initiated charitable program that allows teenagers to raise money for vehicles—cars, vans, motorcycles, bikes, trucks, buses, horses, camels, donkeys, and even airplanes. STL has stated, “If it has wheels or hooves and can carry a missionary to a country, city, town, village, or under a card board [sic] box where someone is waiting to hear about Jesus, Speed the Light has provided it” (General Council 1995–2021). In the first seventy-five years of Speed the Light, Assemblies of God youths have raised more than $300 million for missionary equipment worldwide.

Boys and Girls Missionary Challenge (1949). Introduced at the General Council of 1949, BGMC (originally Boys and Girls Missionary Crusade) was a joint effort of the Foreign Missions and Sunday School departments. It had dual purposes of providing literature for missionaries to use overseas while stirring in children a heart for missions. Its slogan was “The Word for the World.” The first BGMC project was to ship leftover Sunday school materials from Gospel Publishing House to the mission field, where it was desperately needed. Children would be enlisted to raise money for this shipping. At the time, all missionary supplies and materials were shipped overseas in sturdy wooden barrels. These barrels became the symbol of the children’s giving program. Children were given small wooden banks in which to collect their offerings. The animated character Buddy Barrel became the mascot of the program (General Council 2021c).

In 2001, BGMC became the missions education program for Assemblies of God children. BGMC’s mission has expanded to providing literature, tracts, videos, items for children’s ministry, and other evangelism and discipleship related items to missionaries at home and overseas. It helps fund various missions organizations (including Global University), provides Bible schools and new churches with supplies and literature, and helps fund translation efforts. Before Buddy Barrel’s seventieth birthday in 2019, BGMC giving surpassed the $150 million mark, with yearly giving of approximately $8 million (General Council 2021c).

Light for the Lost (1961). In 1953, businessman Sam Cochran saw a vision of people of every race reaching toward heaven, desperate for a message of hope. He felt led to provide evangelism resources, specifically literature and audio/visual materials, to help communicate that message. Sam and three other men started traveling, sharing their vision, and raising funds. Light for the Lost became an official AG missions program in 1961 under leadership of the Men’s Ministries Department (General Council 2021d).

AIM (1966). Ambassadors in Mission was started in 1968 to give young people the opportunity to get involved in short-term mission trips. Assemblies of God educator Dr. Ward Williams saw a need for young people (called Christ’s Ambassadors, or CAs) to gain exposure to missions work, and he felt that the best way to achieve this result was to have them serve as temporary workers in the field. After a three-day orientation period, the CAs were sent on four-week witnessing trips to foreign countries like Brazil, El Salvador, Germany, and others. Since then, tens of thousands of AG youth have participated in AIM trips around the world, learning about missions work through short-term experiences in the field (Oberg 2017b).

U.S. Missions

In 1926, a young missionary named Arthur Berg came up with an idea that would launch the Assemblies of God Home Missions program. In order to expand the base of home churches that were the backbone of AG World Missions support, Berg suggested sending back to the originating district a small portion of every missions gift not designated for a specific missionary or ministry. The plan and the programs associated with it quickly produced significant growth in missions giving as new churches were started that soon became missions-supporting churches.

Almost a century after these humble beginnings, U.S. Missions is going strong, making an impact in many ways and places, touching countless thousands of lives each year. The focus is on the Windows of U.S. Missions, or the main paths to ministry across the United States:

1. Adult and Teen Challenge International, USA . There are over two hundred Teen Challenge programs across the country, in almost every state. Teen Challenge reaches individuals whom society has given up on or sees no value in. Through Teen Challenge, men and women find freedom from addiction and freedom in Christ.

2. Chaplaincy Ministries. AG chaplains serve the military, police and fire departments, prisons, schools, and other specialized areas.

3. Chi Alpha Campus Ministries, USA. Chi Alpha has the opportunity to reach and build relationships with the more than eight hundred thousand international students on US university campuses. Often international students will find Christ here when they would not have had opportunity to hear of Him in their own country. As they return to their homeland, they take their faith with them and spread the love of Christ. The secular university campus is the most strategic mission field in the world. Every religion, race, creed, and culture is represented there.

4. Church Mobilization (Formerly MAPS) . Church teams participate in evangelism projects, construction projects, or both. Missionary associates (MAs) usually commit to one to two years of service and work alongside a ministry leader. You will often find an MA helping with administration or maintenance work. RVers volunteer to travel across America in their own recreational vehicles (RVs) to assist missionaries and ministries with construction projects

5. Gospel Outreach. Meeting the immediate needs of those in crisis is a top priority of Gospel Outreach Ministries personnel. This is accomplished through partnerships with AG districts/networks and churches to serve in-need communities, providing essential resources to homeless individuals, offering care and spiritual support to children affected by poverty, neglect or trauma and more.

6. Youth Alive. Youth Alive missionaries equip students to reach other students for Christ. Nearly eight of every ten decisions for Christ will be made by those under the age of eighteen. More than ninety-eight percent of the American population will pass through at least one of the sixty-seven thousand junior high and high schools in the nation. There is no better place in America to reach the largest group of unreached students and their families in one place and at one time (General Council 2021e).

**Q:** The primary concern with the Indigenous church principles is that churches be locally empowered to multiply and fully participate in the Great Commission. Given that information, would you say that most churches in your area are indigenous?

**A:** Answers may vary. It would be good to mention how churches of different denominations/organizations participate in the Great Commission.

**Q:** How might your church support a member of the body who is called into missionary service?

**A:** Through prayer, financial support, encouragement, providing accountability, assistance with preparation, short term onsite assistance.

**Q:** Evaluate what would happen if most Christians saw the Bible as one united story of God redeeming creation, rather than as a collection of somewhat related stories and instructions.

**A:** Answers may vary, may include more involvement in local evangelism and support of missionaries.

**Q:** Evaluate why it is important for those at home to support missions.

**A:** Answers may vary.

**Q:** Within the Assemblies of God, there are several ministries with the goal of reaching the lost and equipping missionaries for ministering in their countries. How can you, or your church, become more involved in supporting these ministries?

**A:** Prayer, financial support, attending events, sponsoring these programs within the church.

**Q:** Who came up with the ingenious idea that would increase the number of supporting churches and that would become the start of Assemblies of God U.S. Missions, and what was the idea?

**A:** Arthur Berg suggested that missionaries should send their home districts a small portion of undesignated missionary gifts (offerings) which the districts could use to launch new church plants that would then support missionaries. This expanded the base of supporting churches.

#### 6.3.3 — Enumerate various ways people on the home front did and still can contribute to missions.

In the months preceding the important 1921 General Council, Luce wrote a series of three articles for the Pentecostal Evangel promoting the indigenous church principles and New Testament missionary practices. She articulated the importance of establishing churches that were self-supporting, self-governing, and self-propagating. She advocated for training local believers who were empowered by the Holy Spirit and sufficient in Him to sustain and advance work independently of Western funds and governance.

She explained that leadership in newly planted works should be based on spiritual wisdom and experience rather than on race or nationality. She argued that the goal of AG missionaries should be to win and train indigenous leaders who would plant multiplying indigenous churches to reach their nations and the world.

She emphasized our Pentecostal convictions, declaring that both locals and missionaries must be empowered by the Holy Spirit. She also noted that such Spirit-empowered ministry would be accompanied by manifestations of the Spirit’s power—miracles, deliverances, signs and wonders, and spiritual gifts. Her teaching brought the principles of New Testament missionary practices to the forefront at a key moment when the Assemblies of God was making important decisions regarding its missionary practice.

Noel Perkin—the Promoter . Noel Perkin led the Missionary Department from 1927 through 1959. The Lord used his background in banking and missions, along with his kind and friendly personality, to make the changes needed to set the Assemblies of God on a strong foundation biblically and in practice. He promoted indigenous church principles, encouraging all missionaries to read Roland Allen’s book and apply its principles.

Melvin Hodges—the Professor . Melvin Hodges was a missionary in Latin America who applied indigenous church principles with great success. He understood that the church multiplied its effectiveness and honored God’s plan for redeeming mankind when it trained and empowered national workers. He stressed that churches needed to be indigenous from the beginning. Hodges warned that it was far better to build on a foundation of indigeneity than to attempt correcting the situation after straying from indigenous church principles.

In 1953, the Division of Foreign Missions asked Hodges to share the indigenous church principles that had led to such phenomenal growth in Central America. He wrote The Indigenous Church , the first missionary theology written from a Pentecostal perspective. The widely read book was used in missionary training both inside and outside the Assemblies of God.

Prior to Hodges, the Assemblies of God was, in large part, considered a fringe movement with little, if anything, to offer the broader Christian world. Hodges’ writings opened the door for the Assemblies of God to be viewed as a legitimate member of the broader Christian and missions communities.

The Cost of the Commission

AG Missionary Ivan Voronaev was killed in the Siberian Gulag on November 5, 1937. He left behind hundreds of newly planted and united churches in the Soviet Union, which have since multiplied into the thousands.

In the fall of 1964, Assemblies of God missionary J. W. Tucker was bludgeoned to death by Congolese rebels. His body was thrown into a river to be consumed by crocodiles. God used Tucker’s death to open the door for the gospel among the Mangbetu tribe of the Republic of The Congo.

In October of 1969, Mark and Gladys Bliss tragically lost all three of their children in an automobile crash in Iran. Mark and Gladys refused to give in to despair or stop believing in God’s goodness. Mark sang a hymn about the love of God at the funeral of his three children. Today, the underground church in Iran is growing faster than any other church in the world.

In recent years, an AGWM missionary was detained in North Africa, and his family was forced to evacuate. He was eventually released, but his local partners remain imprisoned. This family is now heading to another restricted-access Islamic country to make Jesus known.

Heroes at Home

As was made clear at the General Council of 1921, the Assemblies of God was to be a cooperative missionary fellowship. Not all can go, but every believer and every church shares responsibility for reaching the world with the full gospel. Every person has some part to play, whether by giving money, praying, encouraging, or other avenues of support. Many missionaries testify to times when they were keenly aware of the prayer support back home during critical moments. Countless weary and homesick workers overseas have been encouraged by a letter, news from home, or a gift. Here are just some of the Assemblies of God programs developed over the years to allow those on the home front to help fulfill the Great Commission.

Women’s Missionary Council (1925). Etta Calhoun (1870–1940) had learned much about leadership, public speaking, and organizing women for action in her role as a temperance leader. She was first exposed to the message of Pentecost when Charles Parham visited her Texas town, where she received the baptism and led her pastor and church to do the same. In 1925, Calhoun organized a women’s intercessory prayer group to pray for missionaries. She encouraged the women to consider practical ways in which they could offer support. When Calhoun learned that the children at Lillian Trasher’s orphanage needed clothing, Calhoun’s group sewed three hundred sets of clothing to supply the need. Soon Calhoun was traveling and speaking to women in other AG churches and districts, encouraging them to start similar women’s groups. First the Texico (Texas and New Mexico) District and then the General Council quickly recognized the grassroots groups as extensions of AG ministries. In 1951, the Women’s Missionary Council (now Women’s Ministries) became an official national department. One missionary emphasis has continued to be collecting money to furnish missions institutions with indoor equipment (Oberg 2017a).

Speed the Light (1944). The youth missions ministry of the AG was founded in 1944 by National Youth Ministries director Ralph Harris to give young people a chance to help “speed the light” to a world in darkness. Speed the Light (STL) is a student-initiated charitable program that allows teenagers to raise money for vehicles—cars, vans, motorcycles, bikes, trucks, buses, horses, camels, donkeys, and even airplanes. STL has stated, “If it has wheels or hooves and can carry a missionary to a country, city, town, village, or under a card board [sic] box where someone is waiting to hear about Jesus, Speed the Light has provided it” (General Council 1995–2021). In the first seventy-five years of Speed the Light, Assemblies of God youths have raised more than $300 million for missionary equipment worldwide.

Boys and Girls Missionary Challenge (1949). Introduced at the General Council of 1949, BGMC (originally Boys and Girls Missionary Crusade) was a joint effort of the Foreign Missions and Sunday School departments. It had dual purposes of providing literature for missionaries to use overseas while stirring in children a heart for missions. Its slogan was “The Word for the World.” The first BGMC project was to ship leftover Sunday school materials from Gospel Publishing House to the mission field, where it was desperately needed. Children would be enlisted to raise money for this shipping. At the time, all missionary supplies and materials were shipped overseas in sturdy wooden barrels. These barrels became the symbol of the children’s giving program. Children were given small wooden banks in which to collect their offerings. The animated character Buddy Barrel became the mascot of the program (General Council 2021c).

In 2001, BGMC became the missions education program for Assemblies of God children. BGMC’s mission has expanded to providing literature, tracts, videos, items for children’s ministry, and other evangelism and discipleship related items to missionaries at home and overseas. It helps fund various missions organizations (including Global University), provides Bible schools and new churches with supplies and literature, and helps fund translation efforts. Before Buddy Barrel’s seventieth birthday in 2019, BGMC giving surpassed the $150 million mark, with yearly giving of approximately $8 million (General Council 2021c).

Light for the Lost (1961). In 1953, businessman Sam Cochran saw a vision of people of every race reaching toward heaven, desperate for a message of hope. He felt led to provide evangelism resources, specifically literature and audio/visual materials, to help communicate that message. Sam and three other men started traveling, sharing their vision, and raising funds. Light for the Lost became an official AG missions program in 1961 under leadership of the Men’s Ministries Department (General Council 2021d).

AIM (1966). Ambassadors in Mission was started in 1968 to give young people the opportunity to get involved in short-term mission trips. Assemblies of God educator Dr. Ward Williams saw a need for young people (called Christ’s Ambassadors, or CAs) to gain exposure to missions work, and he felt that the best way to achieve this result was to have them serve as temporary workers in the field. After a three-day orientation period, the CAs were sent on four-week witnessing trips to foreign countries like Brazil, El Salvador, Germany, and others. Since then, tens of thousands of AG youth have participated in AIM trips around the world, learning about missions work through short-term experiences in the field (Oberg 2017b).

U.S. Missions

In 1926, a young missionary named Arthur Berg came up with an idea that would launch the Assemblies of God Home Missions program. In order to expand the base of home churches that were the backbone of AG World Missions support, Berg suggested sending back to the originating district a small portion of every missions gift not designated for a specific missionary or ministry. The plan and the programs associated with it quickly produced significant growth in missions giving as new churches were started that soon became missions-supporting churches.

Almost a century after these humble beginnings, U.S. Missions is going strong, making an impact in many ways and places, touching countless thousands of lives each year. The focus is on the Windows of U.S. Missions, or the main paths to ministry across the United States:

1. Adult and Teen Challenge International, USA . There are over two hundred Teen Challenge programs across the country, in almost every state. Teen Challenge reaches individuals whom society has given up on or sees no value in. Through Teen Challenge, men and women find freedom from addiction and freedom in Christ.

2. Chaplaincy Ministries. AG chaplains serve the military, police and fire departments, prisons, schools, and other specialized areas.

3. Chi Alpha Campus Ministries, USA. Chi Alpha has the opportunity to reach and build relationships with the more than eight hundred thousand international students on US university campuses. Often international students will find Christ here when they would not have had opportunity to hear of Him in their own country. As they return to their homeland, they take their faith with them and spread the love of Christ. The secular university campus is the most strategic mission field in the world. Every religion, race, creed, and culture is represented there.

4. Church Mobilization (Formerly MAPS) . Church teams participate in evangelism projects, construction projects, or both. Missionary associates (MAs) usually commit to one to two years of service and work alongside a ministry leader. You will often find an MA helping with administration or maintenance work. RVers volunteer to travel across America in their own recreational vehicles (RVs) to assist missionaries and ministries with construction projects

5. Gospel Outreach. Meeting the immediate needs of those in crisis is a top priority of Gospel Outreach Ministries personnel. This is accomplished through partnerships with AG districts/networks and churches to serve in-need communities, providing essential resources to homeless individuals, offering care and spiritual support to children affected by poverty, neglect or trauma and more.

6. Youth Alive. Youth Alive missionaries equip students to reach other students for Christ. Nearly eight of every ten decisions for Christ will be made by those under the age of eighteen. More than ninety-eight percent of the American population will pass through at least one of the sixty-seven thousand junior high and high schools in the nation. There is no better place in America to reach the largest group of unreached students and their families in one place and at one time (General Council 2021e).

**Q:** The primary concern with the Indigenous church principles is that churches be locally empowered to multiply and fully participate in the Great Commission. Given that information, would you say that most churches in your area are indigenous?

**A:** Answers may vary. It would be good to mention how churches of different denominations/organizations participate in the Great Commission.

**Q:** How might your church support a member of the body who is called into missionary service?

**A:** Through prayer, financial support, encouragement, providing accountability, assistance with preparation, short term onsite assistance.

**Q:** Evaluate what would happen if most Christians saw the Bible as one united story of God redeeming creation, rather than as a collection of somewhat related stories and instructions.

**A:** Answers may vary, may include more involvement in local evangelism and support of missionaries.

**Q:** Evaluate why it is important for those at home to support missions.

**A:** Answers may vary.

**Q:** Within the Assemblies of God, there are several ministries with the goal of reaching the lost and equipping missionaries for ministering in their countries. How can you, or your church, become more involved in supporting these ministries?

**A:** Prayer, financial support, attending events, sponsoring these programs within the church.

**Q:** Who came up with the ingenious idea that would increase the number of supporting churches and that would become the start of Assemblies of God U.S. Missions, and what was the idea?

**A:** Arthur Berg suggested that missionaries should send their home districts a small portion of undesignated missionary gifts (offerings) which the districts could use to launch new church plants that would then support missionaries. This expanded the base of supporting churches.
