### AGWM Structure and Governance

#### 6.4.1 — Articulate AGWM's relationship to the Assemblies of God and its primary task.

Assemblies of God World Missions (AGWM) is a division of the Assemblies of God and, under the Assemblies of God, is charged with the responsibility of spreading the gospel in other nations.

AGWM is led by an Executive Director and the World Missions Board. The board consists of the AGWM Executive Director, the General Superintendent, the AGWM Administrator, the AGWM Regional Directors, two Executive Presbyters, and eight local pastors from various regions of the United States. The ongoing global operations of AGWM are overseen by the World Missions Executive Committee which includes committee the Executive Director, the Administrator, the Regional Directors, the International Ministries Director, and the leaders of major AGWM divisions.

AGWM divides the world into five regions, each of which is made up of multiple areas led by Area Directors. The five regions are: Africa, Asia Pacific, Europe, Eurasia, and Latin America Caribbean.

#### 6.4.2 — List the five regions of the world as defined by AGWM.

Assemblies of God World Missions (AGWM) is a division of the Assemblies of God and, under the Assemblies of God, is charged with the responsibility of spreading the gospel in other nations.

AGWM is led by an Executive Director and the World Missions Board. The board consists of the AGWM Executive Director, the General Superintendent, the AGWM Administrator, the AGWM Regional Directors, two Executive Presbyters, and eight local pastors from various regions of the United States. The ongoing global operations of AGWM are overseen by the World Missions Executive Committee which includes committee the Executive Director, the Administrator, the Regional Directors, the International Ministries Director, and the leaders of major AGWM divisions.

AGWM divides the world into five regions, each of which is made up of multiple areas led by Area Directors. The five regions are: Africa, Asia Pacific, Europe, Eurasia, and Latin America Caribbean.

#### 6.4.3 — 6.4.3

### AGWM Missionary Application and Appointment

#### 6.5.1 — List some of the requirements to become a AGWM Missionary.

Globalization and the freedom of travel have created a lot of options for engaging in foreign missions. Numerous reputable mission agencies and faithful locals exist with whom churches and individuals in the United States. can connect. However, some locals and workers overseas operate without accountability or oversight. While some are doing good work, others take advantage of the generosity and trust of Westerner donors. Furthermore, funds from well-intentioned donors can sometimes hinder the long-term sustainability and multiplication of a mission by creating dependency, inhibiting local initiative, and undermining the empowerment of locals.

AGWM is intentional in the process used to vet appointed missionaries. To understand the process, it is essential to define the terms AGWM uses for the various levels of missionary service and appointment.

MAPS Volunteers – This designation is given to those who join short-term teams with churches or serve as volunteers on the field for up to eleven months. Vetting for MAPS workers is conducted by their local pastor or church. List some of the requirements to become an AGWM Missionary.

MA (Missionary Associates)- MAs serve under the leadership of appointed missionaries for one to two years. MAs are often in a time of discerning their call, and an MA term provides both them and the missionaries with whom they work the opportunity to discover God’s direction and assess their spiritual, physical, and professional suitability for career service. Requirements for Missionary Associates include: The application and approval process to become an MA involves the applicant’s testimony, call, work experience, personal, family, and educational backgrounds, references, pastor and district/network recommendations and Area Director/ministry leader approval. List three additional requirements for those applying for career missionary appointment.

The application and approval process to become an MA involves the applicant’s testimony, call, work experience, personal, family, and educational backgrounds, references, pastor and district/network recommendations and Area Director/ministry leader approval. List three additional requirements for those applying for career missionary appointment.

Career Appointment – In addition to the steps noted above for MA applicants, those applying for career appointment complete a personal history paper, a chronological history paper, and provide additional references. Other steps include required reading and training courses. Candidates participate in Candidate Orientation and Pre-Field Orientation and undergo multiple interviews, including one with the World Missions Committee.

You may wonder why the AGWM application process, particularly for appointment, is so thorough and time consuming. The appointment process is purposeful and deliberate. There are two primary reasons guiding these requirements.

AGWM believes that nations are best reached by those who dedicate their lives to the call, learn the language and customs of the people, and are well-equipped to disciple and train locals.

AGWM and AG churches need to trust that AGWM has done everything possible to vet, train, and otherwise prepare missionaries for the field. Explain why the process for becoming an AGWM missionary is so detailed and involved.

The State of the Gospel

John Easter has written:

In today’s world of 8 billion people, there are around 15,000 “nations.” Of these, 7,000 nations (or people groups) are considered unreached. That is 42 percent of the world, 3.4 billion people. Yet only 3 percent of all global missionaries work among them.

God is leading us to send our sons and daughters to make disciples and plant churches where they do not exist. Our vision is to grow AGWM to 4,000 healthy missionaries working to establish the church among all peoples everywhere. We will work with our national church partners in the World Assemblies of God Fellowship and beyond (God’s global family) towards this end. The Church shall indeed take all the gospel to all the world.

Unreached - Less than 2 believers in every 100 people

42% of the World

3.4 Billion People

7,400+ People Groups

3% of World Missionaries

Under-Engaged – Less than 1 believer in every 100 people

3 Billion People

6,590 People Groups

Frontier Peoples – Less than 1 believer in every 1,000 people

2 Billion People

4,890 People Groups

Unengaged – no/few known believers

202 Million People

2,085 People Groups Note the key elements in AGWM's vision to address the need for global access to the gospel.

The Vision:

AGWM’s vision is simple, clear, and audacious “to establish the church among all peoples, everywhere.”

To accomplish this, we call upon the Holy Spirit, who inspired our forebearers to commit themselves to God for the greatest evangelism the world has ever seen. Toward that end, we are believing for 4,000 AGWM workers by 2033.

These workers will come from local churches and ministries. Local AG churches and ministries will disciple the believers God is raising up for the nations. They will help discern and nurture their call. They will celebrate their service and send them to the nations, following the pattern of church in Antioch (Acts 13).

These 4,000 AGWM missionaries will partner with 80 million Assemblies of God believers from 160 nations worldwide. Linking arms with AG missionaries sent from Burkina Faso, Argentina, Romania, the Philippines, and more than 120 nations to proclaim Jesus and plan multiplying churches among all people.

AGWM's Main Thing

While there are many needs around the world and many good organizations addressing them, AGWM is committed to one primary task: establishing the church among all peoples everywhere. We carry out this commitment through four primary spheres of engagement:

Reaching–Reaching involves boots-on-the-ground proclamation of the gospel and intercession. “How can they call on him to save them unless they believe in him? And how can they believe in him if they have never heard about him?” Romans 10:14.

Planting–We plant churches because the church is the center of God’s work in the world. It is in the church that people can most fully experience the life of God and do His will on earth.

Training–The Holy Spirit has been given to all so that all may share in God’s mission in the world. This conviction prompts AGWM missionaries to emphasize training ordinary people everywhere, empowering them for ministry in the harvest. This training is conducted formally and informally. Global University courses have been used in places as diverse as Iran, Ethiopia, Europe and the South Pacific. Few, if any, other Christian organizations have started as many Bible Schools, or trained as many local ministers as have Assemblies of God missionaries. We say this not as a point of pride but in recognition of God’s grace and in credit to the foresight of our AGWM forebears.

Serving–Since Acts 2, the Christian church has been known by the world for its generosity and help to the suffering. We plant churches because local churches are best able to show compassion to their communities. Missionaries and foreign aid agencies will eventually leave, but local churches will remain among their people, demonstrating the love of Christ to one another and their communities. Describe three aspects of the role of the local church in supporting missions.

**Q:** How can you or your church become more involved in supporting missions and sending the church’s own sons and daughters to the nations?

**A:** Answers may vary.

**Q:** How should individual Christians and churches respond when hearing about the number of people in the world without access to the gospel?

**A:** The fourfold strategy is: evangelism (reach), church planting (plant), education (train), and compassion ministries (serve). 7 CHAPTER

#### 6.5.2 — List three additional requirements for those applying for career missionary appointment.

Globalization and the freedom of travel have created a lot of options for engaging in foreign missions. Numerous reputable mission agencies and faithful locals exist with whom churches and individuals in the United States. can connect. However, some locals and workers overseas operate without accountability or oversight. While some are doing good work, others take advantage of the generosity and trust of Westerner donors. Furthermore, funds from well-intentioned donors can sometimes hinder the long-term sustainability and multiplication of a mission by creating dependency, inhibiting local initiative, and undermining the empowerment of locals.

AGWM is intentional in the process used to vet appointed missionaries. To understand the process, it is essential to define the terms AGWM uses for the various levels of missionary service and appointment.

MAPS Volunteers – This designation is given to those who join short-term teams with churches or serve as volunteers on the field for up to eleven months. Vetting for MAPS workers is conducted by their local pastor or church. List some of the requirements to become an AGWM Missionary.

MA (Missionary Associates)- MAs serve under the leadership of appointed missionaries for one to two years. MAs are often in a time of discerning their call, and an MA term provides both them and the missionaries with whom they work the opportunity to discover God’s direction and assess their spiritual, physical, and professional suitability for career service. Requirements for Missionary Associates include: The application and approval process to become an MA involves the applicant’s testimony, call, work experience, personal, family, and educational backgrounds, references, pastor and district/network recommendations and Area Director/ministry leader approval. List three additional requirements for those applying for career missionary appointment.

The application and approval process to become an MA involves the applicant’s testimony, call, work experience, personal, family, and educational backgrounds, references, pastor and district/network recommendations and Area Director/ministry leader approval. List three additional requirements for those applying for career missionary appointment.

Career Appointment – In addition to the steps noted above for MA applicants, those applying for career appointment complete a personal history paper, a chronological history paper, and provide additional references. Other steps include required reading and training courses. Candidates participate in Candidate Orientation and Pre-Field Orientation and undergo multiple interviews, including one with the World Missions Committee.

You may wonder why the AGWM application process, particularly for appointment, is so thorough and time consuming. The appointment process is purposeful and deliberate. There are two primary reasons guiding these requirements.

AGWM believes that nations are best reached by those who dedicate their lives to the call, learn the language and customs of the people, and are well-equipped to disciple and train locals.

AGWM and AG churches need to trust that AGWM has done everything possible to vet, train, and otherwise prepare missionaries for the field. Explain why the process for becoming an AGWM missionary is so detailed and involved.

The State of the Gospel

John Easter has written:

In today’s world of 8 billion people, there are around 15,000 “nations.” Of these, 7,000 nations (or people groups) are considered unreached. That is 42 percent of the world, 3.4 billion people. Yet only 3 percent of all global missionaries work among them.

God is leading us to send our sons and daughters to make disciples and plant churches where they do not exist. Our vision is to grow AGWM to 4,000 healthy missionaries working to establish the church among all peoples everywhere. We will work with our national church partners in the World Assemblies of God Fellowship and beyond (God’s global family) towards this end. The Church shall indeed take all the gospel to all the world.

Unreached - Less than 2 believers in every 100 people

42% of the World

3.4 Billion People

7,400+ People Groups

3% of World Missionaries

Under-Engaged – Less than 1 believer in every 100 people

3 Billion People

6,590 People Groups

Frontier Peoples – Less than 1 believer in every 1,000 people

2 Billion People

4,890 People Groups

Unengaged – no/few known believers

202 Million People

The Vision:

AGWM’s vision is simple, clear, and audacious “to establish the church among all peoples, everywhere.”

To accomplish this, we call upon the Holy Spirit, who inspired our forebearers to commit themselves to God for the greatest evangelism the world has ever seen. Toward that end, we are believing for 4,000 AGWM workers by 2033.

These workers will come from local churches and ministries. Local AG churches and ministries will disciple the believers God is raising up for the nations. They will help discern and nurture their call. They will celebrate their service and send them to the nations, following the pattern of church in Antioch (Acts 13).

These 4,000 AGWM missionaries will partner with 80 million Assemblies of God believers from 160 nations worldwide. Linking arms with AG missionaries sent from Burkina Faso, Argentina, Romania, the Philippines, and more than 120 nations to proclaim Jesus and plan multiplying churches among all people.

We will work with our national church partners in the World Assemblies of God Fellowship and beyond (God’s global family) towards this end. The Church shall indeed take all the gospel to all the world.

The Vision:

AGWM’s vision is simple, clear, and audacious “to establish the church among all peoples, everywhere.”

To accomplish this, we call upon the Holy Spirit, who inspired our forebearers to commit themselves to God for the greatest evangelism the world has ever seen. Toward that end, we are believing for 4,000 AGWM workers by 2033.

These workers will come from local churches and ministries. Local AG churches and ministries will disciple the believers God is raising up for the nations. They will help discern and nurture their call. They will celebrate their service and send them to the nations, following the pattern of church in Antioch (Acts 13).

These 4,000 AGWM missionaries will partner with 80 million Assemblies of God believers from 160 nations worldwide. Linking arms with AG missionaries sent from Burkina Faso, Argentina, Romania, the Philippines, and more than 120 nations to proclaim Jesus and plan multiplying churches among all people.

AGWM's Main Thing

While there are many needs around the world and many good organizations addressing them, AGWM is committed to one primary task: establishing the church among all peoples everywhere. We carry out this commitment through four primary spheres of engagement:

Reaching–Reaching involves boots-on-the-ground proclamation of the gospel and intercession. “How can they call on him to save them unless they believe in him? And how can they believe in him if they have never heard about him?” Romans 10:14.

Planting–We plant churches because the church is the center of God’s work in the world. It is in the church that people can most fully experience the life of God and do His will on earth.

Training–The Holy Spirit has been given to all so that all may share in God’s mission in the world. This conviction prompts AGWM missionaries to emphasize training ordinary people everywhere, empowering them for ministry in the harvest. This training is conducted formally and informally. Global University courses have been used in places as diverse as Iran, Ethiopia, Europe and the South Pacific. Few, if any, other Christian organizations have started as many Bible Schools, or trained as many local ministers as have Assemblies of God missionaries. We say this not as a point of pride but in recognition of God’s grace and in credit to the foresight of our AGWM forebears.

Serving–Since Acts 2, the Christian church has been known by the world for its generosity and help to the suffering. We plant churches because local churches are best able to show compassion to their communities. Missionaries and foreign aid agencies will eventually leave, but local churches will remain among their people, demonstrating the love of Christ to one another and their communities. Describe three aspects of the role of the local church in supporting missions.

**Q:** How can you or your church become more involved in supporting missions and sending the church’s own sons and daughters to the nations?

**A:** Answers may vary.

**Q:** How should individual Christians and churches respond when hearing about the number of people in the world without access to the gospel?

**A:** The fourfold strategy is: evangelism (reach), church planting (plant), education (train), and compassion ministries (serve). 7 CHAPTER

### Working Together to Reach the World

#### 6.6.1 — Describe three aspects of the role of the local church in supporting missions.

Missionaries come from local churches and ministries. They are us, our disciples, our sons and daughters. Missionaries are born again, discipled, called, nurtured, and sent from among us. It is we, the church, who send them, support them, pray for them, and receive them back to bear testimony to what God has accomplished.

Christians from other church backgrounds who visit AG churches frequently comment on the compelling nature of our global mission. They see the flags and banners; they hear the reports and missionary speakers. They listen as missionaries and nations are lifted before the Lord in prayer.

All of these things communicate what we value. They help us establish a culture that says God’s mission to the world is important and we, as a church, are giving ourselves to that mission.

Hosting missionaries for services and events helps keep a missions vision before the people and go a long way toward establishing a missions culture. Highlighting missionary updates and prayer needs using video and other means are also helpful.

Patterns such as a missions Sunday once a month and a special missions event once or twice per year help cast vision for the world. Purposeful, periodic missions trips provide a church and ministry members the opportunity to see the world and God’s work up close. Those who go are motivated to intercede and give to missions. God also uses these trips as a time to call people to a lifetime of service overseas.

Assemblies of God World Missions is committed to establishing the church among all peoples everywhere. The strategy of reaching, planting, training, and serving mentioned above is a useful tool for evaluating local church missions budgets.

Missions budgets and the distribution of funds should be evaluated based on these time-tested priorities.

Reaching - What percentage of our church’s budget is going to the support of frontier missionaries who are proclaiming the Gospel where the church does not exist?

Planting - Does our missions budget include supporting boots on the ground missionaries who are planting churches among the unreached?

Training - Are we supporting missionaries who have given themselves to training locals to serve the churches and further the mission around the world?

Serving - Are we remembering the poor, the suffering, the orphaned and widowed in our missions giving? 6 . 7 LESSON

#### 6.8.1

U.S. Missions: The Windows of Ministry From its earliest days, the Assemblies of God has been committed to fulfilling the Great Commission both internationally and within the United States. While global missions often receive significant attention, U.S. Missions plays an equally vital role in reaching people with the gospel. In 1919, the General Council adopted a resolution to “saturate the neglected districts of this country with the Pentecostal message.” This decision laid the foundation for what would later become the national missions division of the Assemblies of God. Just two years later, in 1921, the Council passed another resolution, establishing a fund to support mission fields within the United States and designating areas outside existing districts as home mission fields. Nearly a century later, the division remains a powerful force in evangelism and church planting. In 2003, it was officially renamed Assemblies of God U.S. Missions (AGUSM), reflecting its ongoing dedication to reaching people across the nation. Today, the division operates through key ministry areas, known as the Windows of U.S. Missions, each addressing spiritual, physical, and emotional needs across the country. The Windows of U.S. Missions

1. Adult & Teen Challenge U.S.A. Adult & Teen Challenge (ATC) is a network of over 220 addiction recovery programs throughout the United States and Canada. Offering a full continuum of care, ATC helps individuals seeking freedom from addictions and other life- controlling issues through the power of Jesus Christ. ATC utilizes a biblically based model, including dynamic curriculum, counseling, work therapy, and other services to help students become mentally sound, emotionally balanced, socially adjusted, physically well, and spiritually alive.

2. Chaplaincy Ministries Chaplaincy is pastoring beyond church walls, meeting people where they are and ministering in life’s most challenging moments. Chaplains serve shoulder to shoulder with those in need, offering hope, truth, and the love of Christ. Chaplains serve in a variety of settings, including: • Emergency Services – Supporting police, fire, and rescue personnel as they navigate crisis situations and high-stress environments. • Military – Providing spiritual guidance to active-duty personnel, veterans, and their families, helping them through the unique demands of military life. • Healthcare – Offering comfort to patients, families, and medical staff facing illness, trauma, or loss. • Correctional – Ministering to the incarcerated, sharing the message of redemption and the value God places on every life. • Specialized – Serving in diverse settings such as professional sports teams, corporate offices, disaster relief efforts, truck stops, motorcycle rallies, and more. Wherever people experience crisis, transition, or hardship, chaplains bring the presence of Christ, reminding them that they are seen, valued, and never alone.

3. Chi Alpha Campus Ministries, U.S.A. Chi Alpha focuses on reaching students on college and university campuses. With over 800,000 international students studying in the United States, many encounter the gospel for the first time through Chi Alpha. These students often take their newfound faith back to their home countries, spreading the message of Christ globally. College campuses represent a diverse and strategic mission field, where students from every background, culture, and belief system gather. Chi Alpha missionaries disciple students and help them develop a biblical worldview, equipping them to become Christian leaders in their communities and professions.

4. Church Mobilization (Formerly MAPS) Church Mobilization operates in four areas: Church Development, Church Projects, Church Teams, and RV Ministries—and serves the Assemblies of God by providing opportunities to be involved in ministry, either as a church group or as individuals. Church Mobilization offers evangelism and construction support to missionaries and AG churches, districts, colleges, and other facilities across the nation.

5. Gospel Outreach Gospel Outreach Ministries helps meet the urgent needs of people in crisis, Focusing on the development and salvation of underserved communities through accessible methods and partnerships. This is more than a priority—it is a calling. In partnership with Assemblies of God districts, networks, and local churches, these missionaries step into vulnerable communities to bring practical help and spiritual hope. This includes providing vital resources for the homeless, offering care and encouragement to children affected by poverty, neglect, or trauma, and responding to a wide range of community needs with compassion. Missionaries and volunteers with Gospel Outreach Ministries are often the first point of contact for those who are hurting. They serve on the front lines, meeting immediate physical needs while extending the love of Christ. Once stability begins to take root, our teams share the gospel and connect individuals with local Assemblies of God fellowships and ministries. This ensures that each person not only receives care in the moment but also finds ongoing discipleship, community, and long-term support.

6. Intercultural Ministries The United States is home to hundreds of diverse people groups, speaking more than 600 languages. Rather than only sending missionaries abroad, God has brought the nations to us. Intercultural missionaries serve among ethnic, tribal, and cultural groups, building relationships and sharing the gospel in ways that respect and honor their unique backgrounds. They invest time in learning cultural norms and understanding the communities they serve, ensuring that ministry is both effective and sustainable. Their goal is to establish strong, thriving churches and ministries that develop local, spiritual leaders who can continue the work, replicating disciples and expanding the reach of the gospel.

7. Youth Alive Youth Alive missionaries equip students to reach their peers for Christ. Studies show that nearly 80 percent of people who make a decision for Christ do so before the age of eighteen. Public schools present an incredible mission field, as over 98 percent of Americans will attend at least one of the 67,000 junior high and high schools in the country. Youth Alive helps Christian students start Bible clubs, organize outreach events, and become missionaries to their own campuses. The Mission of U.S. Missions The vision of U.S. Missions is to seek, save, and send:

1. Seek – Every person in the United States should have the opportunity to experience the gospel of Jesus Christ and become a disciple in a local church.

2. Save – U.S. Missions develops and supports nationwide ministries that focus on evangelism and discipleship. Missionaries work in partnership with Assemblies of God districts and networks to spread the gospel.

3. Send – Missionaries are trained and equipped to engage in strategic outreach efforts, working with churches, districts, and ministry networks to fulfill the Great Commission. Becoming a U.S. Missionary A U.S. missionary is called by God and sent by the Church to serve in a dedicated ministry. Missionaries commit to spending the majority of their time engaged in direct, hands-on outreach and discipleship. U.S. Missions offers several pathways to serve:

1. Appointed Missionary • Full-time ministry opportunity for AG credential holders. • Requires a long-term commitment to missionary service. • Includes benefits, training, and formal appointment.

2. Career Associate • Long-term missions opportunity for credentialed AG ministers. • Requires less fundraising than an appointed missionary role. • Can serve as a stepping stone to full-time missionary appointment.

3. Missions Associate • Three-year service opportunity with or without ministerial credentials. • Provides experience under a seasoned missionary leader. • Helps individuals explore a career in missions.

4. Missions Intern • Up to a ten-month internship for those with no prior ministry experience or credentials. • Interns work under the guidance of experienced ministry leaders. • Designed to provide a foundation for future ministry involvement. U.S. Missions plays a critical role in advancing the gospel across the United States. Through the Windows of U.S. Missions, the Church reaches diverse people groups, serves unique ministry needs, and fulfills the Great Commission within our own borders. Whether through Teen Challenge, Chaplaincy, Chi Alpha, Church Mobilization, Intercultural Ministries, Specialized Ministries, or Youth Alive, each effort is a strategic investment in kingdom work. For those sensing a call to missions, U.S. Missions provides multiple pathways to serve. Whether as a missionary intern, associate, career missionary, or appointed missionary, there is a place for every willing heart to engage in the work of the gospel. If God is calling you to U.S. Missions, take the next step—seek His guidance, prepare for the journey, and step into His mission field right where you are.

## 7

### Assemblies of God Education from the Beginning

#### 7.1.1 — Identify three valid reasons early Pentecostals were wary of higher education.

While studies have shown that the earliest leaders of the Pentecostal Movement actually had more education than average for that time, a stereotype persists that they were backward and unsophisticated (Burgess et al. 1988, 58). This may stem from their concerns that an over-emphasis on education would come at the expense of spiritual fervor. They believed that they were living in the last days, and the urgency of the task was so great that there was no time to waste sitting in classrooms. Likewise, the investment of money would be more effective in the sending of missionaries than the building of schools.

They were also intent on following New Testament practices. The early believers preached boldly and effectively, empowered by the Holy Spirit. Those who heard them speak were amazed that they were unschooled, ordinary men (Acts 4:13). Pentecostals recognized that education was of secondary importance to having been with Jesus and experiencing the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

Third, antibiblical modernism and liberal theology had infiltrated mainline churches through schools and seminaries , robbing them of their power, relevance, and ability to recognize or teach the truth. Pentecostals were determined to guard their own movement against a similar fate.

Despite these real concerns, forward-thinking founders of the Assemblies of God recognized the importance of education for training workers and perpetuating Pentecostal distinctives for the organization’s survival, success, and growth. This was clearly evidenced at the first General Council in Hot Springs, Arkansas (April, 1914).

Sunday School: Ensuring a Biblically Literate Fellowship

One of the main original reasons for calling for the organization of the Assemblies of God was this: “ We come together that we may know how to conserve the work, that we may build up and not tear down ” (Word and Witness, December 1913). From the beginning of the Assemblies of God, Sunday school was recognized as an important way to conserve the work, building upon the established foundation and passing on the full gospel message to future generations.

The Sunday school movement, begun in the late 1700s in England to teach reading and Christian morals to those who would otherwise have had no education, saw some of its greatest success in America. Much of the growth of the Methodist and Baptist churches in the 1800s was due to the training of laypeople to teach organized Sunday School classes, even in the remotest areas.

At the turn of the twentieth century, while many other churches were moving away from lay involvement and toward professional clergy and workers, the newly-formed Assemblies of God emphasized the Holy Spirit’s calling and gifting on every believer and did not follow this trend. In fact, as it became clear how effective Sunday school was at evangelizing the community, disciplining the converted, and instructing children and youth in matters of doctrine, Sunday school growth exploded in the 1930s, '40s, and '50s, until by 1967, the number of Sunday school enrollees was twice that of church members in the Assemblies of God (Menzies 1971, 271).

Recognizing the importance of Sunday school, Alice Reynolds Flower, the wife of the first General Secretary of the AG, published Sunday school lesson commentary in their weekly paper, The Christian Evangel (later The Pentecostal Evangel) , even before the Assemblies of God was formed. When their paper became the official publication of the Assemblies of God, this practice was continued.

By 1919, the General Council had approved the production of the AG’s first Sunday school curriculum, to be published through Gospel Publishing House, under the direction of J. Z. Kamerer. E. N. Bell, the first general superintendent, wrote the adult and intermediate age (youth) quarterlies, while Alice Flower wrote the quarterlies for juniors and primaries.

In 1921, the AG printed and distributed its first Sunday school take-home paper, Our Pentecostal Boys and Girls . By 1924, a complete line of Sunday school curriculum, written by Assemblies of God authors teaching the denomination’s distinctive beliefs and doctrines, was being produced. The total circulation of these quarterlies and papers had reached eight million by 1927 (Menzies 1971, 136).

In 1933, Ralph Riggs, pastor of Central Assembly in Springfield, Missouri, and future general superintendent, wrote the Pentecostal Movement’s first teacher training course, A Successful Sunday School (Burgess et al. 1988, 836).

Much of that early growth was due to the enthusiasm of a Sunday school teacher from Springfield, Missouri. Marcus Grable was a janitor at the Gospel Publishing House who started several Sunday schools in different parts of the city. With such explosive growth taking place in the young fellowship, Grable was often asked to respond to letters from churches asking for information or help about their own Sunday schools. He was given a desk and typewriter so that he could respond during his time at work. This eventually led, in 1935, to the establishment of the Sunday School Promotion Department, with Marcus Grable providing leadership.

In his fourteen years in office, Grable enthusiastically promoted Sunday school, earning the moniker, “Mr. Sunday School.” He focused on educating, training, and equipping teachers and superintendents, instituting training magazines ( Our Sunday School Counselor and Superintendent’s Assistant ). He travelled frequently to train teachers, eventually laying the foundation in the 1950s for the national Worker’s Training Program. He oversaw the golden age of annual Sunday school conventions, and under Grable’s leadership, AG Sunday schools expanded by 300 percent, leading all other church groups in growth (McGee 2014, 247).

Sunday school’s growth began to crest in the 1960s due to many factors, including declining birth rates, a proliferation of other AG ministries and programs that competed for attention, and the end of national conventions. Many districts continued holding their own conventions into the 1990s, and the strength of Sunday school varied across the fellowship, depending on the emphasis it received from leadership.

In 1984, a study by the Assemblies of God national Sunday school leadership in Springfield, Missouri outlined the dire consequences for churches when adults failed to attend Sunday school (Burgess 1988, 837). These adults:

Lacked basic Bible knowledge,

Were not committed to the church,

Did not embrace many beliefs of Pentecostal Christianity and the AG, and

Were less likely to volunteer in the church.

Additionally, when Sunday school did not receive support from adults, it affected the attendance and commitment of young people to the church.

Historically, no Christian education program has ever involved more people in consistent weekly Bible study than Sunday school (Burgess et al., 837). While the term Sunday school has often been replaced by trendier names— cell groups, life groups, discipleship tracts, Kid Zone, Xtreme , and so on—an intentional, systematic study of God’s Word presented at the level of the believer’s understanding is of vital importance for church growth and conserving the work—passing on Assemblies of God doctrines to subsequent generations.

Higher Education: Teaching and Training for Ministry

In spite of their wariness of the potential dangers of institutions, early Assemblies of God leaders recognized the necessity of both educational and denominational organization to ensure right teaching and strength through unity. Three key purposes for which Assemblies of God schools were vital included (1) training leaders for ministry, (2) perpetuating Assemblies of God beliefs and doctrine, and (3) forging community, unity, and commitment—conserving the effective work of these fervent Pentecostals (Burgess et al., 58).

As with the stated goal of “conserving the work” in calling for the first General Council, E. N. Bell also stated the need to establish “a general Bible Training School with a literary department for our people.” This demonstrated that the goal was not only to train ministers but also to provide a place for academic instruction.

Although undoubtedly it was their goal to create such a school in the future, the organizational and financial requirements for such an endeavor were too much for the grassroots movement to bear at such an early stage. Therefore, delegates at the first General Council recommended two existing schools that aligned with their doctrines—Neshoba Holiness School in Neshoba, Mississippi, which was comparable to today’s Christian schools for elementary through high school, and T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, which was a minister training program. These were just the first of many that would come and go with varying degrees of success and support as the Assemblies of God moved toward its goal of establishing effective schools of its own.

**Q:** Analyze how continuing education is important for ministry.

**A:** It enables the minister to enlarge his or her knowledge by receiving a variety of training (in missions work, prison ministry, industrial ministry, street witnessing, etc.), conserves the work of Pentecostals by forging community and maintains a focus on the Spirit’s leading in the future.

**Q:** Describe the methods used for training teachers, leaders, or laypeople in your church.

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** List resources your church can provide to teach, train, and disciple new believers.

**A:** Answers may include Sunday school, Bible studies, cell groups, and seminars.

#### 7.1.2 — Summarize two of E. N. Bell's reasons for organizing the AG, and explain how they relate to Sunday school and Assemblies of God schools of higher learning.

While studies have shown that the earliest leaders of the Pentecostal Movement actually had more education than average for that time, a stereotype persists that they were backward and unsophisticated (Burgess et al. 1988, 58). This may stem from their concerns that an over-emphasis on education would come at the expense of spiritual fervor. They believed that they were living in the last days, and the urgency of the task was so great that there was no time to waste sitting in classrooms. Likewise, the investment of money would be more effective in the sending of missionaries than the building of schools.

They were also intent on following New Testament practices. The early believers preached boldly and effectively, empowered by the Holy Spirit. Those who heard them speak were amazed that they were unschooled, ordinary men (Acts 4:13). Pentecostals recognized that education was of secondary importance to having been with Jesus and experiencing the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

Third, antibiblical modernism and liberal theology had infiltrated mainline churches through schools and seminaries , robbing them of their power, relevance, and ability to recognize or teach the truth. Pentecostals were determined to guard their own movement against a similar fate.

Despite these real concerns, forward-thinking founders of the Assemblies of God recognized the importance of education for training workers and perpetuating Pentecostal distinctives for the organization’s survival, success, and growth. This was clearly evidenced at the first General Council in Hot Springs, Arkansas (April, 1914).

Sunday School: Ensuring a Biblically Literate Fellowship

One of the main original reasons for calling for the organization of the Assemblies of God was this: “ We come together that we may know how to conserve the work, that we may build up and not tear down ” (Word and Witness, December 1913). From the beginning of the Assemblies of God, Sunday school was recognized as an important way to conserve the work, building upon the established foundation and passing on the full gospel message to future generations.

The Sunday school movement, begun in the late 1700s in England to teach reading and Christian morals to those who would otherwise have had no education, saw some of its greatest success in America. Much of the growth of the Methodist and Baptist churches in the 1800s was due to the training of laypeople to teach organized Sunday School classes, even in the remotest areas.

At the turn of the twentieth century, while many other churches were moving away from lay involvement and toward professional clergy and workers, the newly-formed Assemblies of God emphasized the Holy Spirit’s calling and gifting on every believer and did not follow this trend. In fact, as it became clear how effective Sunday school was at evangelizing the community, disciplining the converted, and instructing children and youth in matters of doctrine, Sunday school growth exploded in the 1930s, '40s, and '50s, until by 1967, the number of Sunday school enrollees was twice that of church members in the Assemblies of God (Menzies 1971, 271).

Recognizing the importance of Sunday school, Alice Reynolds Flower, the wife of the first General Secretary of the AG, published Sunday school lesson commentary in their weekly paper, The Christian Evangel (later The Pentecostal Evangel) , even before the Assemblies of God was formed. When their paper became the official publication of the Assemblies of God, this practice was continued.

By 1919, the General Council had approved the production of the AG’s first Sunday school curriculum, to be published through Gospel Publishing House, under the direction of J. Z. Kamerer. E. N. Bell, the first general superintendent, wrote the adult and intermediate age (youth) quarterlies, while Alice Flower wrote the quarterlies for juniors and primaries.

In 1921, the AG printed and distributed its first Sunday school take-home paper, Our Pentecostal Boys and Girls . By 1924, a complete line of Sunday school curriculum, written by Assemblies of God authors teaching the denomination’s distinctive beliefs and doctrines, was being produced. The total circulation of these quarterlies and papers had reached eight million by 1927 (Menzies 1971, 136).

In 1933, Ralph Riggs, pastor of Central Assembly in Springfield, Missouri, and future general superintendent, wrote the Pentecostal Movement’s first teacher training course, A Successful Sunday School (Burgess et al. 1988, 836).

Much of that early growth was due to the enthusiasm of a Sunday school teacher from Springfield, Missouri. Marcus Grable was a janitor at the Gospel Publishing House who started several Sunday schools in different parts of the city. With such explosive growth taking place in the young fellowship, Grable was often asked to respond to letters from churches asking for information or help about their own Sunday schools. He was given a desk and typewriter so that he could respond during his time at work. This eventually led, in 1935, to the establishment of the Sunday School Promotion Department, with Marcus Grable providing leadership.

In his fourteen years in office, Grable enthusiastically promoted Sunday school, earning the moniker, “Mr. Sunday School.” He focused on educating, training, and equipping teachers and superintendents, instituting training magazines ( Our Sunday School Counselor and Superintendent’s Assistant ). He travelled frequently to train teachers, eventually laying the foundation in the 1950s for the national Worker’s Training Program. He oversaw the golden age of annual Sunday school conventions, and under Grable’s leadership, AG Sunday schools expanded by 300 percent, leading all other church groups in growth (McGee 2014, 247).

Sunday school’s growth began to crest in the 1960s due to many factors, including declining birth rates, a proliferation of other AG ministries and programs that competed for attention, and the end of national conventions. Many districts continued holding their own conventions into the 1990s, and the strength of Sunday school varied across the fellowship, depending on the emphasis it received from leadership.

In 1984, a study by the Assemblies of God national Sunday school leadership in Springfield, Missouri outlined the dire consequences for churches when adults failed to attend Sunday school (Burgess 1988, 837). These adults:

Lacked basic Bible knowledge,

Were not committed to the church,

Did not embrace many beliefs of Pentecostal Christianity and the AG, and

Were less likely to volunteer in the church.

Additionally, when Sunday school did not receive support from adults, it affected the attendance and commitment of young people to the church.

Historically, no Christian education program has ever involved more people in consistent weekly Bible study than Sunday school (Burgess et al., 837). While the term Sunday school has often been replaced by trendier names— cell groups, life groups, discipleship tracts, Kid Zone, Xtreme , and so on—an intentional, systematic study of God’s Word presented at the level of the believer’s understanding is of vital importance for church growth and conserving the work—passing on Assemblies of God doctrines to subsequent generations.

Higher Education: Teaching and Training for Ministry

In spite of their wariness of the potential dangers of institutions, early Assemblies of God leaders recognized the necessity of both educational and denominational organization to ensure right teaching and strength through unity. Three key purposes for which Assemblies of God schools were vital included (1) training leaders for ministry, (2) perpetuating Assemblies of God beliefs and doctrine, and (3) forging community, unity, and commitment—conserving the effective work of these fervent Pentecostals (Burgess et al., 58).

As with the stated goal of “conserving the work” in calling for the first General Council, E. N. Bell also stated the need to establish “a general Bible Training School with a literary department for our people.” This demonstrated that the goal was not only to train ministers but also to provide a place for academic instruction.

Although undoubtedly it was their goal to create such a school in the future, the organizational and financial requirements for such an endeavor were too much for the grassroots movement to bear at such an early stage. Therefore, delegates at the first General Council recommended two existing schools that aligned with their doctrines—Neshoba Holiness School in Neshoba, Mississippi, which was comparable to today’s Christian schools for elementary through high school, and T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, which was a minister training program. These were just the first of many that would come and go with varying degrees of success and support as the Assemblies of God moved toward its goal of establishing effective schools of its own.

**Q:** Analyze how continuing education is important for ministry.

**A:** It enables the minister to enlarge his or her knowledge by receiving a variety of training (in missions work, prison ministry, industrial ministry, street witnessing, etc.), conserves the work of Pentecostals by forging community and maintains a focus on the Spirit’s leading in the future.

**Q:** Describe the methods used for training teachers, leaders, or laypeople in your church.

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** List resources your church can provide to teach, train, and disciple new believers.

**A:** Answers may include Sunday school, Bible studies, cell groups, and seminars.

### Classes and Courses of AG Schools

#### 7.2.1 — Explain the pros and cons of short-term Bible schools before and after the birth of the Assemblies of God.

Short-Term Schools. Some of the earliest Pentecostal schools were temporary ones, whether by design or because they lacked support or viability. Early leader Daniel (D. C. O.) Opperman’s schools were primary examples of deliberately short-term and mobile schools. Some characteristics and benefits of these schools included the following:

Schools lasted four to eight weeks, which was long enough to make lasting changes in students’ lives but not so long as to make it impossible for laymen and women to participate.

Their mobile nature made it possible for students in various regions to attend school who otherwise would have been unable to do so.

Their status as “faith schools” meant that anyone who wished could enroll, regardless of their ability to pay. Students, staff, and faculty prayed, worked, and trusted God to provide for their needs.

No one was excluded due to inadequate academic achievement. A high school diploma was not required. Emphasis was on spiritual development and preparation more than academics.

The schools were committed to discerning biblical truth with the illumination of the Holy Spirit. The Bible was the textbook, and the Holy Spirit was considered the foremost teacher.

Prayer was a primary activity, and revivals and the moves of the Spirit were expected, welcome, and common.

Students received practical, hands-on training in various types of ministry.Days were spent in Bible study along with practical work in prison ministry, industrial ministry, street witnessing, or door-to-door evangelism, and often concluded with an evangelistic service in the evening, followed by altar services that could last all night.

At the conclusion of such programs, students were often sent out in gospel bands—teams of fervent, newly trained workers—to evangelize new territory (Menzies 1971, 88–89).

In spite of the effectiveness of this intense type of school, their small size, limited faculty, and even their exhausting intensity limited their long-term viability.

Institutes. By 1921, the General Council had endorsed six Bible schools, including Pacific Bible and Missionary Training School (1919—later Bethany University) and Southern California Bible College (1920—later Vanguard University), but these schools were supported by their local districts and focused on training for their regions. In 1922, the Assemblies of God opened a national school in Springfield, Missouri, which would be owned and operated by the General Council. Central Bible Institute (CBI, Central Bible College after 1965) began in the basement of Central Assembly of God church with two classrooms and forty students. Local businessmen gave $5,000 to purchase fifteen acres in north Springfield, and in 1924, its first building was completed

These early institutes typically held a three-year program with the sole focus of the training of ministers and missionaries. Although they shared many common goals and concerns with the earlier short-term schools of Opperman and others, they had taken a step toward greater structure and permanence with permanent buildings and campuses.

As the schools were not accredited and had a very specific purpose, admission was not based on academic qualifications. Any Christian who wanted to study the Bible and was committed to ministry was likely to be accepted. Students were expected to live holy lives free from vice and sin. Daily attendance at chapel and prayer meetings were priorities, as was involvement in outside ministry. Many nearby out-station churches were pioneered or nurtured by Bible institute students as they received practical ministry experience as well as academic instruction.

The Bible was the primary textbook and its study the center of the curriculum, although courses in biblical languages, music, and applied courses in ministry, soulwinning, apologetics, and missions were typically included with great emphasis placed on spiritual development.

Teachers were successful evangelists, missionaries, or pastors. Few had college degrees or much formal training themselves. Their experience in the field and fervor for God were their main qualifications. Both students and their instructors learned to live by faith, many working jobs or pastoring churches alongside their teaching duties.

While many Bible institutes came and went, those that survived tended to have strong leaders. God used such leaders to shepherd their fledgling schools through periods of growth and into stability. These included W. I. Evans at CBI, P. C. Nelson at Southwestern Bible School (later Nelson University), Christine Gibson at Zion Bible Institute (later Northpoint Bible College), Alice Luce of Latin American Bible Institute (later LABI College), and Frank Lindquist of North Central Bible Institute (later North Central University).

The Bible Institutes of the Assemblies of God succeeded in the purpose envisioned for them. Their graduates pioneered the majority of AG churches in the USA and produced most of the missionaries that opened entire countries to the Assemblies of God. In contrast to the early years, when few AG ministers had been trained, by 1953, 60 percent of ordained AG ministers and 93 percent of missionaries had been trained in AG Bible schools (Menzies 1971, 355).

Colleges. World War II was an important turning point for Assemblies of God higher education. During the war, only Southern California Bible Institute had been able to prepare chaplains whose training would be accepted in the US military. In 1939, the school had expanded its curriculum, offering a fourth year and awarding a degree in Bible. This earned the school, now called Southern California College (SCC), recognition by the state of California as a degree-awarding institution (Menzies 1971, 359).

After World War II, the government paid for returning soldiers to get an education through the GI Bill. However, to qualify for GI loans, schools needed to meet certain standards. Recognizing the opportunity, Southwestern in 1946 and Northwest and CBI in 1947 followed SCC’s lead in expanding their curriculum and offering a four-year degree. While there was some concern about allowing an outside organization to set standards for Spirit-led schools, by 1951, all AG schools were accredited by the newly formed Accrediting Association of Bible Institutes and Bible Colleges at either the college or institute level (Menzies 1971, 357–358).

Accreditation required significant changes, starting with additional course offerings in the sciences and humanities. These changes also included higher standards for libraries, record keeping, and faculty education, bringing a new level of quality to Assemblies of God ministerial training (Burgess et al. 1988, 63).

The educational opportunities offered by the GI Bill and the increasing cultural demand for higher education led to greater percentages of AG young people seeking college degrees in their field of choice. However, students who attended secular colleges were exposed to the influences of modernism, liberal theology, and hostility to religion, especially to Pentecostalism. Many students who attended such colleges struggled to maintain their faith. As early as 1929, the General Council Committee on Bible Schools had considered establishing “academic schools of our faith in different parts of our country to provide education without contamination of worldly and antichristian influences” (“The General Council Minutes 1929”).

Therefore, greater attention was focused on providing training for the professions in an atmosphere that supported Christian students’ religious beliefs and cultural perspectives.

Most AG schools by this time were providing some level of professional and vocational training. A proposal was first considered in 1944, and in 1953, the General Council approved the launching of a national liberal arts college. On September 1, 1955, Evangel College (now Evangel University) became the first Pentecostal liberal arts college chartered in the United States (McGee 2014, 286).

The school’s property and first buildings were originally a wartime prison hospital, which was no longer needed by the government. Its fifty-nine acres and sixty-eight buildings were sold to the Assemblies of God for one dollar (365).

Universities. While colleges often focus solely on one area of study, such as Central Bible College, which is provided solely for the training of ministry students, well-established degree-conferring educational institutions with many branches of learning fall under the broader name “ universities ” – one unified school offering a diversity of programs. Beginning in 1993, many Assemblies of God colleges made this transition, with International Correspondence Institute being the first. Southwestern (now Nelson University) followed in 1994, and then Berean, Evangel, North Central, Vanguard, Northwest, and Southeastern Universities, and then the University of Valley Forge in 2014. They added graduate studies and masters-level programs to meet the growing demand of students for more advanced learning and qualifications for an ever-broadening range of professions and career choices.

A Seminary. In spite of advances in the educational quality of Assemblies of God Bible schools, colleges, and universities, ministerial students wanting a deeper understanding of theology, biblical languages, exegesis, or other religious subjects needed to look outside the fellowship for advanced training. Without a seminary of its own, the Assemblies of God’s leading thinkers, writers, and teachers were being trained by other denominations. Many of those institutions had decidedly more liberal theological perspectives that clashed with Assemblies of God’s doctrine and beliefs.

At the 1961 General Council in Portland, Oregon, a resolution was approved giving the Board of Education with the Executive Presbytery authority to establish a seminary (Menzies 1971, 367). There were some concerns expressed that the existence of a seminary would lead to rigid educational requirements for those wishing to be ordained ministers in the Assemblies of God. As in earlier generations, there was a fear that ministers could begin to lean on their education for success rather than dependence on the Holy Spirit. Resolutions were passed to safeguard against these concerns, and the school was called a graduate school rather than a seminary to further allay these worries.

On September 4, 1973, the Assemblies of God Graduate School opened on the top two floors of the distribution center of the Assemblies of God Headquarters. Its first master’s degrees were awarded in 1974. Its name was changed to Assemblies of God Theological Seminary (AGTS) in 1984 to better reflect its mission. AGTS moved to its current location next to Evangel University in July 1997 and awarded its first doctoral degrees in September of that year, with the first PhD program launching in 2009 (PhD in Intercultural Studies).

Consolidation. In 2013, the three General Council–owned schools in Springfield, Missouri—Central Bible College, Evangel University, and Assemblies of God Theological Seminary—were consolidated into one entity under the name Evangel University. As early as the 1960s, there had been discussion about consolidating Evangel and CBC. However, it was not until 2005 that the subject began to be studied officially, with AGTS included in the consideration (Wood 2011, 5).

In 2010, after much prayer and discussion, the Alliance for Higher Education, along with the highest leadership of the Assemblies of God, agreed upon the goal of consolidation and it was presented for approval at the 2011 General Council meeting. The reasons cited for consolidation included (1) ministerial preparation— they felt that the combined schools offered the strongest, best-integrated ministerial training program; (2) enrollment growth; (3) financial and organizational stewardship; and (4) twenty-first century challenges and opportunities.

The three institutions’ missions—providing training for ministry, liberal arts education from a Christian perspective, and advanced theological study—have continued with greater efficiency, integration of learning, and unwavering focus on Pentecostal empowerment for service in all vocations (McGee 2014, 517).

Distance Education/Online Learning. Correspondence schools that allowed students to study the Bible and prepare for ministry regardless of their location were part of the Assemblies of God from its inception. T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, one of two schools recommended at the first General Council in 1914, had a “Home Bible Study” course that allowed students to complete a study of the entire Bible in just one year (Book 2003, 28).

In 1947, the General Council Correspondence School was founded, which later became Berean School of the Bible (1958), Berean College (1985), and finally Berean University (1995). Meanwhile, the International Correspondence Institute (ICI) was envisioned by Dr. George M. Flattery as a distance-learning school that would evangelize, disciple, train, and award bachelor’s degrees to unreached people around the globe. Launched in Springfield, Missouri, in 1967, ICI moved to Brussels, Belgium, in 1972 and then to Irving, Texas, in 1991. In 2000, ICI returned to Springfield and merged with Berean University to form Global University.

Today, Global University is a premier distance-learning resource for pastors, evangelists, scholars, and students. It is an accredited institution that includes five schools under one umbrella:

The School for Evangelism and Discipleship offers entry-level education for new Christians and training for lay workers.

Berean School of the Bible is an adult continuing-education program that is a popular choice for many seeking credentials with the Assemblies of God.

School for Ministry Development offers many of the same courses as Berean at college level in a web-based format.

Undergraduate School of Bible and Theology offers associate of arts and bachelor degree programs.

Graduate School of Theology offers post-graduate degrees, including a doctor of ministry.

Since Global University’s beginning (in 1967 as ICI), more than 4.7 million people have documented a decision for Christ. In the first three years of the 2020s Global University was able to impact more than ten million people for Jesus as recorded by students, partners, and staff. From 2007–2017, Global University students had served and contributed to almost seventeen thousand new churches worldwide (Kozak 2017).

**Q:** Recount the impact Bible schools had on the Assemblies of God in the first half of the twentieth century.

**A:** Most of the new church plants (in the USA and worldwide) were started by Bible school graduates. By 1953, 60 percent of ordained ministers and 93 percent of missionaries were trained in AG Bible schools.

**Q:** Name two ways bi-vocational training benefits pastors today.

**A:** It provides a secondary source of income and serves as a point of contact with people in the community.

**Q:** State some benefits gained by AG colleges becoming universities.

**A:** The benefits encompassed: expansion of the schools’ branches of learning, including graduate degrees for continuing education; students better qualified for a broader range of ministry professions and career choices; and recognition brought on via the name changes. 8 CHAPTER
