The reasons cited for consolidation included (1) ministerial preparation— they felt that the combined schools offered the strongest, best-integrated ministerial training program; (2) enrollment growth; (3) financial and organizational stewardship; and (4) twenty-first century challenges and opportunities.

The three institutions’ missions—providing training for ministry, liberal arts education from a Christian perspective, and advanced theological study—have continued with greater efficiency, integration of learning, and unwavering focus on Pentecostal empowerment for service in all vocations (McGee 2014, 517).

Distance Education/Online Learning. Correspondence schools that allowed students to study the Bible and prepare for ministry regardless of their location were part of the Assemblies of God from its inception. T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, one of two schools recommended at the first General Council in 1914, had a “Home Bible Study” course that allowed students to complete a study of the entire Bible in just one year (Book 2003, 28).

In 1947, the General Council Correspondence School was founded, which later became Berean School of the Bible (1958), Berean College (1985), and finally Berean University (1995). Meanwhile, the International Correspondence Institute (ICI) was envisioned by Dr. George M. Flattery as a distance-learning school that would evangelize, disciple, train, and award bachelor’s degrees to unreached people around the globe. Launched in Springfield, Missouri, in 1967, ICI moved to Brussels, Belgium, in 1972 and then to Irving, Texas, in 1991. In 2000, ICI returned to Springfield and merged with Berean University to form Global University.

Today, Global University is a premier distance-learning resource for pastors, evangelists, scholars, and students. It is an accredited institution that includes five schools under one umbrella:

The School for Evangelism and Discipleship offers entry-level education for new Christians and training for lay workers.

Berean School of the Bible is an adult continuing-education program that is a popular choice for many seeking credentials with the Assemblies of God.

School for Ministry Development offers many of the same courses as Berean at college level in a web-based format.

Undergraduate School of Bible and Theology offers associate of arts and bachelor degree programs.

Graduate School of Theology offers post-graduate degrees, including a doctor of ministry.

Since Global University’s beginning (in 1967 as ICI), more than 4.7 million people have documented a decision for Christ. In the first three years of the 2020s Global University was able to impact more than ten million people for Jesus as recorded by students, partners, and staff. From 2007–2017, Global University students had served and contributed to almost seventeen thousand new churches worldwide (Kozak 2017).

**Q:** Recount the impact Bible schools had on the Assemblies of God in the first half of the twentieth century.

**A:** Most of the new church plants (in the USA and worldwide) were started by Bible school graduates. By 1953, 60 percent of ordained ministers and 93 percent of missionaries were trained in AG Bible schools.

**Q:** Name two ways bi-vocational training benefits pastors today.

**A:** It provides a secondary source of income and serves as a point of contact with people in the community.

**Q:** State some benefits gained by AG colleges becoming universities.

**A:** The benefits encompassed: expansion of the schools’ branches of learning, including graduate degrees for continuing education; students better qualified for a broader range of ministry professions and career choices; and recognition brought on via the name changes. 8 CHAPTER

#### 7.2.3 — Summarize the conditions and circumstances that spurred the change from institutes to colleges after World War II.

Short-Term Schools. Some of the earliest Pentecostal schools were temporary ones, whether by design or because they lacked support or viability. Early leader Daniel (D. C. O.) Opperman’s schools were primary examples of deliberately short-term and mobile schools. Some characteristics and benefits of these schools included the following:

Schools lasted four to eight weeks, which was long enough to make lasting changes in students’ lives but not so long as to make it impossible for laymen and women to participate.

Their mobile nature made it possible for students in various regions to attend school who otherwise would have been unable to do so.

Their status as “faith schools” meant that anyone who wished could enroll, regardless of their ability to pay. Students, staff, and faculty prayed, worked, and trusted God to provide for their needs.

No one was excluded due to inadequate academic achievement. A high school diploma was not required. Emphasis was on spiritual development and preparation more than academics.

The schools were committed to discerning biblical truth with the illumination of the Holy Spirit. The Bible was the textbook, and the Holy Spirit was considered the foremost teacher.

Prayer was a primary activity, and revivals and the moves of the Spirit were expected, welcome, and common.

Students received practical, hands-on training in various types of ministry.Days were spent in Bible study along with practical work in prison ministry, industrial ministry, street witnessing, or door-to-door evangelism, and often concluded with an evangelistic service in the evening, followed by altar services that could last all night.

At the conclusion of such programs, students were often sent out in gospel bands—teams of fervent, newly trained workers—to evangelize new territory (Menzies 1971, 88–89).

In spite of the effectiveness of this intense type of school, their small size, limited faculty, and even their exhausting intensity limited their long-term viability.

Institutes. By 1921, the General Council had endorsed six Bible schools, including Pacific Bible and Missionary Training School (1919—later Bethany University) and Southern California Bible College (1920—later Vanguard University), but these schools were supported by their local districts and focused on training for their regions. In 1922, the Assemblies of God opened a national school in Springfield, Missouri, which would be owned and operated by the General Council. Central Bible Institute (CBI, Central Bible College after 1965) began in the basement of Central Assembly of God church with two classrooms and forty students. Local businessmen gave $5,000 to purchase fifteen acres in north Springfield, and in 1924, its first building was completed

These early institutes typically held a three-year program with the sole focus of the training of ministers and missionaries. Although they shared many common goals and concerns with the earlier short-term schools of Opperman and others, they had taken a step toward greater structure and permanence with permanent buildings and campuses.

As the schools were not accredited and had a very specific purpose, admission was not based on academic qualifications. Any Christian who wanted to study the Bible and was committed to ministry was likely to be accepted. Students were expected to live holy lives free from vice and sin. Daily attendance at chapel and prayer meetings were priorities, as was involvement in outside ministry. Many nearby out-station churches were pioneered or nurtured by Bible institute students as they received practical ministry experience as well as academic instruction.

The Bible was the primary textbook and its study the center of the curriculum, although courses in biblical languages, music, and applied courses in ministry, soulwinning, apologetics, and missions were typically included with great emphasis placed on spiritual development.

Teachers were successful evangelists, missionaries, or pastors. Few had college degrees or much formal training themselves. Their experience in the field and fervor for God were their main qualifications. Both students and their instructors learned to live by faith, many working jobs or pastoring churches alongside their teaching duties.

While many Bible institutes came and went, those that survived tended to have strong leaders. God used such leaders to shepherd their fledgling schools through periods of growth and into stability. These included W. I. Evans at CBI, P. C. Nelson at Southwestern Bible School (later Nelson University), Christine Gibson at Zion Bible Institute (later Northpoint Bible College), Alice Luce of Latin American Bible Institute (later LABI College), and Frank Lindquist of North Central Bible Institute (later North Central University).

The Bible Institutes of the Assemblies of God succeeded in the purpose envisioned for them. Their graduates pioneered the majority of AG churches in the USA and produced most of the missionaries that opened entire countries to the Assemblies of God. In contrast to the early years, when few AG ministers had been trained, by 1953, 60 percent of ordained AG ministers and 93 percent of missionaries had been trained in AG Bible schools (Menzies 1971, 355).

Colleges. World War II was an important turning point for Assemblies of God higher education. During the war, only Southern California Bible Institute had been able to prepare chaplains whose training would be accepted in the US military. In 1939, the school had expanded its curriculum, offering a fourth year and awarding a degree in Bible. This earned the school, now called Southern California College (SCC), recognition by the state of California as a degree-awarding institution (Menzies 1971, 359).

After World War II, the government paid for returning soldiers to get an education through the GI Bill. However, to qualify for GI loans, schools needed to meet certain standards. Recognizing the opportunity, Southwestern in 1946 and Northwest and CBI in 1947 followed SCC’s lead in expanding their curriculum and offering a four-year degree. While there was some concern about allowing an outside organization to set standards for Spirit-led schools, by 1951, all AG schools were accredited by the newly formed Accrediting Association of Bible Institutes and Bible Colleges at either the college or institute level (Menzies 1971, 357–358).

Accreditation required significant changes, starting with additional course offerings in the sciences and humanities. These changes also included higher standards for libraries, record keeping, and faculty education, bringing a new level of quality to Assemblies of God ministerial training (Burgess et al. 1988, 63).

The educational opportunities offered by the GI Bill and the increasing cultural demand for higher education led to greater percentages of AG young people seeking college degrees in their field of choice. However, students who attended secular colleges were exposed to the influences of modernism, liberal theology, and hostility to religion, especially to Pentecostalism. Many students who attended such colleges struggled to maintain their faith. As early as 1929, the General Council Committee on Bible Schools had considered establishing “academic schools of our faith in different parts of our country to provide education without contamination of worldly and antichristian influences” (“The General Council Minutes 1929”).

Therefore, greater attention was focused on providing training for the professions in an atmosphere that supported Christian students’ religious beliefs and cultural perspectives.

Most AG schools by this time were providing some level of professional and vocational training. A proposal was first considered in 1944, and in 1953, the General Council approved the launching of a national liberal arts college. On September 1, 1955, Evangel College (now Evangel University) became the first Pentecostal liberal arts college chartered in the United States (McGee 2014, 286).

The school’s property and first buildings were originally a wartime prison hospital, which was no longer needed by the government. Its fifty-nine acres and sixty-eight buildings were sold to the Assemblies of God for one dollar (365).

Universities. While colleges often focus solely on one area of study, such as Central Bible College, which is provided solely for the training of ministry students, well-established degree-conferring educational institutions with many branches of learning fall under the broader name “ universities ” – one unified school offering a diversity of programs. Beginning in 1993, many Assemblies of God colleges made this transition, with International Correspondence Institute being the first. Southwestern (now Nelson University) followed in 1994, and then Berean, Evangel, North Central, Vanguard, Northwest, and Southeastern Universities, and then the University of Valley Forge in 2014. They added graduate studies and masters-level programs to meet the growing demand of students for more advanced learning and qualifications for an ever-broadening range of professions and career choices.

A Seminary. In spite of advances in the educational quality of Assemblies of God Bible schools, colleges, and universities, ministerial students wanting a deeper understanding of theology, biblical languages, exegesis, or other religious subjects needed to look outside the fellowship for advanced training. Without a seminary of its own, the Assemblies of God’s leading thinkers, writers, and teachers were being trained by other denominations. Many of those institutions had decidedly more liberal theological perspectives that clashed with Assemblies of God’s doctrine and beliefs.

At the 1961 General Council in Portland, Oregon, a resolution was approved giving the Board of Education with the Executive Presbytery authority to establish a seminary (Menzies 1971, 367). There were some concerns expressed that the existence of a seminary would lead to rigid educational requirements for those wishing to be ordained ministers in the Assemblies of God. As in earlier generations, there was a fear that ministers could begin to lean on their education for success rather than dependence on the Holy Spirit. Resolutions were passed to safeguard against these concerns, and the school was called a graduate school rather than a seminary to further allay these worries.

On September 4, 1973, the Assemblies of God Graduate School opened on the top two floors of the distribution center of the Assemblies of God Headquarters. Its first master’s degrees were awarded in 1974. Its name was changed to Assemblies of God Theological Seminary (AGTS) in 1984 to better reflect its mission. AGTS moved to its current location next to Evangel University in July 1997 and awarded its first doctoral degrees in September of that year, with the first PhD program launching in 2009 (PhD in Intercultural Studies).

Consolidation. In 2013, the three General Council–owned schools in Springfield, Missouri—Central Bible College, Evangel University, and Assemblies of God Theological Seminary—were consolidated into one entity under the name Evangel University. As early as the 1960s, there had been discussion about consolidating Evangel and CBC. However, it was not until 2005 that the subject began to be studied officially, with AGTS included in the consideration (Wood 2011, 5).

In 2010, after much prayer and discussion, the Alliance for Higher Education, along with the highest leadership of the Assemblies of God, agreed upon the goal of consolidation and it was presented for approval at the 2011 General Council meeting. The reasons cited for consolidation included (1) ministerial preparation— they felt that the combined schools offered the strongest, best-integrated ministerial training program; (2) enrollment growth; (3) financial and organizational stewardship; and (4) twenty-first century challenges and opportunities.

The three institutions’ missions—providing training for ministry, liberal arts education from a Christian perspective, and advanced theological study—have continued with greater efficiency, integration of learning, and unwavering focus on Pentecostal empowerment for service in all vocations (McGee 2014, 517).

Distance Education/Online Learning. Correspondence schools that allowed students to study the Bible and prepare for ministry regardless of their location were part of the Assemblies of God from its inception. T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, one of two schools recommended at the first General Council in 1914, had a “Home Bible Study” course that allowed students to complete a study of the entire Bible in just one year (Book 2003, 28).

In 1947, the General Council Correspondence School was founded, which later became Berean School of the Bible (1958), Berean College (1985), and finally Berean University (1995). Meanwhile, the International Correspondence Institute (ICI) was envisioned by Dr. George M. Flattery as a distance-learning school that would evangelize, disciple, train, and award bachelor’s degrees to unreached people around the globe. In 2000, ICI returned to Springfield and merged with Berean University to form Global University.

Today, Global University is a premier distance-learning resource for pastors, evangelists, scholars, and students. It is an accredited institution that includes five schools under one umbrella:

The School for Evangelism and Discipleship offers entry-level education for new Christians and training for lay workers.

Berean School of the Bible is an adult continuing-education program that is a popular choice for many seeking credentials with the Assemblies of God.

School for Ministry Development offers many of the same courses as Berean at college level in a web-based format.

Undergraduate School of Bible and Theology offers associate of arts and bachelor degree programs.

Graduate School of Theology offers post-graduate degrees, including a doctor of ministry.

Since Global University’s beginning (in 1967 as ICI), more than 4.7 million people have documented a decision for Christ. In the first three years of the 2020s Global University was able to impact more than ten million people for Jesus as recorded by students, partners, and staff. From 2007–2017, Global University students had served and contributed to almost seventeen thousand new churches worldwide (Kozak 2017).

**A:** Most of the new church plants (in the USA and worldwide) were started by Bible school graduates. By 1953, 60 percent of ordained ministers and 93 percent of missionaries were trained in AG Bible schools.

The Bible was the primary textbook and its study the center of the curriculum, although courses in biblical languages, music, and applied courses in ministry, soulwinning, apologetics, and missions were typically included with great emphasis placed on spiritual development.

Teachers were successful evangelists, missionaries, or pastors. Few had college degrees or much formal training themselves. Their experience in the field and fervor for God were their main qualifications. Both students and their instructors learned to live by faith, many working jobs or pastoring churches alongside their teaching duties.

While many Bible institutes came and went, those that survived tended to have strong leaders. God used such leaders to shepherd their fledgling schools through periods of growth and into stability. These included W. I. Evans at CBI, P. C. Nelson at Southwestern Bible School (later Nelson University), Christine Gibson at Zion Bible Institute (later Northpoint Bible College), Alice Luce of Latin American Bible Institute (later LABI College), and Frank Lindquist of North Central Bible Institute (later North Central University).

The Bible Institutes of the Assemblies of God succeeded in the purpose envisioned for them. Their graduates pioneered the majority of AG churches in the USA and produced most of the missionaries that opened entire countries to the Assemblies of God. In contrast to the early years, when few AG ministers had been trained, by 1953, 60 percent of ordained AG ministers and 93 percent of missionaries had been trained in AG Bible schools (Menzies 1971, 355).

Colleges. World War II was an important turning point for Assemblies of God higher education. During the war, only Southern California Bible Institute had been able to prepare chaplains whose training would be accepted in the US military. In 1939, the school had expanded its curriculum, offering a fourth year and awarding a degree in Bible. This earned the school, now called Southern California College (SCC), recognition by the state of California as a degree-awarding institution (Menzies 1971, 359).

After World War II, the government paid for returning soldiers to get an education through the GI Bill. However, to qualify for GI loans, schools needed to meet certain standards. Recognizing the opportunity, Southwestern in 1946 and Northwest and CBI in 1947 followed SCC’s lead in expanding their curriculum and offering a four-year degree. While there was some concern about allowing an outside organization to set standards for Spirit-led schools, by 1951, all AG schools were accredited by the newly formed Accrediting Association of Bible Institutes and Bible Colleges at either the college or institute level (Menzies 1971, 357–358).

Accreditation required significant changes, starting with additional course offerings in the sciences and humanities. These changes also included higher standards for libraries, record keeping, and faculty education, bringing a new level of quality to Assemblies of God ministerial training (Burgess et al. 1988, 63).

The educational opportunities offered by the GI Bill and the increasing cultural demand for higher education led to greater percentages of AG young people seeking college degrees in their field of choice. However, students who attended secular colleges were exposed to the influences of modernism, liberal theology, and hostility to religion, especially to Pentecostalism. Many students who attended such colleges struggled to maintain their faith. As early as 1929, the General Council Committee on Bible Schools had considered establishing “academic schools of our faith in different parts of our country to provide education without contamination of worldly and antichristian influences” (“The General Council Minutes 1929”).

Therefore, greater attention was focused on providing training for the professions in an atmosphere that supported Christian students’ religious beliefs and cultural perspectives.

Most AG schools by this time were providing some level of professional and vocational training. A proposal was first considered in 1944, and in 1953, the General Council approved the launching of a national liberal arts college. On September 1, 1955, Evangel College (now Evangel University) became the first Pentecostal liberal arts college chartered in the United States (McGee 2014, 286).

The school’s property and first buildings were originally a wartime prison hospital, which was no longer needed by the government. Its fifty-nine acres and sixty-eight buildings were sold to the Assemblies of God for one dollar (365).

Universities. While colleges often focus solely on one area of study, such as Central Bible College, which is provided solely for the training of ministry students, well-established degree-conferring educational institutions with many branches of learning fall under the broader name “ universities ” – one unified school offering a diversity of programs. Beginning in 1993, many Assemblies of God colleges made this transition, with International Correspondence Institute being the first. Southwestern (now Nelson University) followed in 1994, and then Berean, Evangel, North Central, Vanguard, Northwest, and Southeastern Universities, and then the University of Valley Forge in 2014. They added graduate studies and masters-level programs to meet the growing demand of students for more advanced learning and qualifications for an ever-broadening range of professions and career choices.

A Seminary. In spite of advances in the educational quality of Assemblies of God Bible schools, colleges, and universities, ministerial students wanting a deeper understanding of theology, biblical languages, exegesis, or other religious subjects needed to look outside the fellowship for advanced training. Without a seminary of its own, the Assemblies of God’s leading thinkers, writers, and teachers were being trained by other denominations. Many of those institutions had decidedly more liberal theological perspectives that clashed with Assemblies of God’s doctrine and beliefs.

At the 1961 General Council in Portland, Oregon, a resolution was approved giving the Board of Education with the Executive Presbytery authority to establish a seminary (Menzies 1971, 367). There were some concerns expressed that the existence of a seminary would lead to rigid educational requirements for those wishing to be ordained ministers in the Assemblies of God. As in earlier generations, there was a fear that ministers could begin to lean on their education for success rather than dependence on the Holy Spirit. Resolutions were passed to safeguard against these concerns, and the school was called a graduate school rather than a seminary to further allay these worries.

On September 4, 1973, the Assemblies of God Graduate School opened on the top two floors of the distribution center of the Assemblies of God Headquarters. Its first master’s degrees were awarded in 1974. Its name was changed to Assemblies of God Theological Seminary (AGTS) in 1984 to better reflect its mission. AGTS moved to its current location next to Evangel University in July 1997 and awarded its first doctoral degrees in September of that year, with the first PhD program launching in 2009 (PhD in Intercultural Studies).

Consolidation. In 2013, the three General Council–owned schools in Springfield, Missouri—Central Bible College, Evangel University, and Assemblies of God Theological Seminary—were consolidated into one entity under the name Evangel University. As early as the 1960s, there had been discussion about consolidating Evangel and CBC. However, it was not until 2005 that the subject began to be studied officially, with AGTS included in the consideration (Wood 2011, 5).

In 2010, after much prayer and discussion, the Alliance for Higher Education, along with the highest leadership of the Assemblies of God, agreed upon the goal of consolidation and it was presented for approval at the 2011 General Council meeting. The reasons cited for consolidation included (1) ministerial preparation— they felt that the combined schools offered the strongest, best-integrated ministerial training program; (2) enrollment growth; (3) financial and organizational stewardship; and (4) twenty-first century challenges and opportunities.

The three institutions’ missions—providing training for ministry, liberal arts education from a Christian perspective, and advanced theological study—have continued with greater efficiency, integration of learning, and unwavering focus on Pentecostal empowerment for service in all vocations (McGee 2014, 517).

Distance Education/Online Learning. Correspondence schools that allowed students to study the Bible and prepare for ministry regardless of their location were part of the Assemblies of God from its inception. T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, one of two schools recommended at the first General Council in 1914, had a “Home Bible Study” course that allowed students to complete a study of the entire Bible in just one year (Book 2003, 28).

In 1947, the General Council Correspondence School was founded, which later became Berean School of the Bible (1958), Berean College (1985), and finally Berean University (1995). Meanwhile, the International Correspondence Institute (ICI) was envisioned by Dr. George M. Flattery as a distance-learning school that would evangelize, disciple, train, and award bachelor’s degrees to unreached people around the globe. Launched in Springfield, Missouri, in 1967, ICI moved to Brussels, Belgium, in 1972 and then to Irving, Texas, in 1991. In 2000, ICI returned to Springfield and merged with Berean University to form Global University.

Today, Global University is a premier distance-learning resource for pastors, evangelists, scholars, and students. It is an accredited institution that includes five schools under one umbrella:

The School for Evangelism and Discipleship offers entry-level education for new Christians and training for lay workers.

Berean School of the Bible is an adult continuing-education program that is a popular choice for many seeking credentials with the Assemblies of God.

School for Ministry Development offers many of the same courses as Berean at college level in a web-based format.

Undergraduate School of Bible and Theology offers associate of arts and bachelor degree programs.

Graduate School of Theology offers post-graduate degrees, including a doctor of ministry.

Since Global University’s beginning (in 1967 as ICI), more than 4.7 million people have documented a decision for Christ. In the first three years of the 2020s Global University was able to impact more than ten million people for Jesus as recorded by students, partners, and staff. From 2007–2017, Global University students had served and contributed to almost seventeen thousand new churches worldwide (Kozak 2017).

**Q:** Recount the impact Bible schools had on the Assemblies of God in the first half of the twentieth century.

**A:** Most of the new church plants (in the USA and worldwide) were started by Bible school graduates. By 1953, 60 percent of ordained ministers and 93 percent of missionaries were trained in AG Bible schools.

**Q:** Name two ways bi-vocational training benefits pastors today.

**A:** It provides a secondary source of income and serves as a point of contact with people in the community.

**Q:** State some benefits gained by AG colleges becoming universities.

**A:** The benefits encompassed: expansion of the schools’ branches of learning, including graduate degrees for continuing education; students better qualified for a broader range of ministry professions and career choices; and recognition brought on via the name changes. 8 CHAPTER

#### 7.2.6 — Explain the reasons given for consolidating CBC, Evangel, and AGTS as Evangel University.

Short-Term Schools. Some of the earliest Pentecostal schools were temporary ones, whether by design or because they lacked support or viability. Early leader Daniel (D. C. O.) Opperman’s schools were primary examples of deliberately short-term and mobile schools. Some characteristics and benefits of these schools included the following:

Schools lasted four to eight weeks, which was long enough to make lasting changes in students’ lives but not so long as to make it impossible for laymen and women to participate.

Their mobile nature made it possible for students in various regions to attend school who otherwise would have been unable to do so.

Their status as “faith schools” meant that anyone who wished could enroll, regardless of their ability to pay. Students, staff, and faculty prayed, worked, and trusted God to provide for their needs.

No one was excluded due to inadequate academic achievement. A high school diploma was not required. Emphasis was on spiritual development and preparation more than academics.

The schools were committed to discerning biblical truth with the illumination of the Holy Spirit. The Bible was the textbook, and the Holy Spirit was considered the foremost teacher.

Prayer was a primary activity, and revivals and the moves of the Spirit were expected, welcome, and common.

Students received practical, hands-on training in various types of ministry.Days were spent in Bible study along with practical work in prison ministry, industrial ministry, street witnessing, or door-to-door evangelism, and often concluded with an evangelistic service in the evening, followed by altar services that could last all night.

At the conclusion of such programs, students were often sent out in gospel bands—teams of fervent, newly trained workers—to evangelize new territory (Menzies 1971, 88–89).

In spite of the effectiveness of this intense type of school, their small size, limited faculty, and even their exhausting intensity limited their long-term viability.

By 1921, the General Council had endorsed six Bible schools, including Pacific Bible and Missionary Training School (1919—later Bethany University) and Southern California Bible College (1920—later Vanguard University), but these schools were supported by their local districts and focused on training for their regions. The reasons cited for consolidation included (1) ministerial preparation— they felt that the combined schools offered the strongest, best-integrated ministerial training program; (2) enrollment growth; (3) financial and organizational stewardship; and (4) twenty-first century challenges and opportunities.

The three institutions’ missions—providing training for ministry, liberal arts education from a Christian perspective, and advanced theological study—have continued with greater efficiency, integration of learning, and unwavering focus on Pentecostal empowerment for service in all vocations (McGee 2014, 517).

Distance Education/Online Learning. Correspondence schools that allowed students to study the Bible and prepare for ministry regardless of their location were part of the Assemblies of God from its inception. T. K. Leonard’s Gospel School in Findlay, Ohio, one of two schools recommended at the first General Council in 1914, had a “Home Bible Study” course that allowed students to complete a study of the entire Bible in just one year (Book 2003, 28).

In 1947, the General Council Correspondence School was founded, which later became Berean School of the Bible (1958), Berean College (1985), and finally Berean University (1995). Meanwhile, the International Correspondence Institute (ICI) was envisioned by Dr. George M. Flattery as a distance-learning school that would evangelize, disciple, train, and award bachelor’s degrees to unreached people around the globe. Launched in Springfield, Missouri, in 1967, ICI moved to Brussels, Belgium, in 1972 and then to Irving, Texas, in 1991. In 2000, ICI returned to Springfield and merged with Berean University to form Global University.

Today, Global University is a premier distance-learning resource for pastors, evangelists, scholars, and students. It is an accredited institution that includes five schools under one umbrella:

The School for Evangelism and Discipleship offers entry-level education for new Christians and training for lay workers.

Berean School of the Bible is an adult continuing-education program that is a popular choice for many seeking credentials with the Assemblies of God.

School for Ministry Development offers many of the same courses as Berean at college level in a web-based format.

Undergraduate School of Bible and Theology offers associate of arts and bachelor degree programs.

Graduate School of Theology offers post-graduate degrees, including a doctor of ministry.

Since Global University’s beginning (in 1967 as ICI), more than 4.7 million people have documented a decision for Christ. In the first three years of the 2020s Global University was able to impact more than ten million people for Jesus as recorded by students, partners, and staff. From 2007–2017, Global University students had served and contributed to almost seventeen thousand new churches worldwide (Kozak 2017).

**Q:** Recount the impact Bible schools had on the Assemblies of God in the first half of the twentieth century.

**A:** Most of the new church plants (in the USA and worldwide) were started by Bible school graduates. By 1953, 60 percent of ordained ministers and 93 percent of missionaries were trained in AG Bible schools.

**Q:** Name two ways bi-vocational training benefits pastors today.

**A:** It provides a secondary source of income and serves as a point of contact with people in the community.

**Q:** State some benefits gained by AG colleges becoming universities.

**A:** The benefits encompassed: expansion of the schools’ branches of learning, including graduate degrees for continuing education; students better qualified for a broader range of ministry professions and career choices; and recognition brought on via the name changes. 8 CHAPTER

### The Path for the Future

#### 7.3.1 — Outline the original goal of AG higher education, and explain how schools have adapted to fulfill those goals in our changing times.

Several factors, such as declining birth rates, rising costs of a college education, and increasing pressure from accreditation agencies and government to conform to shifting cultural norms that conflict with biblical teaching, are bringing uncertainty regarding the future of AG schools and colleges. However, the schools remain committed to their original goal of training workers to evangelize and win the world, the nation, and the college campus for Christ.

Dr. John Davidson, former director of the Alliance for AG Higher Education and director of CMN (Church Multiplication Network) Discovery and Development, summed it up this way in 2018:

The Assemblies of God has been shaped by higher education. The original call to Hot Springs, Arkansas, that resulted in the formation of the AG listed five reasons why ministers and laymen should gather to discuss how Pentecostal churches could best collaborate. One of those reasons was to discuss the potential of starting a Bible training school. From that day until now, the AG has prioritized the training of ministers and missionaries, and more recently, of marketplace ministers as well.

Due to cultural, educational, and financial factors, AG schools today are offering an ever-wider array of majors in professional disciplines such as business, education, social work, medicine, and more. The availability of online education and an increasing selection of graduate degrees make these schools both widely accessible and deeply helpful. The common thread that continues to make Assemblies of God institutions of higher learning unique in the vast landscape of education is their unwavering commitment to the integration of faith and learning. (John Davidson, e-mail message to the author, June 24, 2018).

## 8

### God’s Servants: Men and Women Alike

#### 8.1.1 — Give examples of women God used in leadership in the New Testament and in the young Assemblies of God.

In the early days of the Pentecostal revival, as in the days following the first Pentecost as recorded in Acts, the Holy Spirit was poured out upon and chose to work through women. Women taught, like Priscilla (Acts 18:24–26, Romans 16:3–4; 1 Corinthians 16:19); prophesied, like Philip’s daughters (Acts 21:8–9); started benevolence programs, like Dorcas (Acts 9:36); labored in ministry, like Euodia and Syntyche (Philippians 4:2–3) and Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis (Romans 16:6,12); and were church leaders, ministers, or even apostles like Phoebe (Romans 16:1–2) and Junia (Romans 16:7).

The first person to be baptized in the Holy Spirit in the 1900s, the spark that ignited the Pentecostal revival, was a woman: Agnes Ozman. Half of the elders at the Azusa Street Mission were women (Wood 2018). A year before the Assemblies of God was founded and five years before it moved its headquarters to Springfield, Missouri, Rachel Sizelove, who had been instrumental in bringing the Pentecostal message to Springfield six years earlier, had a prophetic vision. She saw a “beautiful, bubbling, sparkling fountain” in the heart of Springfield and flowing in all directions “until the whole land was deluged with living water” (Gohr and Rodgers 2017–2018, 7). Through the 1930s, two-thirds of AG missionaries and twenty percent of AG pastors were women (McGee 2014, 188). These Pentecostal people saw this as a continuing fulfillment of the prophecy of Joel 2:28-30 on the Day of Pentecost and continuing in the Pentecostal ministry of their day.

In the beginning, the Pentecostal Movement valued women and validated their ministry. However, women’s involvement in the Assemblies of God has also been subject to many changes and growing pains and has been the topic of much disagreement and tension.

**Q:** Make a list of men and women who have influenced your spiritual formation.

**A:** Answers will vary.

**Q:** Describe the role women have in your local assembly.

**A:** Answers will vary.

### Historical Tensions: Opportunities and Opposition

#### 8.2.1 — Summarize four key reasons for early opportunities for women in ministry and leadership in the Assemblies of God.

Opportunities

Along with their understanding that the Scriptures prophesied a last days outpouring of the Spirit that would include the ministry of women, there are four key reasons for the early leadership opportunities for women in the Assemblies of God:

Holiness Influence . As noted earlier in this text, many of those who became part of the Pentecostal Movement had come from the Holiness Movement of the previous century. Holiness was coupled with the idea of social reform; therefore, its people eagerly fought for human rights, an end to inequality, and equal justice for all. Its central text was Galatians 3:28: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” In America, during the 1800s, Holiness men and women were leading abolitionists and advocates of women’s suffrage , and some, such as the Church of God (Anderson, Indiana) and the Church of the Nazarene ordained women pastors.

Therefore, many Holiness women who experienced Pentecost and came to the AG had already established themselves in preaching, teaching, evangelism, missions, and a host of other ministry roles. Holiness men were largely accustomed to and generally more accepting of women taking an active role in ministry.

Restorationism/Revival . Holiness was a Restorationist movement whose goal was to return to the pre-fallen state through the transforming grace of God through sanctification. Its members believed the subordination of women was not part of God’s creation but part of the curse brought by the Fall. Therefore, the church— and women—were not bound by this curse but were redeemed and restored to equality.

During times of revival, women commonly enjoy more freedom (Burgess et al. 1988, 898), as the overflow of enthusiasm and the moving of the Spirit is too expansive and widespread to limit.

Ministry as a Calling/Passion . In the early 1900s, when believers were baptized in the Holy Spirit, they immediately felt called to share their experience and the gospel with others. During the early days of the Pentecostal revival, few could dispute that the Holy Spirit was empowering women for all aspects of ministry, as was promised in Joel 2. In this atmosphere, women’s calling and giftings were sufficient grounds for their effective ministry.

Expediency . Pentecostals felt the urgency of the harvest (John 4:35). The coming of the Lord was near, but first, the gospel of Christ had to be preached to the whole world (Matthew 24:14). More workers were needed to complete the task (Luke 10:2). Every believer shares the responsibility to reach the lost for Christ. Eliminating half of the potential workforce would have been a foolish act of disobedience and poor stewardship.

Opposition

In spite of the reasons for opportunities for women previously mentioned, other forces worked to limit their participation.

Fundamentalist Influence . Perhaps second only to the positive influence of the Holiness Movement on the formation of the Assemblies of God was that of Fundamentalism. While Fundamentalists happily encouraged women to serve in some ministry capacities, they resisted leadership opportunities for women. This is influenced by their complementarian view of men and women, which is explained in Lesson 8.3.

While the majority of early Pentecostals and their leaders came from Holiness backgrounds, some came from Fundamentalist traditions. E. N. Bell, the first elected leader of the Assemblies of God, was one of these—a graduate of the Southern Baptist Seminary in Louisville (Menzies 1971, 89). Although the first General Council in 1914 authorized the ordination of women as evangelists and missionaries, it excluded them from voting and being ordained as pastors. The first woman credentialed by the Assemblies of God was reported to be Dollie Drain Simms, an evangelist and future church planter who was ordained at age 15 on the last day of the first General Council in Hot Springs, Arkansas (Gohr 2004, 16).

The Status Quo . For centuries, the default position in the church world, as well as the world at large, was for women to be excluded from positions of prestige, authority, and public speaking. Although Pentecostals understood that God was doing something exciting outside the old norms, not everyone agreed about where the new boundary lines should be drawn.

Ministry as a Profession . In the early years, much of the Pentecostal ministry had few professional requirements and little compensation. All that was required was a call of God and the dedication to work through difficult circumstances for the Kingdom of God. However, over time, Pentecostals became more accepted and prominent in the church world. Ministry gradually brought more prestige and better pay, especially for those with education and training. While this brought more acceptance for Pentecostals from the fundamental churches, it also became less likely that women were considered for ministry positions within churches.

Cultural Backlash . When the Assemblies of God was formed in 1914, women were not yet permitted to vote in American politics. In 1920, the nineteenth Amendment to the US Constitution granted women’s suffrage. The 1920s also saw a change in women’s fashions and involvement in activities that Holiness churches believed to be sinful, such as smoking, drinking alcohol, and dancing. There was considerable pushback against these trends, and women were urged to hold instead to the old standards of modest dress and sexual prudence.

During World War II, many women stepped into the jobs that men had to leave when they went to war. When these soldiers returned, there was a renewed emphasis on the role of men in the workplace and women in the home. Also, as more families were moving into cities and leaving agricultural life—where women’s work was vital to the success of the farm - there was more emphasis on the idea of a working father and stay-at-home mother. These cultural emphases greatly influenced the view of Pentecostals about the role women should play, not only in the home but in the church. This view was especially cemented in the 1960s as a backlash against excesses in the American feminist movement. Unfortunately, it was hard for some Christians to separate offensive behaviors from the concept of greater standing and opportunities for women.

Even through these shifting times, the Assemblies of God maintained its position that it was Scriptural principles of inclusion for all Spirit-filled men and women, rather than cultural trends, that must guide the practice of the church.

**Q:** What aspects of the Holiness Movement should we continue to pursue in today’s age?

**A:** Answers can include: working towards equality, human rights, and equal justice for all.

**Q:** Explain how the call of God is an integral aspect of Christian service.

**A:** It gives a strong source of motivation and a passion to serve.

**Q:** Name some gender biases that are still prevalent today and can prevent women from advancing into ministry or leadership positions.

**A:** Answers may include: women are nurturers and should be working in the home or in the nurseries, children’s ministries, and women’s ministries in churches; gender prejudice (the idea that men can do a better job); women only need to fill in where no man is available.

**Q:** What sacrifices did women in ministry make in the early days of the Assemblies of God?

**A:** They worked long hours in ministry with little to no recognition and often with a lack of finances, education, and material goods.

**Q:** List some Scripture verses that promote gender equality.

**A:** These may include: Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28; 1 Corinthians 11:11

### Developing an Understanding of the Bible’s Teaching on Women in Ministry

#### 8.3.1 — Contrast the complementarian and egalitarian views of the Bible's teaching on women in ministry.

From the beginning, the Assemblies of God has pledged its firm commitment to looking to God’s Word as the guiding authority on theology and practice. If all are sincerely committed to this principle, why has there been such disagreement regarding women’s roles in ministry?

Although multiple Bible passages validate women’s participation in ministry philosophically ([especially, and practically] many examples of women in leadership exist in both the Old and New Testament), others seem to limit their involvement. How can these verses be reconciled? What does the Bible really say about women’s roles in ministry, and why have sincere students of God’s Word reached such different conclusions? Let us briefly examine the two predominant views that influence the interpretation of these particular passages.

The Complementarian View: Biblical Manhood and Womanhood

Complementarianism teaches that while God created men and women equal in dignity and standing with God, they have distinct roles in the home and church. Although it acknowledges God’s gifting of women for certain ministry capacities, it holds that only men are to act in most roles of teaching and leadership, specifically in leadership over men. Complementarians also typically hold a patriarchal perspective of the family structure, with the husband as the head to whose authority the wife should submit.

The Egalitarian View: Biblical Equality

The egalitarian view teaches that God created men and women equal in all things. While it acknowledges that men and women are distinct from each other, it rejects the idea that this difference means that women are disqualified from any leadership or ministry roles in the church. Egalitarians also believe that spouses are to be equally responsible for the family, and that marriage is a partnership of two equals submitting to each other.

The Lens of Pentecostal Experience

Using the Jerusalem Council, where the decision was made to include Gentiles in the church on equal footing with Jews as a pattern for New Testament Christians, General Superintendent George O. Wood clarified how we should resolve issues when Bible passages seem to contradict each other:

Since the Scriptures cannot be broken (set against each other), it became the task of the Jerusalem church—and it is ours today as well on other matters—to harmoniously resolve texts that appear to be contrarily engaging each other.

The “much discussion” of Acts 15:7 dealt first with the question, What does the text of Scripture say? The Judaizers answered one way; Paul and Barnabas answered in another way. How do you affirm truth when believers are throwing texts at each other?

Here is where the Jerusalem Council has a most important lesson for us: We must listen to the experience of seasoned leadership who give testimony to being guided by the Holy Spirit.

Following the textual debate, Peter stood and recounted his testimony of years earlier with Cornelius at Caesarea. His clinching line is, “God, who knows the heart showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us” (verse 8). Peter quoted no Scripture; he simply restated his experience.

Then Paul and Barnabas stepped to the microphone. They too spoke of their experience. “The whole assembly became silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul telling about the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them” (verse 12).

The Judaizers have no testimony to share. Their arguments are based solely on proof texts, and they completely ignore what the Spirit has done.

James, presiding at the Council, drew a conclusion supported by those assembled. He affirmed the testimony of Gentile inclusion and attested it by reference to key texts from Amos 9:11–12 and Isaiah 45:21, pointing to the ingathering of the nations and God’s eternal plan for such (Acts 15:16–18). (Wood 2018)

Thousands of women have attested to a clear calling to ministry. They have been empowered and their ministries blessed by the Holy Spirit. These truths must be fully considered when we look to God’s Word regarding the ministry of women.

Interactive Question #9 : Recall biblical leaders who were women and what their ministries were.

The Assemblies of God Position

At the request of many church members and leaders, the Assemblies of God published a paper in 1990 outlining its official position on the matter. After a deep exposition of the various Bible passages related to women in ministry, the updated 2010 version concluded:

We cannot find convincing evidence that the ministry of women is restricted according to some sacred or immutable principle.

We are aware that the ministry and leadership of women are not accepted by some individuals, both within and outside the Christian community. We condemn all prejudice and self-promotion by men or women. The existence of bigotry against women in our world, and all too often in the church, cannot be denied. But there is no place for such an attitude in the body of Christ. We acknowledge that attitudes of secular society, based on long-standing practice and tradition, have influenced the application of biblical principles to local circumstances. We desire wisely to respect yet help redeem cultures that are at variance with Kingdom principles. Like Paul, we affirm that the Great Commission takes priority over every other consideration. (General Council 2010)

George P. Wood, executive editor of Assemblies of God Publications and coordinator of Religious Freedom Initiatives, wrote an important series of articles comparing the complementarian and egalitarian views called “What Paul Really Says About Women in Ministry.” He concluded: “In all the New Testament, the passages most commonly cited as affirmative answers to this question [Does the New Testament limit the ministries women can perform in the church?]. The first addresses how women minister in the church, not whether they can minister. The second addresses how women should learn in the church, not whether they can teach. And the third prohibits assuming or usurping the authority to teach, not teaching per se” (Wood 2017).

**Q:** Evaluate ways you can be an agent of change in helping women advance in ministry and leadership.

**A:** Answers will vary, but may include: validating women who are called to ministry by helping them obtain their credentials and placing them in ministry positions in your church, making sure that your church board contains women as well as men and engaging their participation, encouraging and supporting them in pursuing ministerial training or education, and voting for qualified women to leadership positions in the district and national levels.

**A:** Answers will vary, but may include: validating women who are called to ministry by helping them obtain their credentials and placing them in ministry positions in your church, making sure that your church board contains women as well as men and engaging their participation, encouraging and supporting them in pursuing ministerial training or education, and voting for qualified women to leadership positions in the district and national levels.

#### 8.3.3 — Describe the Assemblies of God's official position on women in ministry in the context of complementarian and egalitarian views.

From the beginning, the Assemblies of God has pledged its firm commitment to looking to God’s Word as the guiding authority on theology and practice. If all are sincerely committed to this principle, why has there been such disagreement regarding women’s roles in ministry?

Although multiple Bible passages validate women’s participation in ministry philosophically ([especially, and practically] many examples of women in leadership exist in both the Old and New Testament), others seem to limit their involvement. How can these verses be reconciled? What does the Bible really say about women’s roles in ministry, and why have sincere students of God’s Word reached such different conclusions? Let us briefly examine the two predominant views that influence the interpretation of these particular passages.

The Complementarian View: Biblical Manhood and Womanhood

Complementarianism teaches that while God created men and women equal in dignity and standing with God, they have distinct roles in the home and church. Although it acknowledges God’s gifting of women for certain ministry capacities, it holds that only men are to act in most roles of teaching and leadership, specifically in leadership over men. Complementarians also typically hold a patriarchal perspective of the family structure, with the husband as the head to whose authority the wife should submit.

The Egalitarian View: Biblical Equality

The egalitarian view teaches that God created men and women equal in all things. While it acknowledges that men and women are distinct from each other, it rejects the idea that this difference means that women are disqualified from any leadership or ministry roles in the church. Egalitarians also believe that spouses are to be equally responsible for the family, and that marriage is a partnership of two equals submitting to each other.

The Lens of Pentecostal Experience

Using the Jerusalem Council, where the decision was made to include Gentiles in the church on equal footing with Jews as a pattern for New Testament Christians, General Superintendent George O. Wood clarified how we should resolve issues when Bible passages seem to contradict each other:

Since the Scriptures cannot be broken (set against each other), it became the task of the Jerusalem church—and it is ours today as well on other matters—to harmoniously resolve texts that appear to be contrarily engaging each other.

The “much discussion” of Acts 15:7 dealt first with the question, What does the text of Scripture say? The Judaizers answered one way; Paul and Barnabas answered in another way. How do you affirm truth when believers are throwing texts at each other?

Here is where the Jerusalem Council has a most important lesson for us: We must listen to the experience of seasoned leadership who give testimony to being guided by the Holy Spirit.

Following the textual debate, Peter stood and recounted his testimony of years earlier with Cornelius at Caesarea. His clinching line is, “God, who knows the heart showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us” (verse 8). Peter quoted no Scripture; he simply restated his experience.

Then Paul and Barnabas stepped to the microphone. They too spoke of their experience. “The whole assembly became silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul telling about the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them” (verse 12).

The Judaizers have no testimony to share. Their arguments are based solely on proof texts, and they completely ignore what the Spirit has done.

James, presiding at the Council, drew a conclusion supported by those assembled. He affirmed the testimony of Gentile inclusion and attested it by reference to key texts from Amos 9:11–12 and Isaiah 45:21, pointing to the ingathering of the nations and God’s eternal plan for such (Acts 15:16–18). (Wood 2018)

Thousands of women have attested to a clear calling to ministry. They have been empowered and their ministries blessed by the Holy Spirit. These truths must be fully considered when we look to God’s Word regarding the ministry of women.

Interactive Question #9 : Recall biblical leaders who were women and what their ministries were.

The Assemblies of God Position

At the request of many church members and leaders, the Assemblies of God published a paper in 1990 outlining its official position on the matter. After a deep exposition of the various Bible passages related to women in ministry, the updated 2010 version concluded:

We cannot find convincing evidence that the ministry of women is restricted according to some sacred or immutable principle.

We are aware that the ministry and leadership of women are not accepted by some individuals, both within and outside the Christian community. We condemn all prejudice and self-promotion by men or women. The existence of bigotry against women in our world, and all too often in the church, cannot be denied. But there is no place for such an attitude in the body of Christ. We acknowledge that attitudes of secular society, based on long-standing practice and tradition, have influenced the application of biblical principles to local circumstances. We desire wisely to respect yet help redeem cultures that are at variance with Kingdom principles. Like Paul, we affirm that the Great Commission takes priority over every other consideration. (General Council 2010)

George P. Wood, executive editor of Assemblies of God Publications and coordinator of Religious Freedom Initiatives, wrote an important series of articles comparing the complementarian and egalitarian views called “What Paul Really Says About Women in Ministry.” He concluded: “In all the New Testament, the passages most commonly cited as affirmative answers to this question [Does the New Testament limit the ministries women can perform in the church?]. The first addresses how women minister in the church, not whether they can minister. The second addresses how women should learn in the church, not whether they can teach. And the third prohibits assuming or usurping the authority to teach, not teaching per se” (Wood 2017).

**Q:** Evaluate ways you can be an agent of change in helping women advance in ministry and leadership.

**A:** Answers will vary, but may include: validating women who are called to ministry by helping them obtain their credentials and placing them in ministry positions in your church, making sure that your church board contains women as well as men and engaging their participation, encouraging and supporting them in pursuing ministerial training or education, and voting for qualified women to leadership positions in the district and national levels.

### Service with Distinction: Past and Present

#### 8.4.1 — Cite one example of a woman who served with distinction in each of these five categories: missionaries, evangelists, pastors and church planters, writers and editors, and leaders and trailblazers.

Missionaries

Women were a vital and driving force of establishing Pentecostal and AGWM endeavors. Through the 1930s, two-thirds of AG missionaries were women (McGee 2014, 188).

In spite of a lack of official organization and resources, women pressed ahead on foreign fields alone, in teams, or with their husbands and families. Many found greater opportunities for ministry overseas than at home. Some boldly went to dangerous places at the ends of the earth where other missionaries feared to go.

Women missionaries often had to rely only upon God and their own resourcefulness. It was not uncommon for women missionaries to step into traditionally male roles, such as physically building their own homes, churches, or schools; conducting business; or repairing their own equipment and vehicles (Kowalski 2014, 68).

The first Pentecostal missionary to Argentina, Alice Wood (1870-1961), received AG ordination in November 1914. She served more than sixty years on the mission field, the last fifty without a furlough. When she finally retired at age ninety, she left behind a thriving church pastored by Argentinians whom she raised up for the purpose of impacting a country for Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. The stability of the work she helped to establish provided a foundation for the nationwide Argentine revivals of the 1980s and 1990s.

Evangelists

Perhaps fewer barriers existed for women to minister as evangelists than in any other field. For one reason, the Holiness and Pentecostal Movements had given rise to famous and successful female evangelists—Maria Woodworth-Etter, Aimee Semple McPherson, Minnie Draper—before the Assemblies of God was formed. Before 1950, more than one thousand women had traveled the nation evangelizing and planting churches (Rodgers 2014).

The February 2, 1936, edition of the Latter Rain Evangel contained the following announcement of services to be held by a woman evangelist at Chicago’s Stone Church: “Miss Mattie Howard, a converted gangstress, to hold evangelistic services for three weeks or longer. Miss Howard spent seven years in the Missouri Penitentiary, at Jefferson City, and was known in her sordid years as the Queen of Gangland. After serving her term in prison she was living under an assumed name and was converted through hearing a sermon over the radio. She went to the church that broadcasted the message and gave her heart to God. She was later called to preach the Gospel and has been in the evangelistic field for several years.”

Pastors and Church Planters

In some states, as many as 20 percent of new churches in the Assemblies of God were planted by women. Some would stay and pastor the church for many years. Others would turn the work over to someone else and move on to begin another church. In the Iowa district, a full 22 percent of the churches were founded by female church planters. Even today, many AG female pastors are in churches that they planted themselves.

Although there were some well-known female church planters and pastors, most labored in relative obscurity, as did Elva K. Stump (1885–1985). In 1937, she felt led to start a church in the small, poor village of Shadybrook in the mountains of West Virginia. “There are opportunities on every hand,” she wrote. She responded to the call as her heart was drawn to those “left by the wayside to perish because there is no faithful pastor” (McGee 2014, 231–232).

One of today’s AG church planters, Adelita Garza, would understand “the opportunities on every hand” that Stump saw in the 1930s. Citing the statistics that in 1920, there were twenty-seven churches for every ten thousand people in America, but just eleven per ten thousand people in 2014, Garza challenges women as well as men to step up to fill the gap. “We have the potential to do so much more than we have seen before…I believe with all of my heart that we’re in a new season to do new things where there’s no limitation to what the Holy Spirit can do” (Garza 2014).

Writers and Editors

Among women’s most powerful and lasting routes of influence historically in the Assemblies of God has been the written word. Writers and editors have influenced the movement, inspired believers, convicted unbelievers, trained and challenged future workers, and impacted eternity.

Through her series of articles advocating the indigenous church principle, Alice E. Luce was instrumental in setting the course of Assemblies of God missions.

Through her editing and writing of the early Christian Evangel with her husband, J. Roswell Flower, Alice Reynolds Flower helped build the Assemblies of God from its inception. Ada Brownell, a prolific Assemblies of God layperson, wrote almost 200 articles for the Pentecostal Evangel . Joyce Wells Booze not only wrote more than 100 articles for the Evangel but served as the guiding force for the Assemblies of God missions publication, Mountain Movers .

Editors and writers such as Dorothy Morris, Gwen Jones, Billie Davis, Peggy Musgrove, and Sylvia Lee produced effective Sunday school curriculum and training materials that encouraged, inspired, molded, and launched many current AG leaders into greater devotion and ministry. Billie Davis

Billie Davis

Today, a new generation of writers, editors, educators, and church historians is influencing the next generation. They are boldly continuing the great tradition established by influential women of the past.

Leaders and Trailblazers

Even in an era when most people believed a woman’s proper place was in the home, AG and Pentecostal women started schools and Bible colleges (Alice Luce [Latin America Bible Institute], Mary Craig [Bethany University], Christine Gibson [Zion Bible Institute, now Northpoint Bible College and Seminary], and others). Through a calling to reach out to those who were often marginalized, Assemblies of God women launched benevolence programs (such as Lillian Trasher’s Orphanage, Etta Calhoun’s Women’s Missionary Council, Mildred Whitney’s ministries for the blind, and Beth Grant’s Project Rescue).

Alice Luce

The 2007 General Council in Indianapolis marked a step forward in the leadership opportunities available to female ministers. Missionary and educator Beth Grant was one of the top three candidates for assistant general superintendent. At that council, a new position of “ordained female executive presbyter” was approved. In 2009, Grant was elected to that position.

**Q:** Recount the many ways that women have been influential in the Assemblies of God.

**A:** They were: missionaries—often in dangerous places where others feared to go; evangelists—traveling and evangelizing nationwide; pastors and church planters— leading to much of the early growth of the Assemblies of God; writers and editors— influencing the movement powerfully through the written word; and leaders and trailblazers—pioneers in starting Bible schools, launching benevolence programs, and opening new fields of ministry. 9 CHAPTER

### Leading the Way to the Future

#### 8.5.1 — Describe several trends regarding women's roles in the Assemblies of God, and explain their implications for the future.

The church has not always offered equal status or opportunities to women. However, as we have seen in this chapter, revival has always brought great opportunities for women, and God’s love brings freedom beyond anything society can offer. Even when men in the church failed to recognize and accept the call of women to ministry and leadership equal to their own, God provided open doors for women to serve. Exceptional women have done extraordinary things for God in every generation. When a ministry or calling is from God, nothing can defeat it. With God’s empowerment and the Spirit’s leading, women continue to work toward a brighter future for the Assemblies of God.

As the leadership and influence of women have become more widely accepted at all levels and in all arenas in society, it is important for the church to recognize the impact this has on the church as well. Although the Assemblies of God bases its teaching and practice on the Word of God, the church must realize the influence of culture on the perspectives of those in the church. The challenge for the Assemblies of God is to provide a balanced biblical example for the world, showing women and men working together in effective and God-honoring ways.

Further Resources on Women in Ministry

Official Position Paper . The position paper was updated by the General Presbytery in 2010 and can be read in its entirety on the Assemblies of God website (https://ag.org/en/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Women-in-Ministry).

Network of Women Ministers . The Network of Women Ministers exists to mobilize women to fulfill their ministerial call. They connect women ministers and those seeking credentials, build community and support systems, offer resources, and provide opportunities for leadership development. Their belief statement says, “The image of God is best reflected and the church of Jesus Christ is healthiest when both men and women are empowered to fulfill their calling at every level of ministerial leadership” (Network of Women Ministers 2021).

Women in Leadership Cohort . Since 2009, the Assemblies of God Theological Seminary has offered a Women in Leadership cohort in its doctoral program. Qualified and gifted women in ministry across the nation form lifelong connections and support networks through a degree program that combines distance learning with periodic on-site classes. Many accomplished and noteworthy women have already been part of the Women in Leadership cohort. Undoubtedly, many more of tomorrow’s leaders will continue to do so.

National Women's Department . The earliest organized opportunity for women to minister in the Assemblies of God was the Women’s Missionary Council, established in 1925 (see chapter 6, “The Pattern and Practice of Assemblies of God Missions,” for more information). In 1975, the name was changed to Women’s Ministries, reflecting a broader range of ministries.

In 2009, Women’s Ministries was renamed the National Women’s Department, reflecting their focus on ministering to every woman, as evidenced by their Snuff Out Cancer prayer ministry, Touch with Hope ministry to single moms, Her Green Room (an online community for ministry wives), and online ministry training for women in English and Spanish.

## 9

### Rejection and Isolation

#### 9.1.1 — Summarize the response of many liberal churches to the Pentecostal experience in the first half of the twentieth century.

Most early Pentecostals never anticipated leaving their churches, much less starting new denominations. Instead, they first believed that the outpouring of God’s Spirit they had experienced would spread throughout the church world and become a unifying influence.

The refusal of others to associate with Pentecostals or even acknowledge them as true Christians left them isolated. Some Pentecostals took it as proof that they were right and reveled in being approved by God while being scorned by the world.

Holy Rollers: Ridicule by Liberal Churches

Mainline and liberal churches largely ignored Pentecostals, but it was clear they looked down on the “Holy Rollers.” One of the few mainline books that addressed the Pentecostal phenomenon made its position clear in its title: The Gift of Tongues: A Study in Pathological Aspects of Christianity . The author, Alexander Mackie, called Pentecostalism a “crime against intelligence” (Mackie 1921, 274). He concluded his book with the following judgment of Pentecostalism: “Christendom has waited long and patiently to see whether this thing—this gift of tongues—is of God. It is of sickness, of poverty, of fatigue, of disease, of crime. It is not of God” (275).

Instead of viewing it as a manifestation of the Spirit, liberal churches saw speaking in tongues as a manifestation of mental illness, low intelligence, or social dysfunction.

Sensual, Sinful Glossolalia: Rejection by Holiness Groups

Some southern Holiness congregations had embraced Pentecostalism in the early 1900s, and many establishers of the Assemblies of God came from the Holiness tradition. Although Pentecostals were most closely aligned with and owed much to the Holiness Movement, their sense of connection was not returned. While some, such as A. B. Simpson, were cautious in their dismissal and kept an open mind, others were not so kind. Some called speaking in tongues “sensual,” “sinful,” or even “satanic,” considering it a grave danger to the church.

The Menace of Modern Pentecostalism: Rejection by Fundamentalists

Fundamentalism was perhaps the second most influential precursor to modern Pentecostalism. The two groups shared almost all important doctrines. However, while the fledgling Pentecostals considered themselves to be Fundamentalists, Fundamentalists rejected the association. They believed Pentecostals to be fanatics and heretics—a menace to their orthodox beliefs. This rejection was a result of several issues:

Fundamentalists were convinced that speaking in tongues, miracles, and manifestations of the Spirit were part of a past age or dispensation that had come to an end (1 Corinthians 13:8) and had no place in the modern dispensation.

The emotional nature of Pentecostal worship was strange and unsettling to many Fundamentalists. This was compounded by a few fanatical fringe groups who stretched the boundaries of theology and practice.

At the time of the rise of the modern Pentecostal Movement, Fundamentalists were fighting a valiant but losing battle with modernism within the broader church world. This resulted in a general tendency toward hypervigilance and defensiveness. They were perceived as being combative, judgmental, and excluding. As a result of this defensive posture, they were quick to judge Pentecostalism as another threat to orthodox Christianity (Menzies 1971, 179–180).

Pentecostals were stunned and saddened by the rejection of those with whom they so closely identified, and such rejection effectively built a wall separating the Assemblies of God from their Holiness and Fundamentalist brothers and sisters for many years.

**Q:** Respond to the dispensational position that says manifestations of the Spirit had come to an end.

**A:** Paul taught that spiritual gifts would end when “perfection” comes in 1 Corinthians 13. That is when Jesus comes again, and we receive our new bodies and enter the millennial blessings.
