### Bridging the Divide: Associations

#### 9.2.1 — Outline several factors that may have contributed to the National Association of Evangelicals' ignoring pressure to exclude Pentecostals.

The moniker “evangelical” has been in use since the Protestant Reformation of the 1500s. In the 1800s, it was used to refer to those of revivalist leanings with an emphasis on converting sinners. The more modern usage was developed in the 1930s to distinguish those of conservative theology from the stringent fundamentalist camp which tended to be more isolationist and anticultural in their approach to Christianity in America.

These ‘neo-evangelicals” called for a conference of like-minded Christians in St. Louis in 1942. The primary purpose was to unite evangelical Christians in fellowship and purpose: to amplify the effectiveness of their work of spreading the gospel and their voice before civil authorities. This marked the first time any evangelical body had invited the Pentecostals to participate (Menzies 1971, 185). This led to the creation of the National Association of Evangelicals (NAE).

Some leaders of the new evangelical association objected to the inclusion of the Pentecostals. The Assemblies of God delegation, led by General Secretary J. Roswell Flower, General Superintendent E. S. Williams, and Missionary Secretary Noel Perkin, offered to withdraw from membership rather than cause division among other evangelicals. However, the leadership of the NAE refused to abandon their Pentecostal friends. This was due to several factors.

Cofounder and first president of the NAE, Harold John Ockenga, wanted to remain true to the biblical and theological beliefs of Fundamentalism but without the isolationist, defensive, militant, and confrontational personality many Fundamentalists had assumed.

Cofounder and vigorous promotor J. Elwin Wright’s father had been a Pentecostal, and the younger Wright’s cooperative association, the New England Fellowship, which sought to unite evangelicals in an area dominated by Catholics, had welcomed all evangelicals—including Pentecostals.

Early influencer Ralph Davis of the Africa Inland Mission expressed the need for greater cooperation in missions, and Pentecostal groups, particularly the Assemblies of God, were winning admiration with the great success of their indigenous church principle (National Association of Evangelicals, n.d).

World War II had brought evangelicals into closer contact with the Assemblies of God, who for the first time had abandoned its pacifist leanings and provided soldiers and chaplains for the war effort. They also produced a magazine for service men and women, Reveille , which they provided free to 3,500 chaplains of all faiths (Menzies 1971, 188).

Rather than spurning the Pentecostals as outsiders, the broader church world of evangelicals decided at last to embrace them as fellow evangelicals.

The Power of Association

Other than this perception of legitimization in the eyes of the church world and the opportunity for fellowship, what did membership in the NAE do for the Assemblies of God? Perhaps the most important benefit was the power of association. The Assemblies of God was able to amplify its voice and its effectiveness by being a part of the following organizations under the umbrella of the NAE.

National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) . Before the NAE was organized, one area in which the evangelicals and Pentecostals had great success was in the relatively new field of radio broadcasting. It was the practice of the major radio networks to donate free time to churches, but only if they were part of a recognized and approved broadcasting organization. Because they were not part of the larger mainline church association, the Federal Council of Churches, many of these evangelical churches were only able to broadcast on small stations with little reach.

In conjunction with the second convention of the NAE in 1944, the National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) was formed to safeguard the integrity of evangelical broadcasters and ensure that their voices would be heard. Thomas F. Zimmerman, who would serve as general superintendent of the Assemblies of God from 1959 to 1985, was on the original executive committee of the group and later served as its president (Menzies 1971, 190).

By 1946, the NRB had effectively pushed back the threat that would have silenced evangelicals’ voices on the radio. The important work of the NRB continues in the twenty-first century with a broader emphasis on television and internet broadcasting as well. In America, 141 million people interact with some form of Christian media monthly (National Religious Broadcasters, 2021). The NRB continues to grapple with both the incredible ministry opportunities and the ever-increasing threats to evangelicals’ right to share the gospel.

At the 2020 Christian Media Convention in Nashville, Tennessee, Mike Huckabee stated:

We’re living in a day where the polarity of cultures and the clash is so intense that if we do not stand and fight hard for the basic Constitutional liberties of religious freedom, we not only will lose them, but the future generations will lose any understanding or knowledge of what this country was about…The NRB serves a vital, incredibly important role not only in communicating who we as believers are but who we as Americans are…One of the reasons that our culture and society, our civilization itself, is in trouble is because we’re raising a whole generation of younger people who believe that the world revolves around what they think, what they feel, what they believe, and not what the facts of the Word of God are…This as much as anything is a message that I believe NRB has a unique responsibility to help broadcast to the world and to make sure that we don’t lose that fundamental idea that there are some things that may seem right but in the end they are death…We cannot have a generation that lives as it was in the time of the Judges where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, and yet that’s the culture that young people are being raised in and sadly even in what have been and otherwise would be Bible-believing, evangelical churches. (Roach 2020)

National Sunday School Association (NSSA) . The more liberal Federal Council of Churches also oversaw much of the religious education during the 1920s to the 1950s. The lessons produced by their organization, the International Council of Religious Education (ICRE), included little Bible teaching but a great deal of liberal theology and social gospel propaganda (Menzies 1971, 191). The ICRE’s oversight coincided with a significant decline in Sunday school attendance and vitality. So, in 1943, the NAE commissioned a study to explore creating its own uniform Sunday school lesson series from a conservative, evangelical perspective. The Assemblies of God became the guiding force in this endeavor, since in 1937, it had been the first to abandon the ICRE curriculum and develop its own material under the leadership of Editor Stanley Frodsham (Menzies, 191).

Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (EFMA) . In 1945, the NAE launched the Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (now Missio Nexus). The EFMA was an advocate to the US government on behalf of evangelical missions and missionaries, facilitated the acquisition of visas, and mediated sensitive diplomatic matters involving missionaries (Menzies 1971, 192). Currently, Missio Nexus seeks to advance the Great Commission by building relationships, sharing, learning, providing ideas and innovation, missionary advocacy, and collaborative action (Missio Nexus, "Who We Are"). This evangelical missions organization, of which Assemblies of God World Missions remains a part, now operates independently of the NAE, although it is a member organization of the NAE.

Other Fellowships

While membership in the NAE was very beneficial for the growth and acceptance of the Assemblies of God, there were some drawbacks. To maintain this acceptance, some of its earlier distinctives saw less emphasis – such as the ordination of women. The challenge for the Assemblies of God—and Pentecostals in general—was to guard against allowing Pentecostal values and distinctives to be drowned out or lost among broader evangelical teaching (Menzies 1999). One way of safeguarding the Pentecostal message was to freshly articulate it for a new generation. Another way was to join with other Pentecostals in various fellowships. Here are three Pentecostal fellowships that have been of particular significance for the Assemblies of God:

Pentecostal World Fellowship (PWF, 1947) . In 1947, a great international conference of Pentecostals gathered in Zurich, Switzerland. There, the Pentecostal World Fellowship was formed. European Pentecostals had long been pursuing cooperation among continental Pentecostals. At this meeting, the Europeans challenged the American Pentecostals to organize their own cooperative fellowship. This led directly to the birth of the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America the following year.

Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (PFNA, 1948) . Assemblies of God leader J. Roswell Flower was the chairman of a committee assigned by the NAE to frame a tentative Constitution for a new organization that would soon become the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America. Flower was elected the first secretary of the PFNA at its first Constitutional convention in October 1948.

Created to promote fellowship among Pentecostals, the PFNA was made up only of White churches and denominations. This officially cemented the racial divide until 1994, when the PFNA was replaced by the multiracial Pentecostal and Charismatic Churches of North America (see Chapter 10 for a more detailed discussion).

World Assemblies of God Fellowship (WAGF, 1988) . Under the leadership of General Superintendent G. Raymond Carlson, the US Assemblies of God declared the 1990s to be a “Decade of Harvest.” Ambitious goals included winning five million individuals to Christ, training twenty thousand ministers, and establishing five thousand new churches. In 1988, in anticipation of the Decade of Harvest, leaders of sixty national churches met in Springfield, Missouri, to form a network for cooperation to boost global evangelism and church planting. This cooperative body soon became the World Assemblies of God Fellowship (WAGF) (McGee 2014, 390).

Over thirty years later, the Assemblies of God was the largest Pentecostal fellowship in the world, having grown to more than seventy million members worldwide, with more than 160 member fellowships (General Council 2021f). Its purpose remains the same—“To pursue the fulfillment of the Lord’s command to evangelize the lost in the shortest possible time…by encouraging and assisting one another, promoting harmonious relationships and seeking the most effective means of its accomplishment under the dynamic leadership of the Holy Spirit” (General Council 2021f).

With a few notable exceptions (such as Brazil’s Assembl é ias de Deus, which was formed in 1911, three years before the Assemblies of God in the USA), most fellowships that make up the WAGF originated from the missionary success of the Assemblies of God USA (Molenaar 2011, 40–47). The indigenous church principle was clearly an important factor in the establishment of strong, independent national churches that would eventually come to partner with the US Assemblies of God in the WAGF.

**Q:** Analyze how the meaning of the word evangelical has changed over time.

**A:** Martin Luther used it to describe non-Catholic churches; then it went on to be used to describe any Protestant who resisted liberal influences. Later, “evangelicalism” became synonymous with revivalism. During the 1920s and 1930s, some Fundamentalists distanced themselves from certain extreme Fundamentalists. As a result, they called themselves “evangelicals.”

**Q:** Paraphrase how the Assemblies of God benefitted from participating in the National Association of Evangelicals.

**A:** Being part of the association gave them connections they would not have otherwise had. It was legitimizing and caused the Assemblies of God to be stronger and more effective due to the Assemblies of God’s participation in organizations that were part of the National Association of Evangelicals, which included the National Religious Broadcasters, National Sunday School Association, Evangelical Foreign Missions Association, and others.

**Q:** Describe the challenge regarding Pentecostal values in joining other religious associations.

**A:** The challenge was to keep Pentecostal values and distinctives alive in the midst of the Assemblies of God’s associations with other evangelicals and to articulate it for the younger generations. They accomplished this by joining with other Pentecostal fellowships: the Pentecostal World Fellowship, Pentecostal Fellowship of North America, and the World Assemblies of God Fellowship.

#### 9.2.2 — Describe the dilemma of evangelicals that led to the foundation of the National Religious Broadcasters.

The moniker “evangelical” has been in use since the Protestant Reformation of the 1500s. In the 1800s, it was used to refer to those of revivalist leanings with an emphasis on converting sinners. The more modern usage was developed in the 1930s to distinguish those of conservative theology from the stringent fundamentalist camp which tended to be more isolationist and anticultural in their approach to Christianity in America.

These ‘neo-evangelicals” called for a conference of like-minded Christians in St. Louis in 1942. The primary purpose was to unite evangelical Christians in fellowship and purpose: to amplify the effectiveness of their work of spreading the gospel and their voice before civil authorities. This marked the first time any evangelical body had invited the Pentecostals to participate (Menzies 1971, 185). This led to the creation of the National Association of Evangelicals (NAE).

Some leaders of the new evangelical association objected to the inclusion of the Pentecostals. The Assemblies of God delegation, led by General Secretary J. Roswell Flower, General Superintendent E. S. Williams, and Missionary Secretary Noel Perkin, offered to withdraw from membership rather than cause division among other evangelicals. However, the leadership of the NAE refused to abandon their Pentecostal friends. This was due to several factors.

Cofounder and first president of the NAE, Harold John Ockenga, wanted to remain true to the biblical and theological beliefs of Fundamentalism but without the isolationist, defensive, militant, and confrontational personality many Fundamentalists had assumed.

Cofounder and vigorous promotor J. Elwin Wright’s father had been a Pentecostal, and the younger Wright’s cooperative association, the New England Fellowship, which sought to unite evangelicals in an area dominated by Catholics, had welcomed all evangelicals—including Pentecostals.

Early influencer Ralph Davis of the Africa Inland Mission expressed the need for greater cooperation in missions, and Pentecostal groups, particularly the Assemblies of God, were winning admiration with the great success of their indigenous church principle (National Association of Evangelicals, n.d).

World War II had brought evangelicals into closer contact with the Assemblies of God, who for the first time had abandoned its pacifist leanings and provided soldiers and chaplains for the war effort. They also produced a magazine for service men and women, Reveille , which they provided free to 3,500 chaplains of all faiths (Menzies 1971, 188).

Rather than spurning the Pentecostals as outsiders, the broader church world of evangelicals decided at last to embrace them as fellow evangelicals.

The Power of Association

Other than this perception of legitimization in the eyes of the church world and the opportunity for fellowship, what did membership in the NAE do for the Assemblies of God? Perhaps the most important benefit was the power of association. The Assemblies of God was able to amplify its voice and its effectiveness by being a part of the following organizations under the umbrella of the NAE.

National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) . Before the NAE was organized, one area in which the evangelicals and Pentecostals had great success was in the relatively new field of radio broadcasting. It was the practice of the major radio networks to donate free time to churches, but only if they were part of a recognized and approved broadcasting organization. Because they were not part of the larger mainline church association, the Federal Council of Churches, many of these evangelical churches were only able to broadcast on small stations with little reach.

In conjunction with the second convention of the NAE in 1944, the National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) was formed to safeguard the integrity of evangelical broadcasters and ensure that their voices would be heard. Thomas F. Zimmerman, who would serve as general superintendent of the Assemblies of God from 1959 to 1985, was on the original executive committee of the group and later served as its president (Menzies 1971, 190).

By 1946, the NRB had effectively pushed back the threat that would have silenced evangelicals’ voices on the radio. The important work of the NRB continues in the twenty-first century with a broader emphasis on television and internet broadcasting as well. In America, 141 million people interact with some form of Christian media monthly (National Religious Broadcasters, 2021). The NRB continues to grapple with both the incredible ministry opportunities and the ever-increasing threats to evangelicals’ right to share the gospel.

At the 2020 Christian Media Convention in Nashville, Tennessee, Mike Huckabee stated:

We’re living in a day where the polarity of cultures and the clash is so intense that if we do not stand and fight hard for the basic Constitutional liberties of religious freedom, we not only will lose them, but the future generations will lose any understanding or knowledge of what this country was about…The NRB serves a vital, incredibly important role not only in communicating who we as believers are but who we as Americans are…One of the reasons that our culture and society, our civilization itself, is in trouble is because we’re raising a whole generation of younger people who believe that the world revolves around what they think, what they feel, what they believe, and not what the facts of the Word of God are…This as much as anything is a message that I believe NRB has a unique responsibility to help broadcast to the world and to make sure that we don’t lose that fundamental idea that there are some things that may seem right but in the end they are death…We cannot have a generation that lives as it was in the time of the Judges where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, and yet that’s the culture that young people are being raised in and sadly even in what have been and otherwise would be Bible-believing, evangelical churches. (Roach 2020)

National Sunday School Association (NSSA) . The more liberal Federal Council of Churches also oversaw much of the religious education during the 1920s to the 1950s. The lessons produced by their organization, the International Council of Religious Education (ICRE), included little Bible teaching but a great deal of liberal theology and social gospel propaganda (Menzies 1971, 191). The ICRE’s oversight coincided with a significant decline in Sunday school attendance and vitality. So, in 1943, the NAE commissioned a study to explore creating its own uniform Sunday school lesson series from a conservative, evangelical perspective. The Assemblies of God became the guiding force in this endeavor, since in 1937, it had been the first to abandon the ICRE curriculum and develop its own material under the leadership of Editor Stanley Frodsham (Menzies, 191).

Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (EFMA) . In 1945, the NAE launched the Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (now Missio Nexus). The EFMA was an advocate to the US government on behalf of evangelical missions and missionaries, facilitated the acquisition of visas, and mediated sensitive diplomatic matters involving missionaries (Menzies 1971, 192). Currently, Missio Nexus seeks to advance the Great Commission by building relationships, sharing, learning, providing ideas and innovation, missionary advocacy, and collaborative action (Missio Nexus, "Who We Are"). This evangelical missions organization, of which Assemblies of God World Missions remains a part, now operates independently of the NAE, although it is a member organization of the NAE.

We’re living in a day where the polarity of cultures and the clash is so intense that if we do not stand and fight hard for the basic Constitutional liberties of religious freedom, we not only will lose them, but the future generations will lose any understanding or knowledge of what this country was about…The NRB serves a vital, incredibly important role not only in communicating who we as believers are but who we as Americans are…One of the reasons that our culture and society, our civilization itself, is in trouble is because we’re raising a whole generation of younger people who believe that the world revolves around what they think, what they feel, what they believe, and not what the facts of the Word of God are…This as much as anything is a message that I believe NRB has a unique responsibility to help broadcast to the world and to make sure that we don’t lose that fundamental idea that there are some things that may seem right but in the end they are death…We cannot have a generation that lives as it was in the time of the Judges where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, and yet that’s the culture that young people are being raised in and sadly even in what have been and otherwise would be Bible-believing, evangelical churches. (Roach 2020)

National Sunday School Association (NSSA) . The more liberal Federal Council of Churches also oversaw much of the religious education during the 1920s to the 1950s. The lessons produced by their organization, the International Council of Religious Education (ICRE), included little Bible teaching but a great deal of liberal theology and social gospel propaganda (Menzies 1971, 191). The ICRE’s oversight coincided with a significant decline in Sunday school attendance and vitality. So, in 1943, the NAE commissioned a study to explore creating its own uniform Sunday school lesson series from a conservative, evangelical perspective. The Assemblies of God became the guiding force in this endeavor, since in 1937, it had been the first to abandon the ICRE curriculum and develop its own material under the leadership of Editor Stanley Frodsham (Menzies, 191).

Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (EFMA) . In 1945, the NAE launched the Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (now Missio Nexus). The EFMA was an advocate to the US government on behalf of evangelical missions and missionaries, facilitated the acquisition of visas, and mediated sensitive diplomatic matters involving missionaries (Menzies 1971, 192). Currently, Missio Nexus seeks to advance the Great Commission by building relationships, sharing, learning, providing ideas and innovation, missionary advocacy, and collaborative action (Missio Nexus, "Who We Are"). This evangelical missions organization, of which Assemblies of God World Missions remains a part, now operates independently of the NAE, although it is a member organization of the NAE.

Other Fellowships

While membership in the NAE was very beneficial for the growth and acceptance of the Assemblies of God, there were some drawbacks. To maintain this acceptance, some of its earlier distinctives saw less emphasis – such as the ordination of women. The challenge for the Assemblies of God—and Pentecostals in general—was to guard against allowing Pentecostal values and distinctives to be drowned out or lost among broader evangelical teaching (Menzies 1999). One way of safeguarding the Pentecostal message was to freshly articulate it for a new generation. Another way was to join with other Pentecostals in various fellowships. Here are three Pentecostal fellowships that have been of particular significance for the Assemblies of God:

Pentecostal World Fellowship (PWF, 1947) . In 1947, a great international conference of Pentecostals gathered in Zurich, Switzerland. There, the Pentecostal World Fellowship was formed. European Pentecostals had long been pursuing cooperation among continental Pentecostals. At this meeting, the Europeans challenged the American Pentecostals to organize their own cooperative fellowship. This led directly to the birth of the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America the following year.

Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (PFNA, 1948) . Assemblies of God leader J. Roswell Flower was the chairman of a committee assigned by the NAE to frame a tentative Constitution for a new organization that would soon become the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America. Flower was elected the first secretary of the PFNA at its first Constitutional convention in October 1948.

Created to promote fellowship among Pentecostals, the PFNA was made up only of White churches and denominations. This officially cemented the racial divide until 1994, when the PFNA was replaced by the multiracial Pentecostal and Charismatic Churches of North America (see Chapter 10 for a more detailed discussion).

World Assemblies of God Fellowship (WAGF, 1988) . Under the leadership of General Superintendent G. Raymond Carlson, the US Assemblies of God declared the 1990s to be a “Decade of Harvest.” Ambitious goals included winning five million individuals to Christ, training twenty thousand ministers, and establishing five thousand new churches. In 1988, in anticipation of the Decade of Harvest, leaders of sixty national churches met in Springfield, Missouri, to form a network for cooperation to boost global evangelism and church planting. This cooperative body soon became the World Assemblies of God Fellowship (WAGF) (McGee 2014, 390).

Over thirty years later, the Assemblies of God was the largest Pentecostal fellowship in the world, having grown to more than seventy million members worldwide, with more than 160 member fellowships (General Council 2021f). Its purpose remains the same—“To pursue the fulfillment of the Lord’s command to evangelize the lost in the shortest possible time…by encouraging and assisting one another, promoting harmonious relationships and seeking the most effective means of its accomplishment under the dynamic leadership of the Holy Spirit” (General Council 2021f).

With a few notable exceptions (such as Brazil’s Assembl é ias de Deus, which was formed in 1911, three years before the Assemblies of God in the USA), most fellowships that make up the WAGF originated from the missionary success of the Assemblies of God USA (Molenaar 2011, 40–47). The indigenous church principle was clearly an important factor in the establishment of strong, independent national churches that would eventually come to partner with the US Assemblies of God in the WAGF.

**Q:** Analyze how the meaning of the word evangelical has changed over time.

**A:** Martin Luther used it to describe non-Catholic churches; then it went on to be used to describe any Protestant who resisted liberal influences. Later, “evangelicalism” became synonymous with revivalism. During the 1920s and 1930s, some Fundamentalists distanced themselves from certain extreme Fundamentalists. As a result, they called themselves “evangelicals.”

**Q:** Paraphrase how the Assemblies of God benefitted from participating in the National Association of Evangelicals.

**A:** Being part of the association gave them connections they would not have otherwise had. It was legitimizing and caused the Assemblies of God to be stronger and more effective due to the Assemblies of God’s participation in organizations that were part of the National Association of Evangelicals, which included the National Religious Broadcasters, National Sunday School Association, Evangelical Foreign Missions Association, and others.

**Q:** Describe the challenge regarding Pentecostal values in joining other religious associations.

**A:** The challenge was to keep Pentecostal values and distinctives alive in the midst of the Assemblies of God’s associations with other evangelicals and to articulate it for the younger generations. They accomplished this by joining with other Pentecostal fellowships: the Pentecostal World Fellowship, Pentecostal Fellowship of North America, and the World Assemblies of God Fellowship.

#### 9.2.5 — Explain how the creation of Pentecostal fellowships was an important safeguard to balance broader associations with evangelicals.

The moniker “evangelical” has been in use since the Protestant Reformation of the 1500s. In the 1800s, it was used to refer to those of revivalist leanings with an emphasis on converting sinners. The more modern usage was developed in the 1930s to distinguish those of conservative theology from the stringent fundamentalist camp which tended to be more isolationist and anticultural in their approach to Christianity in America.

These ‘neo-evangelicals” called for a conference of like-minded Christians in St. Louis in 1942. The primary purpose was to unite evangelical Christians in fellowship and purpose: to amplify the effectiveness of their work of spreading the gospel and their voice before civil authorities. This marked the first time any evangelical body had invited the Pentecostals to participate (Menzies 1971, 185). This led to the creation of the National Association of Evangelicals (NAE).

Some leaders of the new evangelical association objected to the inclusion of the Pentecostals. The Assemblies of God delegation, led by General Secretary J. Roswell Flower, General Superintendent E. S. Williams, and Missionary Secretary Noel Perkin, offered to withdraw from membership rather than cause division among other evangelicals. However, the leadership of the NAE refused to abandon their Pentecostal friends. This was due to several factors.

Cofounder and first president of the NAE, Harold John Ockenga, wanted to remain true to the biblical and theological beliefs of Fundamentalism but without the isolationist, defensive, militant, and confrontational personality many Fundamentalists had assumed.

Cofounder and vigorous promotor J. Elwin Wright’s father had been a Pentecostal, and the younger Wright’s cooperative association, the New England Fellowship, which sought to unite evangelicals in an area dominated by Catholics, had welcomed all evangelicals—including Pentecostals.

Early influencer Ralph Davis of the Africa Inland Mission expressed the need for greater cooperation in missions, and Pentecostal groups, particularly the Assemblies of God, were winning admiration with the great success of their indigenous church principle (National Association of Evangelicals, n.d).

World War II had brought evangelicals into closer contact with the Assemblies of God, who for the first time had abandoned its pacifist leanings and provided soldiers and chaplains for the war effort. They also produced a magazine for service men and women, Reveille , which they provided free to 3,500 chaplains of all faiths (Menzies 1971, 188).

Rather than spurning the Pentecostals as outsiders, the broader church world of evangelicals decided at last to embrace them as fellow evangelicals.

The Power of Association

Other than this perception of legitimization in the eyes of the church world and the opportunity for fellowship, what did membership in the NAE do for the Assemblies of God? Perhaps the most important benefit was the power of association. The Assemblies of God was able to amplify its voice and its effectiveness by being a part of the following organizations under the umbrella of the NAE.

National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) . Before the NAE was organized, one area in which the evangelicals and Pentecostals had great success was in the relatively new field of radio broadcasting. It was the practice of the major radio networks to donate free time to churches, but only if they were part of a recognized and approved broadcasting organization. Because they were not part of the larger mainline church association, the Federal Council of Churches, many of these evangelical churches were only able to broadcast on small stations with little reach.

In conjunction with the second convention of the NAE in 1944, the National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) was formed to safeguard the integrity of evangelical broadcasters and ensure that their voices would be heard. Thomas F. Zimmerman, who would serve as general superintendent of the Assemblies of God from 1959 to 1985, was on the original executive committee of the group and later served as its president (Menzies 1971, 190).

By 1946, the NRB had effectively pushed back the threat that would have silenced evangelicals’ voices on the radio. The important work of the NRB continues in the twenty-first century with a broader emphasis on television and internet broadcasting as well. In America, 141 million people interact with some form of Christian media monthly (National Religious Broadcasters, 2021). The NRB continues to grapple with both the incredible ministry opportunities and the ever-increasing threats to evangelicals’ right to share the gospel.

At the 2020 Christian Media Convention in Nashville, Tennessee, Mike Huckabee stated:

We’re living in a day where the polarity of cultures and the clash is so intense that if we do not stand and fight hard for the basic Constitutional liberties of religious freedom, we not only will lose them, but the future generations will lose any understanding or knowledge of what this country was about…The NRB serves a vital, incredibly important role not only in communicating who we as believers are but who we as Americans are…One of the reasons that our culture and society, our civilization itself, is in trouble is because we’re raising a whole generation of younger people who believe that the world revolves around what they think, what they feel, what they believe, and not what the facts of the Word of God are…This as much as anything is a message that I believe NRB has a unique responsibility to help broadcast to the world and to make sure that we don’t lose that fundamental idea that there are some things that may seem right but in the end they are death…We cannot have a generation that lives as it was in the time of the Judges where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, and yet that’s the culture that young people are being raised in and sadly even in what have been and otherwise would be Bible-believing, evangelical churches. (Roach 2020)

The lessons produced by their organization, the International Council of Religious Education (ICRE), included little Bible teaching but a great deal of liberal theology and social gospel propaganda (Menzies 1971, 191). Because they were not part of the larger mainline church association, the Federal Council of Churches, many of these evangelical churches were only able to broadcast on small stations with little reach.

In conjunction with the second convention of the NAE in 1944, the National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) was formed to safeguard the integrity of evangelical broadcasters and ensure that their voices would be heard. Thomas F. Zimmerman, who would serve as general superintendent of the Assemblies of God from 1959 to 1985, was on the original executive committee of the group and later served as its president (Menzies 1971, 190).

By 1946, the NRB had effectively pushed back the threat that would have silenced evangelicals’ voices on the radio. The important work of the NRB continues in the twenty-first century with a broader emphasis on television and internet broadcasting as well. In America, 141 million people interact with some form of Christian media monthly (National Religious Broadcasters, 2021). The NRB continues to grapple with both the incredible ministry opportunities and the ever-increasing threats to evangelicals’ right to share the gospel.

At the 2020 Christian Media Convention in Nashville, Tennessee, Mike Huckabee stated:

We’re living in a day where the polarity of cultures and the clash is so intense that if we do not stand and fight hard for the basic Constitutional liberties of religious freedom, we not only will lose them, but the future generations will lose any understanding or knowledge of what this country was about…The NRB serves a vital, incredibly important role not only in communicating who we as believers are but who we as Americans are…One of the reasons that our culture and society, our civilization itself, is in trouble is because we’re raising a whole generation of younger people who believe that the world revolves around what they think, what they feel, what they believe, and not what the facts of the Word of God are…This as much as anything is a message that I believe NRB has a unique responsibility to help broadcast to the world and to make sure that we don’t lose that fundamental idea that there are some things that may seem right but in the end they are death…We cannot have a generation that lives as it was in the time of the Judges where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, and yet that’s the culture that young people are being raised in and sadly even in what have been and otherwise would be Bible-believing, evangelical churches. (Roach 2020)

National Sunday School Association (NSSA) . The more liberal Federal Council of Churches also oversaw much of the religious education during the 1920s to the 1950s. The lessons produced by their organization, the International Council of Religious Education (ICRE), included little Bible teaching but a great deal of liberal theology and social gospel propaganda (Menzies 1971, 191). The ICRE’s oversight coincided with a significant decline in Sunday school attendance and vitality. So, in 1943, the NAE commissioned a study to explore creating its own uniform Sunday school lesson series from a conservative, evangelical perspective. The Assemblies of God became the guiding force in this endeavor, since in 1937, it had been the first to abandon the ICRE curriculum and develop its own material under the leadership of Editor Stanley Frodsham (Menzies, 191).

Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (EFMA) . In 1945, the NAE launched the Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (now Missio Nexus). The EFMA was an advocate to the US government on behalf of evangelical missions and missionaries, facilitated the acquisition of visas, and mediated sensitive diplomatic matters involving missionaries (Menzies 1971, 192). Currently, Missio Nexus seeks to advance the Great Commission by building relationships, sharing, learning, providing ideas and innovation, missionary advocacy, and collaborative action (Missio Nexus, "Who We Are"). This evangelical missions organization, of which Assemblies of God World Missions remains a part, now operates independently of the NAE, although it is a member organization of the NAE.

Other Fellowships

While membership in the NAE was very beneficial for the growth and acceptance of the Assemblies of God, there were some drawbacks. To maintain this acceptance, some of its earlier distinctives saw less emphasis – such as the ordination of women. The challenge for the Assemblies of God—and Pentecostals in general—was to guard against allowing Pentecostal values and distinctives to be drowned out or lost among broader evangelical teaching (Menzies 1999). One way of safeguarding the Pentecostal message was to freshly articulate it for a new generation. Another way was to join with other Pentecostals in various fellowships. Here are three Pentecostal fellowships that have been of particular significance for the Assemblies of God:

Pentecostal World Fellowship (PWF, 1947) . In 1947, a great international conference of Pentecostals gathered in Zurich, Switzerland. There, the Pentecostal World Fellowship was formed. European Pentecostals had long been pursuing cooperation among continental Pentecostals. At this meeting, the Europeans challenged the American Pentecostals to organize their own cooperative fellowship. This led directly to the birth of the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America the following year.

Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (PFNA, 1948) . Assemblies of God leader J. Roswell Flower was the chairman of a committee assigned by the NAE to frame a tentative Constitution for a new organization that would soon become the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America. Flower was elected the first secretary of the PFNA at its first Constitutional convention in October 1948.

Created to promote fellowship among Pentecostals, the PFNA was made up only of White churches and denominations. This officially cemented the racial divide until 1994, when the PFNA was replaced by the multiracial Pentecostal and Charismatic Churches of North America (see Chapter 10 for a more detailed discussion).

World Assemblies of God Fellowship (WAGF, 1988) . Under the leadership of General Superintendent G. Raymond Carlson, the US Assemblies of God declared the 1990s to be a “Decade of Harvest.” Ambitious goals included winning five million individuals to Christ, training twenty thousand ministers, and establishing five thousand new churches. In 1988, in anticipation of the Decade of Harvest, leaders of sixty national churches met in Springfield, Missouri, to form a network for cooperation to boost global evangelism and church planting. This cooperative body soon became the World Assemblies of God Fellowship (WAGF) (McGee 2014, 390).

Over thirty years later, the Assemblies of God was the largest Pentecostal fellowship in the world, having grown to more than seventy million members worldwide, with more than 160 member fellowships (General Council 2021f). Its purpose remains the same—“To pursue the fulfillment of the Lord’s command to evangelize the lost in the shortest possible time…by encouraging and assisting one another, promoting harmonious relationships and seeking the most effective means of its accomplishment under the dynamic leadership of the Holy Spirit” (General Council 2021f).

With a few notable exceptions (such as Brazil’s Assembl é ias de Deus, which was formed in 1911, three years before the Assemblies of God in the USA), most fellowships that make up the WAGF originated from the missionary success of the Assemblies of God USA (Molenaar 2011, 40–47). The indigenous church principle was clearly an important factor in the establishment of strong, independent national churches that would eventually come to partner with the US Assemblies of God in the WAGF.

**Q:** Analyze how the meaning of the word evangelical has changed over time.

**A:** Martin Luther used it to describe non-Catholic churches; then it went on to be used to describe any Protestant who resisted liberal influences. Later, “evangelicalism” became synonymous with revivalism. During the 1920s and 1930s, some Fundamentalists distanced themselves from certain extreme Fundamentalists. As a result, they called themselves “evangelicals.”

**Q:** Paraphrase how the Assemblies of God benefitted from participating in the National Association of Evangelicals.

**A:** Being part of the association gave them connections they would not have otherwise had. It was legitimizing and caused the Assemblies of God to be stronger and more effective due to the Assemblies of God’s participation in organizations that were part of the National Association of Evangelicals, which included the National Religious Broadcasters, National Sunday School Association, Evangelical Foreign Missions Association, and others.

**Q:** Describe the challenge regarding Pentecostal values in joining other religious associations.

**A:** The challenge was to keep Pentecostal values and distinctives alive in the midst of the Assemblies of God’s associations with other evangelicals and to articulate it for the younger generations. They accomplished this by joining with other Pentecostal fellowships: the Pentecostal World Fellowship, Pentecostal Fellowship of North America, and the World Assemblies of God Fellowship.

#### 9.2.8 — Give evidence of the strength of the World Assemblies of God Fellowship today.

The moniker “evangelical” has been in use since the Protestant Reformation of the 1500s. In the 1800s, it was used to refer to those of revivalist leanings with an emphasis on converting sinners. The more modern usage was developed in the 1930s to distinguish those of conservative theology from the stringent fundamentalist camp which tended to be more isolationist and anticultural in their approach to Christianity in America.

These ‘neo-evangelicals” called for a conference of like-minded Christians in St. Louis in 1942. The primary purpose was to unite evangelical Christians in fellowship and purpose: to amplify the effectiveness of their work of spreading the gospel and their voice before civil authorities. This marked the first time any evangelical body had invited the Pentecostals to participate (Menzies 1971, 185). This led to the creation of the National Association of Evangelicals (NAE).

Some leaders of the new evangelical association objected to the inclusion of the Pentecostals. The Assemblies of God delegation, led by General Secretary J. Roswell Flower, General Superintendent E. S. Williams, and Missionary Secretary Noel Perkin, offered to withdraw from membership rather than cause division among other evangelicals. However, the leadership of the NAE refused to abandon their Pentecostal friends. This was due to several factors.

Cofounder and first president of the NAE, Harold John Ockenga, wanted to remain true to the biblical and theological beliefs of Fundamentalism but without the isolationist, defensive, militant, and confrontational personality many Fundamentalists had assumed.

Cofounder and vigorous promotor J. Elwin Wright’s father had been a Pentecostal, and the younger Wright’s cooperative association, the New England Fellowship, which sought to unite evangelicals in an area dominated by Catholics, had welcomed all evangelicals—including Pentecostals.

Early influencer Ralph Davis of the Africa Inland Mission expressed the need for greater cooperation in missions, and Pentecostal groups, particularly the Assemblies of God, were winning admiration with the great success of their indigenous church principle (National Association of Evangelicals, n.d).

World War II had brought evangelicals into closer contact with the Assemblies of God, who for the first time had abandoned its pacifist leanings and provided soldiers and chaplains for the war effort. They also produced a magazine for service men and women, Reveille , which they provided free to 3,500 chaplains of all faiths (Menzies 1971, 188).

Rather than spurning the Pentecostals as outsiders, the broader church world of evangelicals decided at last to embrace them as fellow evangelicals.

The Power of Association

Other than this perception of legitimization in the eyes of the church world and the opportunity for fellowship, what did membership in the NAE do for the Assemblies of God? Perhaps the most important benefit was the power of association. The Assemblies of God was able to amplify its voice and its effectiveness by being a part of the following organizations under the umbrella of the NAE.

National Religious Broadcasters (NRB) . Before the NAE was organized, one area in which the evangelicals and Pentecostals had great success was in the relatively new field of radio broadcasting. ### Uniters and Dividers: New Revival Movements

#### 9.3.1 — Compare and contrast the origins and issues of the New Order of the Latter Rain with the Pentecostal revival of the early 1900s.

In the second half of the twentieth century, new revival movements echoed those of the Pentecostal outpourings that had led to the organization of the Assemblies of God. Some new, exciting spiritual opportunities, as well as some of the same excesses and errors, arose. Would the lessons learned in the early years protect this new generation of Pentecostals from the dangers of error and excess? Would these new revivals unite or divide Pentecostals?

The New Order of the Latter Rain (1948)

As the Assemblies of God grew, leading to increasing structure and organization, some worried about restricting the moving and leading of the Holy Spirit. They feared that Pentecostals’ zeal and spiritual power had declined. Once again, some longed for a fresh revival and a restoration of all the gifts of the Spirit as demonstrated in the New Testament church.

When revival broke out in Saskatchewan, Canada, in 1948, it quickly spread to the United States. Many Pentecostals flocked to meetings to judge for themselves whether this new movement was of God. Among these was Stanley Frodsham, the influential editor of the Pentecostal Evangel . After attending revival meetings in Detroit, Michigan, Frodsham declared, “This is God” (Scott 1967, interview).

But not everyone in the Assemblies of God felt that way. Problems quickly developed that caused division among proponents of Latter Rain and more traditional Pentecostals:

1. Alienation . Latter Rain proponents denounced Pentecostal denominations having lost the fire of the Holy Ghost and becoming apostate.

2. Lack of accountability . The Latter Rain Movement practiced an extreme form of congregationalism that did not recognize denominational authority. This led to many of the same abuses of power that had made it important to organize the Assemblies of God. Some who claimed the titles and authority of modern-day prophets and apostles besmirched the name of Christ with their immorality and controversial doctrines (Rodgers 2014).

3. Erroneous teachings . Below are some doctrines promoted by the Latter Rain Movement that were questionable:

The belief that the church is to be built on present-day prophets and apostles;

Overemphasis on identifying, imparting, and bestowing of gifts by the laying on of hands and prophecy;

Belief in the giving of the gift of tongues for missionary service;

The extreme and unscriptural practice of imparting or imposing personal leadings through gifts of utterance (a personal word of knowledge or wisdom to give personal guidance to another person); and

The practice of confessing sins to and deliverance by man rather than God (Menzies 1971, 325).

The General Council officially condemned the Latter Rain Movement in 1949 (McGee 2014, 488). Decisive action and strong teaching by leaders of the Assemblies of God defused this serious threat to the unity of Pentecostals and the AG. By 1951, the movement had largely subsided, although it would later resurface around the fringes of the charismatic movement in the 1970s and the New Apostolic Reformation of the 2000s.

Even with this official rebuke, there were those who chose to disagree. Stanley Frodsham, who was editor of the Pentecostal Evangel for thirty years, had been instrumental in graciously defending the Assemblies of God against its critics and was swept up in the Latter Rain Movement. When the AG publicly taught against key teachings embraced by the New Order of the Latter Rain, Frodsham resigned his position and AG ministerial credentials to avoid conflict and confusion.

The Salvation and Healing Movement (Late 1940s)

An exciting new revival movement swept the United States in the 1950s and ‘60s. The Salvation and Healing Movement featured vibrant and appealing evangelists who healed the sick and preached the gospel, often in large tents. Many built national or international audiences through radio and television ministries. Some well-known healing evangelists of this time included Oral Roberts, Gordon Lindsay, William Branham, Jack Coe, Walter Vinson (W. V.) Grant, Asa Alonso (A. A.) Allen, and Kathryn Kuhlman. Although many of these had histories with the Assemblies of God, many withdrew from established denominations to conduct independent ministries. Although some experienced well-publicized and harmful moral failures, overall, the impact of the Salvation and Healing Movement was positive (Rodgers 2014) .This movement:

Renewed interest in evangelism and healing.

Sowed seeds of racial unity and reconciliation, as some evangelists (A. A. Allen and Oral Roberts) refused to segregate their crowds and even promoted integrated ministry.

Prepared the way for the Charismatic Movement, as believers in mainline denominations were attracted by the healings and exposed to the working of the Holy Spirit. Explain the tension many classical Pentecostals felt in choosing how to respond to Pentecostals in mainline churches

Oral Roberts

The Charismatic Renewal (1960)

The church world was shocked in 1960 when Rector Dennis Bennett told his congregation at St. Mark’s Episcopal Church in Van Nuys, California, that he had been baptized in the Holy Spirit and spoken in tongues. The real controversy was stirred when he announced that he had no intention of leaving the Episcopal church. Fifty-five years earlier, believers who had been baptized in the Spirit and spoke in other tongues were rejected and forced from their churches. By 1960, however, many traditional Christians had been exposed to the evangelists in the Salvation and Healing Movement, arousing their interest in the power and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Although not all churches, pastors, and members were accepting of these spiritual experiences, renewal began to sweep among many where it was least expected—Episcopalians, Lutherans, Methodists, Greek Orthodox, and, starting in 1967, even Roman Catholics. This revival of spiritual gifts became known as the charismatic renewal (from the Greek word charisma or gift). Many classical Pentecostals expected the newly baptized charismatics to leave their old churches and join with other Pentecostals. However, some Pentecostals recognized it as an opportunity to spread Pentecostal experience to many more churches and encouraged these charismatics to stay within their churches.

As with any new work of God, some people were eager to embrace it, while others were not. For some Pentecostals, the desire for revival within the churches that had once rejected them was strong. After all, was not this the fulfillment of their earliest expectations that the Holy Spirit would bring unity to all believers through a new spiritual awakening? But the need for caution was also strongly felt. Many Pentecostals were concerned that unity with mainline churches would bring compromise and cause Pentecostals to lose their distinctive teachings. Would the Assemblies of God successfully balance the desire for unity with the necessity of maintaining biblical purity and integrity?

In 1972, the AG issued a statement that reflected its cautious embrace of the charismatic renewal: “The winds of the Spirit are blowing freely outside the normally recognized Pentecostal body…The Assemblies of God does not place approval on that which is manifestly not scriptural in doctrine or conduct.

But neither do we categorically condemn everything that does not totally… conform to our standards…It is important to find our way in a scriptural path, avoiding extremes of ecumenism that compromises scriptural principles and an exclusivism that excludes true Christians” (Rodgers 2014).

Although it was confusing for many in the AG to reconcile their understanding of the Pentecostal experience with the liturgy, teaching, and practices of these mainline churches that seemed so contrary to the free moving of the Spirit, the Assemblies of God chose to support their Pentecostal brothers and sisters in other denominations. At the 1975 General Council, the Assemblies of God issued a resolution of support for the Charismatic Renewal. The resolution approved and encouraged Assemblies of God ministers to provide assistance to ministers of other denominations who were seeking to know more about Spirit baptism.

The Toronto Blessing (1994)

In 1994, revival came to the Airport Vineyard Fellowship in Toronto, Canada. Although it brought many positive results, it also stirred controversy. Unusual verbal manifestations—animal sounds, screaming, shouting, weeping, and laughter—as well as physical manifestations—slayings in the Spirit as well as jerking, shaking, and acting drunk—made many uncomfortable and caused some to wonder if it were truly of God. Services were held six nights a week for twelve and a half years, reaching many curious and seeking people. Toronto-style revivals sprung up in congregations around the world, including in Pensacola, Florida.

The Pensacola Outpouring (Brownsville Revival, 1995)

On Father’s Day in 1995, at the Brownsville Assembly of God, a strong presence of the Lord was manifest. Evangelist Steve Hill and Pastor John Kilpatrick began holding meetings seven days a week as crowds were coming from around the nation and the world to experience the moving of the Spirit taking place. By 1998, two and a half million people had come to Brownsville, AG; thousands had been saved or reinvigorated. Many took the Brownsville Revival to their home churches. Again, the unusual manifestations caused controversy. Since the revival had started in an Assemblies of God church and was endorsed by the General Council, its leaders took great care to monitor, advise, and assist Pastor Kilpatrick and the Brownsville Revival (McGee 2014, 488).

At this time, some of the more radical teachings of the New Order of the Latter Rain resurfaced, including the restoration of offices of apostles and prophets, generational curses, and the imparting of personal leadings to others by means of tongues, interpretation, and prophecy. In response, the AG Commission on Doctrinal Purity studied the issue and, on August 11, 2000, reported its conclusions in a position paper titled “Endtime Revival—Spirit-Led and Spirit-Controlled.” Once again, the Assemblies of God carefully balanced openness to new moves of God with measuring everything against the teachings of Scripture, as had the Bereans in Acts 17.

The report stated: “In times of revival God often reminds the Church of neglected truths. When this happens, it is easy for extremes to develop. Some will reject the revival of a doctrine, while others in their zeal will go beyond the teaching of Scripture. Both extremes are harmful and bring reproach on the cause of Christ” (General Council 2000).

Balancing Discernment and Unity

God designed us for fellowship. We are stronger together than when we stand alone, and unity should be a defining characteristic of the church. Ephesians 4:1– 7 (NLT) tells us:

Lead a life worthy of your calling, for you have been called by God. Always be humble and gentle. Be patient with each other, making allowance for each other’s faults because of your love. Make every effort to keep yourselves united in the Spirit, binding yourselves together with peace. For there is one body and one Spirit, just as you have been called to one glorious hope for the future. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, in all, and living through all. However, he has given each one of us a special gift through the generosity of Christ.

Still, discernment is of great importance, lest we open our arms to or bind ourselves in associations with those who would lead us astray from the truth of the full gospel. Assemblies of God educator William Menzies summarized what is needed in charting a balanced course in fellowshipping with non-Pentecostals and relating to new Pentecostal outpourings outside the framework of our own experience: “Certainly Pentecostals are evangelicals, but the unique contribution of Pentecostal understanding needs to be articulated freshly so Pentecostal values are not submerged within evangelical teaching. Pentecostals will also need to develop constructive ways to relate to charismatics, without compromising the authority of Scripture and the importance of historic doctrines of faith” (Menzies 1999).

It all comes down to understanding what the Bible says so that we may come together with others on those points in which we agree while standing firm in our biblical beliefs. Rupertus Meldenius, 1582–1651, a German theologian, gave good counsel when he said: “In essentials, unity; in nonessentials, liberty; in all things, charity."

**Q:** List the issues that caused division during the Latter Rain Movement and describe the Assemblies of God’s response.

**A:** The issues were alienation, lack of accountability, and erroneous teachings, to which the General Council responded by condemning the movement.

**Q:** What lessons in unity can be learned from the Charismatic Renewal?

**A:** God can move among the people of the mainline churches, and the Assemblies of God can support their brothers and sisters in other denominations who are open to the Spirit’s baptism.

**Q:** Paraphrase why discernment is vital for the believer.

**A:** It protects us from error and helps us find the balance between fellowship and unity with others. At the same time, it allows us to maintain our distinctiveness without compromising our beliefs. UNIT 3

They feared that Pentecostals’ zeal and spiritual power had declined. Once again, some longed for a fresh revival and a restoration of all the gifts of the Spirit as demonstrated in the New Testament church.

When revival broke out in Saskatchewan, Canada, in 1948, it quickly spread to the United States. Many Pentecostals flocked to meetings to judge for themselves whether this new movement was of God. Among these was Stanley Frodsham, the influential editor of the Pentecostal Evangel . After attending revival meetings in Detroit, Michigan, Frodsham declared, “This is God” (Scott 1967, interview).

But not everyone in the Assemblies of God felt that way. Problems quickly developed that caused division among proponents of Latter Rain and more traditional Pentecostals:

1. Alienation . Latter Rain proponents denounced Pentecostal denominations having lost the fire of the Holy Ghost and becoming apostate.

2. Lack of accountability . The Latter Rain Movement practiced an extreme form of congregationalism that did not recognize denominational authority. This led to many of the same abuses of power that had made it important to organize the Assemblies of God. Some who claimed the titles and authority of modern-day prophets and apostles besmirched the name of Christ with their immorality and controversial doctrines (Rodgers 2014).

3. Erroneous teachings . Below are some doctrines promoted by the Latter Rain Movement that were questionable:

The belief that the church is to be built on present-day prophets and apostles;

Overemphasis on identifying, imparting, and bestowing of gifts by the laying on of hands and prophecy;

Belief in the giving of the gift of tongues for missionary service;

The extreme and unscriptural practice of imparting or imposing personal leadings through gifts of utterance (a personal word of knowledge or wisdom to give personal guidance to another person); and

The practice of confessing sins to and deliverance by man rather than God (Menzies 1971, 325).

The General Council officially condemned the Latter Rain Movement in 1949 (McGee 2014, 488). Decisive action and strong teaching by leaders of the Assemblies of God defused this serious threat to the unity of Pentecostals and the AG. By 1951, the movement had largely subsided, although it would later resurface around the fringes of the charismatic movement in the 1970s and the New Apostolic Reformation of the 2000s.

Even with this official rebuke, there were those who chose to disagree. Stanley Frodsham, who was editor of the Pentecostal Evangel for thirty years, had been instrumental in graciously defending the Assemblies of God against its critics and was swept up in the Latter Rain Movement. When the AG publicly taught against key teachings embraced by the New Order of the Latter Rain, Frodsham resigned his position and AG ministerial credentials to avoid conflict and confusion.

The Salvation and Healing Movement (Late 1940s)

An exciting new revival movement swept the United States in the 1950s and ‘60s. The Salvation and Healing Movement featured vibrant and appealing evangelists who healed the sick and preached the gospel, often in large tents. Many built national or international audiences through radio and television ministries. Some well-known healing evangelists of this time included Oral Roberts, Gordon Lindsay, William Branham, Jack Coe, Walter Vinson (W. V.) Grant, Asa Alonso (A. A.) Allen, and Kathryn Kuhlman. Although many of these had histories with the Assemblies of God, many withdrew from established denominations to conduct independent ministries. Although some experienced well-publicized and harmful moral failures, overall, the impact of the Salvation and Healing Movement was positive (Rodgers 2014) .This movement:

Renewed interest in evangelism and healing.

Sowed seeds of racial unity and reconciliation, as some evangelists (A. A. Allen and Oral Roberts) refused to segregate their crowds and even promoted integrated ministry.

Prepared the way for the Charismatic Movement, as believers in mainline denominations were attracted by the healings and exposed to the working of the Holy Spirit. Explain the tension many classical Pentecostals felt in choosing how to respond to Pentecostals in mainline churches

Oral Roberts

The Charismatic Renewal (1960)

The church world was shocked in 1960 when Rector Dennis Bennett told his congregation at St. Mark’s Episcopal Church in Van Nuys, California, that he had been baptized in the Holy Spirit and spoken in tongues. The real controversy was stirred when he announced that he had no intention of leaving the Episcopal church. Fifty-five years earlier, believers who had been baptized in the Spirit and spoke in other tongues were rejected and forced from their churches. By 1960, however, many traditional Christians had been exposed to the evangelists in the Salvation and Healing Movement, arousing their interest in the power and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Although not all churches, pastors, and members were accepting of these spiritual experiences, renewal began to sweep among many where it was least expected—Episcopalians, Lutherans, Methodists, Greek Orthodox, and, starting in 1967, even Roman Catholics. This revival of spiritual gifts became known as the charismatic renewal (from the Greek word charisma or gift). Many classical Pentecostals expected the newly baptized charismatics to leave their old churches and join with other Pentecostals. However, some Pentecostals recognized it as an opportunity to spread Pentecostal experience to many more churches and encouraged these charismatics to stay within their churches.

As with any new work of God, some people were eager to embrace it, while others were not. For some Pentecostals, the desire for revival within the churches that had once rejected them was strong. After all, was not this the fulfillment of their earliest expectations that the Holy Spirit would bring unity to all believers through a new spiritual awakening? But the need for caution was also strongly felt. Many Pentecostals were concerned that unity with mainline churches would bring compromise and cause Pentecostals to lose their distinctive teachings. Would the Assemblies of God successfully balance the desire for unity with the necessity of maintaining biblical purity and integrity?

In 1972, the AG issued a statement that reflected its cautious embrace of the charismatic renewal: “The winds of the Spirit are blowing freely outside the normally recognized Pentecostal body…The Assemblies of God does not place approval on that which is manifestly not scriptural in doctrine or conduct.

But neither do we categorically condemn everything that does not totally… conform to our standards…It is important to find our way in a scriptural path, avoiding extremes of ecumenism that compromises scriptural principles and an exclusivism that excludes true Christians” (Rodgers 2014).

Although it was confusing for many in the AG to reconcile their understanding of the Pentecostal experience with the liturgy, teaching, and practices of these mainline churches that seemed so contrary to the free moving of the Spirit, the Assemblies of God chose to support their Pentecostal brothers and sisters in other denominations. At the 1975 General Council, the Assemblies of God issued a resolution of support for the Charismatic Renewal. The resolution approved and encouraged Assemblies of God ministers to provide assistance to ministers of other denominations who were seeking to know more about Spirit baptism.

The Toronto Blessing (1994)

In 1994, revival came to the Airport Vineyard Fellowship in Toronto, Canada. Although it brought many positive results, it also stirred controversy. Unusual verbal manifestations—animal sounds, screaming, shouting, weeping, and laughter—as well as physical manifestations—slayings in the Spirit as well as jerking, shaking, and acting drunk—made many uncomfortable and caused some to wonder if it were truly of God. Services were held six nights a week for twelve and a half years, reaching many curious and seeking people. Toronto-style revivals sprung up in congregations around the world, including in Pensacola, Florida.

The Pensacola Outpouring (Brownsville Revival, 1995)

On Father’s Day in 1995, at the Brownsville Assembly of God, a strong presence of the Lord was manifest. Evangelist Steve Hill and Pastor John Kilpatrick began holding meetings seven days a week as crowds were coming from around the nation and the world to experience the moving of the Spirit taking place. By 1998, two and a half million people had come to Brownsville, AG; thousands had been saved or reinvigorated. Many took the Brownsville Revival to their home churches. Again, the unusual manifestations caused controversy. Since the revival had started in an Assemblies of God church and was endorsed by the General Council, its leaders took great care to monitor, advise, and assist Pastor Kilpatrick and the Brownsville Revival (McGee 2014, 488).

At this time, some of the more radical teachings of the New Order of the Latter Rain resurfaced, including the restoration of offices of apostles and prophets, generational curses, and the imparting of personal leadings to others by means of tongues, interpretation, and prophecy. In response, the AG Commission on Doctrinal Purity studied the issue and, on August 11, 2000, reported its conclusions in a position paper titled “Endtime Revival—Spirit-Led and Spirit-Controlled.” Once again, the Assemblies of God carefully balanced openness to new moves of God with measuring everything against the teachings of Scripture, as had the Bereans in Acts 17.

The report stated: “In times of revival God often reminds the Church of neglected truths. When this happens, it is easy for extremes to develop. Some will reject the revival of a doctrine, while others in their zeal will go beyond the teaching of Scripture. Both extremes are harmful and bring reproach on the cause of Christ” (General Council 2000).

Balancing Discernment and Unity

God designed us for fellowship. We are stronger together than when we stand alone, and unity should be a defining characteristic of the church. Ephesians 4:1– 7 (NLT) tells us:

Lead a life worthy of your calling, for you have been called by God. Always be humble and gentle. Be patient with each other, making allowance for each other’s faults because of your love. Make every effort to keep yourselves united in the Spirit, binding yourselves together with peace. For there is one body and one Spirit, just as you have been called to one glorious hope for the future. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, in all, and living through all. However, he has given each one of us a special gift through the generosity of Christ.

Still, discernment is of great importance, lest we open our arms to or bind ourselves in associations with those who would lead us astray from the truth of the full gospel. Assemblies of God educator William Menzies summarized what is needed in charting a balanced course in fellowshipping with non-Pentecostals and relating to new Pentecostal outpourings outside the framework of our own experience: “Certainly Pentecostals are evangelicals, but the unique contribution of Pentecostal understanding needs to be articulated freshly so Pentecostal values are not submerged within evangelical teaching. Pentecostals will also need to develop constructive ways to relate to charismatics, without compromising the authority of Scripture and the importance of historic doctrines of faith” (Menzies 1999).

It all comes down to understanding what the Bible says so that we may come together with others on those points in which we agree while standing firm in our biblical beliefs. Rupertus Meldenius, 1582–1651, a German theologian, gave good counsel when he said: “In essentials, unity; in nonessentials, liberty; in all things, charity."

**Q:** List the issues that caused division during the Latter Rain Movement and describe the Assemblies of God’s response.

**A:** The issues were alienation, lack of accountability, and erroneous teachings, to which the General Council responded by condemning the movement.

**Q:** What lessons in unity can be learned from the Charismatic Renewal?

**A:** God can move among the people of the mainline churches, and the Assemblies of God can support their brothers and sisters in other denominations who are open to the Spirit’s baptism.

**Q:** Paraphrase why discernment is vital for the believer.

**A:** It protects us from error and helps us find the balance between fellowship and unity with others. At the same time, it allows us to maintain our distinctiveness without compromising our beliefs. UNIT 3
