In response, the AG Commission on Doctrinal Purity studied the issue and, on August 11, 2000, reported its conclusions in a position paper titled “Endtime Revival—Spirit-Led and Spirit-Controlled.” Once again, the Assemblies of God carefully balanced openness to new moves of God with measuring everything against the teachings of Scripture, as had the Bereans in Acts 17.

The report stated: “In times of revival God often reminds the Church of neglected truths. When this happens, it is easy for extremes to develop. Some will reject the revival of a doctrine, while others in their zeal will go beyond the teaching of Scripture. Both extremes are harmful and bring reproach on the cause of Christ” (General Council 2000).

Balancing Discernment and Unity

God designed us for fellowship. We are stronger together than when we stand alone, and unity should be a defining characteristic of the church. Ephesians 4:1– 7 (NLT) tells us:

Lead a life worthy of your calling, for you have been called by God. Always be humble and gentle. Be patient with each other, making allowance for each other’s faults because of your love. Make every effort to keep yourselves united in the Spirit, binding yourselves together with peace. For there is one body and one Spirit, just as you have been called to one glorious hope for the future. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, in all, and living through all. However, he has given each one of us a special gift through the generosity of Christ.

Still, discernment is of great importance, lest we open our arms to or bind ourselves in associations with those who would lead us astray from the truth of the full gospel. Assemblies of God educator William Menzies summarized what is needed in charting a balanced course in fellowshipping with non-Pentecostals and relating to new Pentecostal outpourings outside the framework of our own experience: “Certainly Pentecostals are evangelicals, but the unique contribution of Pentecostal understanding needs to be articulated freshly so Pentecostal values are not submerged within evangelical teaching. Pentecostals will also need to develop constructive ways to relate to charismatics, without compromising the authority of Scripture and the importance of historic doctrines of faith” (Menzies 1999).

It all comes down to understanding what the Bible says so that we may come together with others on those points in which we agree while standing firm in our biblical beliefs. Rupertus Meldenius, 1582–1651, a German theologian, gave good counsel when he said: “In essentials, unity; in nonessentials, liberty; in all things, charity."

**Q:** List the issues that caused division during the Latter Rain Movement and describe the Assemblies of God’s response.

**A:** The issues were alienation, lack of accountability, and erroneous teachings, to which the General Council responded by condemning the movement.

**Q:** What lessons in unity can be learned from the Charismatic Renewal?

**A:** God can move among the people of the mainline churches, and the Assemblies of God can support their brothers and sisters in other denominations who are open to the Spirit’s baptism.

**Q:** Paraphrase why discernment is vital for the believer.

**A:** It protects us from error and helps us find the balance between fellowship and unity with others. At the same time, it allows us to maintain our distinctiveness without compromising our beliefs. UNIT 3

## 10

### A Complicated History

#### 10.1.1 — List four African-American pioneers in the Assemblies of God, and describe their contributions.

The Pentecostal revival burst onto the scene in America at a time when many places in the United States had strict rules about people of differing races – especially Black and White individuals – meeting, working, eating, and living together. This was especially true in the central and southeastern part of the country. However, Pentecostal church services were often a notable exception to these rules. People of every race, color, and ethnicity knelt together during the Azusa Street Revival, led by African-American preacher William Seymour. Frank Bartleman, a White Pentecostal preacher and early chronicler of the revival, marveled, “The color line was washed away in the Blood [of Christ]” (McGee 1999).

Historian Edward Ayres agreed: “Indeed, the Holiness and Pentecostal churches violated more of the cultural shibboleths of the New South than any other organization in that time and place. In many ways, these churches inverted the cultural values being disseminated throughout the South…They stressed the ability of anyone, regardless of race, class, or gender, to experience the most thrilling manifestations of God’s love, ignoring the distinctions that multiplied elsewhere in the New South” (Ayers 2007, 407).

The early history of the Assemblies of God demonstrates some wonderful fruit of this racial unity:

Ellsworth S. Thomas (1866–1936) was the first African American to hold ministerial credentials with the newly formed Assemblies of God. Thomas was a credentialed AG minister from 1915 until his death at age 70.

Isaac S. Neeley (1865–1923) and Mattie A. Board Neeley (1866–1940s?) were commissioned as the Assemblies of God’s first African-American missionaries (Liberia) in 1920.

Cornelia Jones Robertson (1891–1967) , who had been a part of the Azusa Street Revival, was a popular evangelist with a nationwide ministry. She transferred her credentials to the Assemblies of God in 1923, becoming one of the first African-American women ordained by the Fellowship. She planted a church in San Francisco and ran a mission in the notorious Barbary Coast district, where she is credited with helping 100,000 men and boys.

Thoro Harris (1874–1955) made an early and substantial impact on Assemblies of God music. Composing almost 600 songs and publishing many songbooks, some of Harris’s best-known songs include “Jesus Loves the Little Children,” “More Abundantly,” “He’s Coming Soon,” “Pentecost in My Soul,” “I Saw the Light,” “Hide Thou Me,” and “All That Thrills My Soul Is Jesus” (Rodgers 2015 and 2017).

But these positive examples were just the vestigial fruit of a racial unity that had already started to wither by the birth of the Assemblies of God in 1914. African- American leader, Charles Harrison Mason, founder and senior bishop of the Church of God in Christ (COGIC), was invited to preach at the AG organizational meeting in 1914, bringing his choir from Memphis to perform at the Hot Springs meeting. Even though he initially blessed the formation of the Assemblies of God, he later expressed concern and disappointment about the racial division he foresaw as the inevitable result of founding another Pentecostal fellowship (Newman 2007, 13).

### The Door to Racial Unity Slammed Shut

#### 10.2.1 — Explain what happened to diversity in the early years of the Assemblies of God, and summarize what led to segregation and exclusion.

For some in the Assemblies of God, the spirit of racial unity and fellowship of all believers continued—as evidenced by the cited examples of Ellsworth Thomas, the Neeleys, Cornelia Jones Robertson, and Thoro Harris, as well as those who supported them and their ministries. Still, the gulf between the races steadily widened.

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, many laws (called Jim Crow laws) were passed in the southern states, limiting rights of Black Americans, including the right to freely integrate into White gatherings, such as churches. In the Great Migration (1916- 1940), many African Americans left the southern United States for areas in the northern, Midwestern, and western states. Most of the Black ministers in the Assemblies of God were in these northern and western states.

A particular problem arose when Black ministers who carried full Assembly of God ordination in northern and western districts came into southern districts and found that their credentials did not automatically provide the same level of freedom to preach. Some southern churches found they had difficulty reaching their communities if the Assemblies of God became widely known as a fully integrated church.

Finally, in 1939, the General Presbytery went on record as disapproving the ordination of African Americans at the national level, while affirming that African Americans could still be licensed at the district level. Northern and western districts continued to grant the more limiting level of licensed credentials, but other districts were not bound to recognize these district credentials or to grant ministry opportunities to those holding them.

The reaction to this policy was mixed. Some felt that it was an appropriate compromise that would only be in place until racial tensions died down. Others felt it was an unacceptable moral compromise with the evil of racial prejudice. Some Assemblies of God people questioned how a fellowship born of the Holy Spirit and with a burning passion for the lost in Africa could fail to love their African-American brothers and sisters in Christ or make room for them in the pulpit and the pew. The following are a few explanations for this inconsistency:

All have sinned (Romans 3:23) .

At its core, racial discrimination is sin. We all fall short of God’s glorious standards. The failings of individual leaders, ministers, and members of the Assemblies of God who were racist or were uncomfortable with breaking social taboos were reflected in the organization they created. The consequences of this sin can still be felt in our nation and fellowship today.

They loved human praise more than praise from God (John 12:43).

Early Pentecostals gladly endured the scorn—even beatings, tarring and feathering, or death—of the world and other churches rather than give up their doctrine and practice of speaking in tongues. But at least in this one area, they were afraid or unwilling to defy social convention. Some argued that it was dangerous to grant full credentials to Black brothers and sisters because it would encourage the breaking of segregation laws. These decisions show how easy it is, even for Spirit-filled believers, to value the approval of their sinful society more than the approval of God and faithfulness to biblical principles.

The church followed societal trend rather than raising the standard of God's greater plan.

Well into the 1960s, many public schools in the United States did not allow Black and White children to attend school together, even though this enforced segregation became illegal in 1954. Some members feared that if the Assemblies of God was known as a church that had integrated Sunday schools, many unsaved neighbors would never allow their children to attend. As late as 1958, some Assemblies of God leaders made it clear that they believed integrated churches would not be effective in reaching the lost, and thus they would embrace desegregation only if convinced that it would not interfere with the “progress and expansion of the movement” (Newman 2007, 10).

They deceived themselves that the evangelism of the Black community was not their responsibility (Galatians 6:3-5).

Few White believers in the Assemblies of God were likely to have considered themselves or their church to be racist. Yet the policies and practices of many were actively pushing African Americans away from the Fellowship. No matter how kindly stated or what the reasoning given, the message was clear: African-Americans were not equally welcome in the Assemblies of God. Before the early 1960s, fewer than ten African Americans were listed as Assemblies of God ministers at any given time (Newman 2007, 11).

**Q:** How did Jesus’ encounter with the Samaritan woman break with the social norms of His day?

**A:** Racial and religious prejudices separated the Jewish and Samaritan people. The Jews did not associate with Samaritans (Acts 10:28; John 4:9).

**Q:** What influences have shaped your view of racial segregation?

**A:** Answers will vary.

### Knocking Until the Doors Open

#### 10.3.1 — Describe Bob Harrison's role in opening the door to integration in the Assemblies of God.

While some local churches through the years may have opened their arms to African-American individuals, it is easy to understand why few Black believers persisted or pursued ministry or leadership roles. Yet some did, making inroads and opening doors for others to follow. One of these was Robert E. (Bob) Harrison (1920–2012).

In 1951, Harrison became the first African American to graduate from Bethany Bible College (receiving a certificate of theology). Although graduates were eligible for district licensing, Harrison’s application was denied because of his race. He and his wife, Marilyn, pastored an independent church until, through the efforts of Northern California–Nevada District Superintendent Leonard Palmer, Harrison was licensed with the district in 1957. He was, however, still denied credentials by the national body due to the 1939 policy denying ordination to Black people.

Harrison’s ministerial gifts soon led to an invitation from Billy Graham to join his crusade team. Motivated by the changing societal standards amid the success of the Civil Rights Movement and embarrassed that the Graham organization was willing to platform a minister they had refused ordination, the General Council reversed its 1939 policy and ordained Harrison in 1962 (McGee 2004, 304). His highly-visible ordination and success as a missionary and evangelist brought into public focus the existence of racism and racial exclusion within the Assemblies of God. The graciousness of Bob Harrison in accepting ordination from the church that had rejected him became a catalyst for change.

In 1965, the General Council officially condemned racial discrimination:

“RESOLVED, that we reaffirm our belief in the teachings of Christ including His emphasis upon the inherent worth and intrinsic value of every man, regardless of race, class, creed, or color, and we urge all our constituency to discourage unfair and discriminatory practices wherever they exist and, be it further RESOLVED, that we believe those in authority in political, social, and particularly in evangelical groups, have a moral responsibility toward the creation of those situations which will provide equal rights and opportunities for every individual.” (General Council Minutes 1965, 61)

As a clear indicator of progress, in 1967, Harrison was invited to speak at the General Council in Long Beach, California (Hufman 2020). And in 1972, at the Council on Spiritual Life in Minneapolis, Harrison was a featured speaker again, urging the AG to go further and highlighting the Spirit’s ministry of racial reconciliation (McGee 2004, 383).

**Q:** In what way can the local church address the issue of segregation? How can you and your church overcome racial division?

**A:** Repent and seek reconciliation. Be intentional in reaching out to those of different races. Develop a multicultural staff. Provide bilingual services. Organize and attend services across racial lines.

### Steps in the Right Direction

#### 10.4.1 — Outline some of the progress made under Thomas F. Zimmerman and in the years to follow toward becoming more inclusive.

Along with changing attitudes nationwide and the push for inclusion from within the ministerial ranks, a new, younger general superintendent enlarged the AG commitment to diversity. Under the leadership of Thomas F. Zimmerman (in office 1959–1985) and then G. Raymond Carlson (in office 1986-1993), the Assemblies of God made great efforts to improve on its record by embracing ministry to and by African-Americans.

In the 1960s, Zimmerman dialogued with the Fellowship’s few African-American ministers to better understand their concerns.

The organization’s colleges began aggressively recruiting African-American ministerial students.

In the 1970s and ‘80s, the Pentecostal Evangel highlighted the establishment of new outreach ministries targeting African Americans in inner cities (Newman 2007, 11).

After decades of small beginnings, AG African Americans officially organized as the Inner City Workers Conference in 1980. Spencer Jones was the first president. The name was changed to the National Black Fellowship on July 28-30, 1998. This was to be “a network of urban churches and Christian leaders committed to community transformation and positively impacting people’s lives through the Spirit of God…by implementing strategies through existing and new urban churches; by raising indigenous leaders and revitalizing under-resourced neighborhoods” (National Black Fellowship 2021).

In 1989, the 43rd General Council adopted "Resolution 20. Racism":

WHEREAS, Racism is an issue that continues to confront the church and American society today; and

WHEREAS, Racism continues to confront our brothers and sisters in other countries; and

WHEREAS, The Bible recognizes that all people are created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27; 5:1,2); and

WHEREAS, The Bible declares that the barriers that separate us from one another have been broken down through Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:26–28; Colossians 3:11); and

WHEREAS, In the Early Church the Holy Spirit confronted divisions along racial lines and brought reconciliation (Acts 6:1–7; 10:1–22); therefore be it

RESOLVED, That the Assemblies of God oppose the sin of racism in any form; and be it further

RESOLVED, That we call any and all to repentance who have participated in the sin of racism through personal thought or action, or through church and social structures, or through inactivity in addressing racism as individuals or as a church; and be it further

RESOLVED, That we pray for God to give us the courage to confront the sin of racism where it may be found in our own lives, in our churches, in our society structures, and in our world; and be it further

RESOLVED, That we participate with the work of the Holy Spirit in actively working against racism at home and abroad, and that we seek the reconciliation of man to God and man to man. ( AG OFFICIAL )

From the Assemblies of God’s early failure to stand against racism before it became popular to do so, we can learn an important lesson. We would be wise to resist embracing any popular idea, belief, attitude, or action that does not line up with God’s Word—no matter how appealing and timely it may seem or how difficult it feels to go against the flow of popular culture.

After more than thirty years of progress and attempting to make amends, the stage was set for one of the most necessary and significant miracles ever experienced in the Assemblies of God and the broader Pentecostal movement.

**Q:** In what ways did the early church confront social divisions?

**A:** The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) met to resolve differences between Jewish and Gentile believers. See: Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–18.

### Recognition, Repentance, and Reconciliation: The Memphis Miracle

#### 10.5.1 — Summarize what happened surrounding the Memphis Miracle and why it was necessary.

As mentioned in Chapter 8, when representatives of various Pentecostal denominations met in 1948 to form an association, not a single Black denomination was invited. The Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (PFNA), which was created to promote fellowship among Pentecostals, purposefully disfellowshipped a large portion of its potential members. This officially cemented the racial divide and was a blot on Pentecostalism for more than forty years.

Finally, in the early 1990s, preparations were made to correct this transgression and bring Black and White Pentecostals back into fellowship by dissolving the PFNA and replacing it with a new, inclusive organization.

After a series of preparatory meetings over the course of more than a year, representatives from Black and White Pentecostal denominations met together in October 1994 in Memphis, Tennessee—a city known for great racial conflict. Scholars from many of the organizations—Black and White—presented carefully researched papers identifying the causes and particulars of racism that had done great damage to the body of Christ and to Pentecostals’ witness to the world.

The airing of grievances opened old wounds; voices were raised in anger and defensiveness. The grievances were legitimate; so were the feelings of defensiveness.

The tension and frustration were finally broken in the afternoon session, when Bishop Charles E. Blake of the Church of God in Christ tearfully announced, “Brothers and Sisters, I commit my love to you. There are problems down the road, but a strong commitment to love will overcome them all” (Synan 2021).

With that, the Holy Spirit moved upon the entire assembly. A young Black brother in the audience gave a message in tongues, which was interpreted by White pastor Jack Hayford of the International Church of the Foursquare Gospel:

“Look, for I, by my Spirit, am flowing the two streams into one. And the two becoming one, if you can see from the heaven side of things, are being purified and not only is there a new purity coming in your midst, but there will be multitudes more who will gather at this one mighty river because they will see the purity of the reality of my love manifest in you. And so, know that as heaven observes and tells us what is taking place, there is reason for you to rejoice and prepare yourself for there shall be multitudes more than ever before come to this joint surging of my grace among you, says the Lord” (Synan 2021).

Moved by the Spirit, Pastor Don Evans, a White pastor from a multicultural church in Tampa, Florida, approached the head table with a tin of water and a janitor’s rag. He tearfully washed Bishop Ithiel Clemmons’s (COGIC) feet, pleading for forgiveness for the sins of White people against their Black brothers and sisters. A wave of weeping and repentance swept through the room. Bishop Blake then turned and tearfully washed the feet of Assemblies of God General Superintendent Thomas Trask in repentance for the animosity Black brothers and sisters had harbored toward their White counterparts. People wept and embraced, as the Lord broke down walls of misunderstanding, hard feelings, and prejudice and poured out a healing spirit of love and grace.

The next day, the group convened for one last meeting of the PFNA—just long enough to vote unanimously to dissolve it and replace it with a new, multiracial fellowship, the Pentecostal and Charismatic Churches of North America (PCCNA), governed by an interracial executive committee. “We cannot undo the racism of the past,” said Trask, “but we can with the Lord’s help write a new and better chapter” (McGee 2004, 485).

Racial Reconciliation Manifesto

The delegates in Memphis adopted the following covenant to commit themselves to racial reconciliation:

I. I pledge in concert with my brothers and sisters of many hues to oppose racism prophetically in all its various manifestations within and without the Body of Christ and to be vigilant in the struggle with all my God-given might.

II. I am committed personally to treat those in the Fellowship who are not of my race or ethnicity, regardless of color, with love and respect as my sisters and brothers in Christ. I am further committed to work against all forms of personal and institutional racism, including those which are revealed within the very structures of our environment.

III. With complete boldness and courageous honesty, we mutually confess that racism is sin and as a blight in the Fellowship must be condemned for having hindered the maturation of spiritual development and mutual sharing among Pentecostal-Charismatic believers for decades.

IV. We openly confess our shortcomings and our participation in the sin of racism by our silence, denial and blindness. We admit the harm it has brought to generations born and unborn. We strongly contend that the past does not always completely determine the future. New horizons are emerging. God wants to do a new thing through His people.

V. We admit that there is no single solution to racism in the Fellowship. We pray and are open to tough love and radical repentance with deep sensitivity to the Holy Spirit as Liberator.

VI. Together we will work to affirm one another’s strengths and acknowledge our own weaknesses and inadequacies, recognizing that all of us only “see in a mirror dimly” what God desires to do in this world. Together, we affirm the wholeness of the Body of Christ as fully inclusive of Christians regardless of color. We, therefore, commit ourselves “to love one another with mutual affection, outdoing one another in showing honor (Romans 12:10).”

VI. We commit ourselves not only to pray but also to work for genuine and visible manifestations of Christian unity.

VIII. We hereby commit ourselves not only to the task of making prophetic denouncement of racism in word and creed, but to live by acting in deed. We will fully support and encourage those among us who are attempting change.

IX. We pledge that we will return to our various constituencies and appeal to them for logistical support and intervention as necessary in opposing racism. We will seek partnerships and exchange pulpits with persons of a different hue, not in a paternalistic sense, but in the Spirit of our Blessed Lord who prayed that we might be one (John 17:21).

X. We commit ourselves to leaving our comfort zones, lay aside our warring, racial allegiances, respecting the full humanity of all, live with an openness to authentic liberation which is a product of Divine Creation, until the shackles fall and all bondage ceases.

XI. At the beginning of the twentieth century, the Azusa Street Mission was a model of preaching and living the Gospel message in the world. We desire to drink deeply from the well of Pentecost as it was embodied in that mission. We, therefore, pledge our commitment to embrace the essential commitments of that mission in evangelism and mission, in justice and holiness, in spiritual renewal and empowerment, and in the reconciliation of all Christians regardless of race or gender as we move into the new millennium. (Pentecostal-Charismatic Theological Inquiry International, n.d)

**Q:** What role did the Holy Spirit play in opening the gospel to the Gentiles? What was the role of the Spirit in breaking the social divide?

**A:** Peter was sent to Cornelius’s household to preach the gospel. They received the gift of the Holy Spirit as Peter spoke (Acts 10:44-47).

**Q:** Write and adopt a resolution of reconciliation that can be applied in your local church.

**A:** Answers will vary.

### Beyond Memphis: The Memphis Mandate

#### 10.6.1 — Analyze the post-Memphis Miracle progress of the Assemblies of God as related to inclusion, unity, and racial healing.

True to General Superintendent Trask’s word, the Assemblies of God immediately started writing a new and better chapter in race relations:

General Council leaders began inviting COGIC bishops to speak at their conferences and events.

The Assemblies of God Theological Seminary named its new chapel after William J. Seymour.

Analyze the post-Memphis Miracle progress of the Assemblies of God as related to inclusion, unity, and racial healing. In 2009, Zollie Smith was elected director of Assemblies of God U.S. Missions, the first African-American to hold an executive leadership position.

At the time of a 2015 Pew Research Center Report, the Assemblies of God was the most diverse Evangelical denomination in the United States ( AG News 2015).

In August 2015, the General Council unanimously voted to approve the creation of a designated African-American executive presbyter. After the positive vote, delegates stood and applauded. A standing ovation was also given to Superintendent Wood in recognition of his ongoing efforts toward racial reconciliation. (Kennedy 2015).

In 2017, Samuel M. Huddleston was elected the first designated African-American executive presbyter (Kennedy 2017).

In 2019, at the twenty-five-year anniversary celebration of the Memphis Miracle, AG General Superintendent Doug Clay served communion with COGIC Bishop Charles Blake and Samuel Rodriguez, president of the National Hispanic Christian Leadership Conference. “May we who come to the table of the Lord as one body do more than just talk the talk but recognize that we are brothers and sisters in Christ because of His shed blood,” Clay said. “Communion reminds us that never again does there have to be a separation between God and man. I pray that we will make a commitment that there never needs to be separation in the body of Christ because of the color of skin” (Faith News Network 2019).

In 2020, Evangel University created a new full-tuition scholarship named after Bob Harrison, the AG Bible college graduate who was instrumental in opening the door for African-Americans to be ordained in the Assemblies of God. The Bob and Marilyn Harrison Emerging Leaders Scholarship is awarded to an African-American student with the potential to have as great an impact on the Assemblies of God and race relations as did the scholarship’s namesakes (Huffman 2020). S elect two of the steps forward for African Americans after the Memphis Miracle that you think are most significant, and tell why you chose them.

In 2020, a record 44.3 percent of AG adherents were ethnic minorities, including an all-time high of 11.1 percent who are Black (Kennedy 2020b). That is a significant increase since 2001, when just 6.2 percent of AG adherents were African-American (Kennedy 2020b). 10 . 7 LESSON

### The Individual Mandate

#### 10.7.1 — Reexamine your own attitudes and actions with regard to racism, and create and implement a biblical personal plan for healing racial divisions.

Years ago, a growing community struggled to keep its streets free of litter. They strategically placed trash cans to make doing the right thing easier. It helped some, but the problem persisted. An ad campaign reminding people to stop littering changed little. It seemed that the litterers were never going to be persuaded to stop. Finally, the town changed its message and audience. Those who cared about keeping the streets clean and conscientiously avoided littering were asked to help solve the problem by picking up litter—even though they were not responsible and had not caused the mess. This worked; the streets soon improved dramatically.

The sin of racism has littered the streets of the Assemblies of God for generations. It must be acknowledged, addressed, and atoned for. The Memphis Miracle; official resolutions and executive statements on racism; aggressive recruitment of black students and leaders; outreach to black denominations, churches, communities, and individuals; and recent structural efforts to ensure inclusion and representation are good starting steps toward those goals that must be continued.

When Spencer Jones started his ministry in Chicago, he won over his White neighbors by grilling T-bone steaks for them and shoveling their snowy sidewalks (Morgan 2020). What can you do today to demonstrate love and build unity with your brothers and sisters of another race? What can you do to help clean up the racism littering your “street”—even if it is not technically your mess to clean up?

If you truly want to be a part of racial reconciliation and understanding in your church, your denomination, your city, your nation, and your world, consider the counsel of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. who gave commitment cards to people who wanted to do their part in the quest for racial justice. The card called for participants to pledge to do the following:

1. Meditate daily on the teachings and life of Jesus.

2. Remember always to seek justice and reconciliation—not victory.

3. Walk and talk in the manner of love, for God is love.

4. Pray daily to be used by God.

5. Sacrifice personal wishes in order that all people might be free.

6. Observe with both friend and foe the ordinary rules of courtesy.

7. Seek to perform regular service for others.

8. Refrain from the violence of fist, tongue, or heart.

9. Strive to be in good spiritual and bodily health (King 1963).

The plan was a game changer then, and it is still relevant today. Will you commit to doing your part to advance racial reconciliation and harmony in the church and the nation?

**Q:** List several biblical principles and verses that you can apply to your own life in regards to racism.

**A:** These may include: look at the heart (1 Sam. 16:7), bear one another’s burdens (Gal. 6:2), do not judge (Matt. 7:1), be forgiving (Eph. 4:32), remember that all have sinned (Rom. 3:23 ), and understand that revenge is not yours to give and justice must be left in God’s hands (Rom. 12:19). ## 11

### Ethnic Transformation

#### 11.1.1 — Contrast the growth and vitality of ethnic minorities with those of Whites within the Assemblies of God.

¿Hablas español? (Do you speak Spanish?) As of 2020, around 580 million people in the world speak Spanish; it is the native language of 483 million of those, making it the second most common mother tongue in the world (behind Mandarin Chinese; English is third) (Ghosh 2020). In 2018, more than 41 million in the United States spoke Spanish rather than English in the home (United States Census Bureau 2019). Many resources from the Assemblies of God National Office are now available in Spanish as well as English.

日本語は話せますか ? (Do you speak Japanese?)

هل تتحدث العربية (Do you speak Arabic?)

Koj puas paub hais lus Hmoob? (Do you speak Hmong?)

Stii sa vorbesti romaneste? (Do you speak Romanian?) C ontrast the growth and vitality of ethnic minorities with those of Whites within the Assemblies of God

Whether you speak Spanish, Japanese, Arabic, Hmong, Romanian, or one of more than a dozen other languages, you can find an Assemblies of God church that will minister to you in your heart language.

If you are thinking that the Assemblies of God is still a white, Anglo fellowship, you need to catch up with the transformation. In 2021, 44 percent of Assemblies of God people were ethnic minorities (General Council 1995–2021); that is an even greater proportion than in the United States as a whole. And the numbers have been growing steadily for decades.

Here are a few aspects of this transformation that are important for you to know:

Growth and Vitality

Hispanic, Black, and ethnic minorities are fueling the growth and vitality of the Assemblies of God. The importance of this fact cannot be overstated, as growth and vitality are not the typical conditions of churches in the West. To illustrate, according to Arizona Christian University’s American Worldview Inventory 2021, fully 43 percent of millennials do not believe God exists, do not know, or do not care (Barna Group 2021).

Because of this diminishing acknowledgement of God, the membership of many churches in America continues to decline. From 1975 to 2015, the Presbyterian Church (USA) lost 56 percent of its adherents, while the United Church of Christ (48 percent), Episcopal Church (36 percent), Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (30 percent), and United Methodist Church (27 percent) also suffered significant losses (Rodgers 2016). Even some evangelical churches have showed worrying declines. But during this same period, the Assemblies of God increased by 158 percent!

This increase would not be possible without the vigorous growth of Hispanic, Black, and other ethnic fellowships within the Assemblies of God. Although from 2001 to 2015 the number of non-White adherents increased by 76.8 percent, the number of White adherents declined by 1.6 percent. The decline would have been greater if not for the fast growth among White Slavic immigrants (Rodgers 2016). Additionally, the white demographic is the oldest in the United States, while the Hispanic demographic is the youngest. It has become increasingly clear that the future of the Assemblies of God looks less White.

The growing importance of ethnic minorities is reflected in their increased representation in AG leadership, including expanded representation among the Executive Presbytery and Executive Leadership team. The Office of Hispanic Relations and Office of Ethnic Relations within the National Office act as resources for and liaisons between the national office and ethnic minority and immigrant ministers, churches, and fellowship groups.

The growing list of ethnic minority fellowships within the Assemblies of God includes country groups (Myanmar, Ethiopia, Fiji, the Philippines, Ghana, Haiti, India, Indonesia, Japan, Nigeria, Romania, Tonga, and Vietnam), regional groups (Africa, Caribbean, Southern Asia), language groups (Chinese, Hmong, Korean), and culture groups (Black, Native American, Jewish, deaf). Approximately 25 percent of Assemblies of God districts are Hispanic or other ethnic/language groups, including Korean, Samoan, German, Slavic, Brazilian, and multinational (General Council 2019).

Immigration and Missions

Although the presence of some ethnic minority groups in the USA long preceded the founding of the Assemblies of God, the remarkable growth of minority adherents in the twenty-first century is largely due to two factors: immigration and missions. It has often been said that America is a nation of immigrants. Today, immigrants from nearly every country live in the United States, and their numbers are growing. Many are unchurched, disadvantaged, poor, or fleeing violence; they bring the mission field to our own backyard. However, many others are highly educated professionals—doctors, scientists, and educators. Some are Christians whose faith has been refined and strengthened in the fires of persecution in their homelands. Such Christians have been quick to start vibrant churches in their new homeland. They bring renewed vitality and unique flavors to the Assemblies of God.

Darrin J. Rodgers, Director of the Flower Pentecostal Heritage Center, explained the role of missions in the current growth of the Assemblies of God via immigration:

The Assemblies of God is growing in America, due largely to a transformative demographic shift that has been underway for decades. The founding fathers and mothers of the Assemblies of God laid the foundation for this ethnic shift when they committed the Assemblies of God in November 1914 to “the greatest evangelism that the world has ever seen.” In 1921 the Assemblies of God adopted the indigenous church principle as its official missions strategy, in order to better carry out world evangelism. The implementation of this strategy—which recognizes that each national church is autonomous and not controlled by Western interests—resulted in the development of strong national churches and leaders. And now, in a fitting turn of events, those churches are sending missionaries to America. (Rodgers 2016)

Through immigration, God has given the Assemblies of God in America an opportunity to reach the nations within their own nation. And, in God’s divine providence, He has called people from many evangelized nations to the mission field of the United States and other Western nations.

In another interesting turn, there is a growing trend toward multiculturalism and multilingualism within many ethnic minority churches. Some have found that becoming multiethnic and even multilingual is necessary if they wish to keep their second and third generations, as each becomes successively more Americanized. Many of their members have married husbands or wives of a different ethnic group or language. Some of these churches have three services: one in their original language, one bilingual (popular for couples where one speaks only English), and one in English. Interestingly, it is often the English services that are seeing the most growth, as it opens the door for other ethnic minorities to also be included (Kilpatrick 2020).

**Q:** Has your church experienced ethnic transformation? If so, describe the transformation process. What ethnic groups in your community need to be reached?

**Q:** Summarize how your church can help immigrants in your community.
