### Technological Transformation

#### 11.2.1 — Describe at least four ways in which advancing technology has transformed and increased the reach and effectiveness of Assemblies of God ministry.

The voice of the Assemblies of God in America, spoken in more languages than ever, is now “louder” and reaches farther than ever. The wholehearted embrace of new technology to effectively accomplish the work of the church is a second major trend that has transformed the Assemblies of God in the twenty-first century.

Technological advances have revolutionized many areas of life, such as communication, education, production and distribution, agriculture, transportation, and power generation. Technology is also transforming many Assemblies of God churches and the Assemblies of God as a whole.

When the heavenly messenger God sent to interpret Daniel’s vision spoke of “the time of the end,” he described it as a time “when many will rush here and there, and knowledge will increase” (Daniel 12:4 NLT). This might impress you as being a good description of our increasingly fast-paced world and the exponential increase in knowledge demonstrated in new technologies that sounded like science fiction only a few years ago.

Below are a few of the changes, blessings, and challenges advancing technology is bringing.

The Assemblies of God has adapted to today’s digital culture, using the Internet to simplify contact and communication; strengthen connections and provide support; extend reach; and increase access to news, resources, encouragement, and teaching.

Contributions and other financial transactions can be made easily and securely online.

AG News (https://news.ag.org/) tells inspiring stories of cutting-edge ministries, churches, and people of the Assemblies of God.

Curriculum and other resources can be ordered or accessed online.

Many individual ministries have regular podcasts , videos, blogs, webinars , and virtual events, enabling inexpensive, effective, personal teaching, training, encouragement, and community building.

Technology has dramatically transformed the ministries and operations of the Assemblies of God National Office. A large portion of its Springfield, Missouri, footprint was taken up by a massive production, printing, and binding plant, as well as a distribution center. However, the technological transformation has made it possible to streamline the process of producing and mailing ministry resources, books, curricula, and other publications. Approximately a century of Assemblies of God printing plant history wound down; the hum of massive presses and binding machines fell silent as literature and resources became mostly digital.

The changes at the national office are dwarfed by the technological transformation of the ministry at the local level. Ordinary churches and people in the Assemblies of God are leading the way in finding ways to amplify their ministry’s reach and effectiveness using new technologies. Even the smallest church with a simple smartphone and a Facebook page can stream a service live that has the potential to reach around the world. Here are a few examples:

In less than five years, online attendance at Arkansas’ First Assembly North Little Rock grew from one thousand to thirty-five thousand using surprisingly inexpensive click-on social media ads. During the COVID-19 pandemic, online audiences reached seventy-five thousand (Alford 2020). Additionally, online pastor Parker Loy monitors the weather, and pushes ads to people who may be stuck at home due to bad weather. The church also places ads targeting Mexico, where many tune in each week to learn English. (There are Spanish subtitles on sermons streamed into Mexico.) “Social media is the largest mission field in the history of the world,” according to Loy. Now he’s sharing the secrets of that success with others. Loy teaches interested individuals and churches how to use social media to reach the nation and world for Christ (Alford 2019).

When the Civil Air Patrol shut down all facilities in March 2020 due to the pandemic, Captain Leia Eisenhower, an Assemblies of God U.S. Missions chaplain, found an innovative way to take her ministry online. Her ministry starts with direct messages on Instagram, followed by a Saturday morning class. Participants are then invited to her Telegram group, where they receive a link to a YouTube course on discipleship. Interest was so great that she started recording the class in multiple languages. In the first year, more than one hundred thousand people followed her—far more than her in-person ministry as a chaplain would have allowed her to reach; more than one hundred accepted Christ (Ellis 2021).

**Q:** Describe ways that Assemblies of God ministries have benefited from today’s digital age.

**Q:** Identify tools your church can use to expand its reach through social media.

### Transformation of Purpose

#### 11.3.1 — List the four purposes of the Assemblies of God and summarize your understanding of why the addition of the fourth purpose is important.

We don’t need to write to you about the importance of loving each other, for God himself has taught you to love one another (1 Thessalonians 4:9 NLT).

In 1971, when future General Superintendent George O. Wood wrote the bylaws for his own church, he adopted a statement of purpose that flowed from the mission of Jesus: He came to save (evangelize), make followers (disciple), give glory to God (worship), and do acts of mercy (compassion). Because the Assemblies of God’s mission statement included only the first three, Wood sought to change the General Council Constitution to add compassion. He proposed doing just that when he chaired his first General Council in 2009. To Wood’s disappointment, the resolution failed.

“After a sleepless night,” Wood recalled, “I stepped away from the chair and went down to a floor microphone—taking my place not as the general superintendent, but as a delegate. I asked for the resolution to be reconsidered. A kindly pastor who had voted against the resolution came to a microphone and moved the reconsideration. It was seconded and passed by an overwhelming vote. Adding that fourth reason for being provided a stimulus for our churches, ministries, and missionary endeavors to further unleash compassion ministries and helped our Fellowship realize that compassion and evangelism are both required” (George O. Wood, personal e-mail, July 8, 2018).

As a whole, Assemblies of God people have been loving and compassionate, quick to give and show God’s love to those in need in the community and around the world. Since 2009, the Constitution has better reflected the heart of God and the hearts of His people, as it formalizes compassion as a priority for the Fellowship. Clichés such as, “people don’t care what you know until they know that you care,” and “nourish the body, feed the soul” are true.

Living Proof Church, a struggling AG church of nine in a small Texas town learned that firsthand—and that no church is too small to help others. In conjunction with Rural Compassion, the church reached out to meet needs in the community, including hosting a support group for young mothers, hosting a barbecue, scrubbing statues, cleaning graffiti, supporting the school and fire department, and helping community members with after-storm yard cleanup. That caught people’s attention and let the community know that the church cared about them. Attendance quickly grew from nine to 170, stretching their building facilities to the breaking point. That was when a local church with no pastor and only six elderly members stepped up, joining Living Proof and giving them their facility—almost five times larger than their current church! This gift will further enable the compassion outreaches of Living Proof. Parts of the old property will become a women’s safe house, a clothes closet, a food pantry, and an emergency shelter. A community garden and sports parks are planned for an additional piece of land donated to the church (Alford 2016). This small church’s compassion for others transformed their community—and their own church as well.

On a local level, Assemblies of God churches are engaged in countless compassion projects impacting hurting, needy people in the community and abroad. Here are some Assemblies of God programs at the national level that are helping local churches and individuals reach out in compassion with the love of God:

Aged Ministers Assistance provides aged Assemblies of God ministers the support to afford daily needs, like food, housing, and medicine.

Center for the Blind (Special Touch Ministry) retools and develops programs and services specifically to meet the needs of people who are blind or have visual impairments.

Compassion Link (formerly HealthCare Ministries) partners with missionaries and national churches to restore community health. Their vision is to see communities around the world lift themselves out of poverty and know the love of Jesus.

Serving more than 130 million people since 1994, Convoy of Hope feeds and cares for people in need through Community Events, Disaster Services, Children’s Feeding, Women’s Empowerment, Agriculture program, and Rural Initiative.

Disaster Relief assists communities and churches affected by disasters such as hurricanes, earthquakes, and flooding.

COMPACT Family Services is comprised of Hillcrest Children’s Home and Highlands Adoption and ministers through various aspects of family care including maternal care, foster care, and developmental disability treatment.

Global AIDS Partnership provides resources and training for those ministering to people affected by HIV/AIDS.

Child Hope transforms children by means of a relationship with Jesus Christ through a quality education and other ministries of compassion.

Rural Compassion resources, empowers, and partners with rural churches through training, mentoring, and coaching to strengthen and enrich rural communities.

Asia’s Little Ones assists compassion projects (feeding programs, children’s homes, schools) in Asia Pacific.

Interactive Question #7 : Read through the list of compassion programs in the Assemblies of God and come up with a plan on how you or your church can become more engaged in specific compassion ministries

A dramatic transformation has come to the Assemblies of God in recent years. Its adherents, churches, and leaders are becoming more diverse ethnically and culturally. The ways in which it communicates with its members and pursues its mission are being transformed by a digital revolution. And its purpose has been transformed from a singularly spiritual focus to one that more completely matches the heart of Christ and of compassionate AG people and churches. These changes have opened wider the arms—and the doors—of the Assemblies of God to more effectively minister to increasing numbers of people. As demographic and technological shifts continue, the Assemblies of God will continue transforming to meet the needs of our changing world.

**Q:** List and define the four pillars of the statement of purpose of the Assemblies of God.

**Q:** What are some ways a rural church can show compassion to the community?

## 12

### Revitalizing Core Principles: AGTrust

#### 12.1.1 — Describe the charge of the AGTrust, listing three key initiatives.

Those who have been given a trust must prove faithful. 1 Corinthians 4:2

To resource and encourage the Fellowship to act on these values, AGTrust was launched in 2008, under the leadership of Assistant General Superintendent Alton Garrison.

The Assemblies of God Trust (AGTrust) exists to ensure our Fellowship has a healthy church and a healthy minister in every community so that all people may have an opportunity to know Jesus. AG Trust is charged with the following initiatives from the Office of the General Superintendent:

Called—to discover and equip those called to vocational ministry,

Bible Engagement Project (BEP)—to eradicate biblical illiteracy in the Fellowship,

Church Multiplication Network (CMN)—to plant vibrant AG churches,

Church Health—to help strengthen existing AG churches, and

Legacy Transition Group—to help churches successfully plan for a smooth pastoral change. (https://agtrust.org/)

With support from more than twelve thousand members—individuals, families, churches, districts, organizations, and colleges—AGTrust invests in the future as it helps to revitalize communities, churches, and believers. It provides funding, expertise, connections, and resources to equip local churches, pastors, and believers to succeed.

**Q:** Describe the spiritual habit that is vital to maintaining a healthy spiritual life for ourselves personally, our churches, and our fellowship.

**A:** Seeking after revival, renewal, and revitalization (review, reassess, and realign goals)

### Revitalizing Communities: The Church Multiplication Network

#### 12.2.1 — Describe how the Church Multiplication Network has counteracted the decline of the church in America.

Christians understand the importance of the local church because they have experienced the spiritual and personal benefits of corporate worship, education, and fellowship. The unchurched are less likely to have shared those experiences or appreciation for the value of the church. But what both are likely overlooking is the irreplaceable value and positive influence the church has had on the community in indirect—but huge—ways. Increasing numbers of people believe that they can be spiritual without being religious—that they do not need the church to be (or do) good. But they likely are unaware that they are living in grace borrowed from the church. Have you ever seen videos from non-Christian nations where an accident victim lies injured in the middle of a busy street but absolutely no one stops to help? Recently in China, a student fell into a river, where she flailed for a while and finally stopped moving, drowning while hundreds of people watched passively. A newly arrived British diplomat saw the dire situation, dove in, and saved her (Landale 2020). Christianity teaches the value of all lives. The contrast with the worldview of other religions is stark.

The worldview that flows out of faith in Christ and obedience to the Bible is responsible for some of the best, most uplifting parts of our society.

The early church’s respect for life inspired them to raise strong voices against infanticide, slavery, the degradation of women, and the cruelty of the gladiatorial games. This was in stark contrast to the prevailing attitudes and disregard for human life that prevailed in Roman culture.

In AD 252, Christians in Corinth risked their lives to save those suffering from plague who had callously been dumped into the streets to die (Williams 2000).

Hospitals and universities are largely products of the Christian Church. In the Middle Ages, monasteries served as hospitals, places of refuge, education, knowledge preservation, agricultural advancement, and the furthering of art and literature.

The abolition of slavery, prison reform, labor reform, and the founding of organizations that cared for the poor and broken of society were largely driven by Christians and the church (Williams 2000).

It seems likely that the decay currently seen in our communities mirrors the decline of the church in America. Signs that the grace of the church age is fading, and our communities need revitalizing, are everywhere today—increasing crime and violence, a skyrocketing homeless population, urban decay, isolation, and increased fracturing of communities are just some of the major problems widely evident. To stop the decline, the church must step up.

“The Church is truly the hope of America,” General Superintendent Doug Clay wrote. “I’m such a fan of the local church because I am a product of the local church. I’ve seen firsthand in my life and the lives of so many others the lasting difference of an encounter with Jesus. That’s the heart of AGTrust—making sure there is a healthy church and healthy minister in every community, so that all may have an opportunity to meet Jesus” (Clay 2021).

“Churches are perceived to be an important element of a community, even among the unchurched. This positive view is partly due to the fact that most unchurched adults are de-churched, or former churchgoers. So, although they may be wary of personal involvement, they have an understanding of the service and assistance that churches can provide to their communities,” says David Kinnaman, President of the Barna Group (Barna Group 2011).

The Church Multiplication Network (CMN) was pioneered by Steve Pike, an Assemblies of God US missionary, in 2008 to meet communities’ needs for churches in direct response to Wood’s articulated core value of vigorously planting new churches. The vision of the Church Multiplication Network is to see a healthy, Spirit-empowered church in every community marked by spiritual and numerical growth. God has blessed the efforts. Since the beginning of CMN’s existence, it has facilitated the launch of more than 5,000 new AG churches and trained more than 8,000 leaders. Amazingly, 20 percent of all AG churches were established between 2008 and 2019. In conjunction with AGTrust, CMN distributed more than 20 million dollars in matching funds to nearly 700 churches (Church Multiplication Network 2021b).

In spite of these encouraging successes, the task requires much more of us. Two-thirds of US cities still do not have an Assemblies of God church. The need for churches is even more pressing as many cities continue to move from church to post-church to something former CMN Director Jeffrey Portman (starting in 2020) describes as pre-churched. This is due to a long-term lack of gospel penetration. “Many local residents don’t know anyone who goes to church,” Portman said (Kennedy 2020a). Church is not a part of many Americans’ lives or even part of their thinking at all. CMN is doing something to stop the slide into a post-Christian, churchless world lacking the positive, godly presence of the church.

“We are called to minister to a fractured world,” General Superintendent Doug Clay said. “This fracture is a result of being alienated from God. Only Jesus can heal that fracture” (Kennedy 2017).

“We believe that a generation of church planters and missions-minded pastors and leaders will change the face of this country by discipling their congregations and reaching out down their blocks, across their towns, throughout their communities, and into the world,” wrote CMN Director Chris Railey (2014–2020) and Director of Leadership Development John Davidson. Their goal was to see ten thousand AG churches planted from 2020 to 2030 (Railey and Davidson 2019).

Thanks to the Church Multiplication Network and AGTrust, church planters do not have to do it all on their own. Every AG church planting project can apply for up to $75,000 in matching funds, and another $25,000 for building-related expenses in the first year. Matching Fund Churches pay back 10 percent of their non-designated income until the entire amount of the initial investment has been paid back. This replenishes the fund so others can be blessed. Matching Fund Churches have an amazing planting success rate of 90 percent (Church Multiplication Network 2021a).

Every healthy, vibrant church that is planted represents another community impacted and revitalized through the power of the gospel. Every healthy, vibrant church and believer can impact their community—or others—by joining the church-planting mission. As in the Early Church, church multiplication should not be just what we do; it should be part of who we are. Even those who are not called to be church planters have a part to play in starting churches that will revitalize our communities. Everyone can give to CMN and AGTrust to help start churches. Every church can send workers to start a church. Church plants today include parent-affiliated churches, multi-site campuses, and collaborative networks, all of which make starting new churches faster and easier—and more effective.

**Q:** Throughout church history, what effects has the Christian worldview had on society?

**A:** The church has raised its voice in valuing human life and against infanticide, slavery, and the degradation of women. It has reached out to those who were suffering by developing many hospitals and clinics. Christians and the church have been a driving force in abolishing slavery, prison reform, labor reform, and the founding of organizations to care for the poor and broken of society.

**Q:** Appraise the church planting task in America. What are ways you can encourage and support the church plants in your area?

**A:** Two-thirds of US cities have no AG church. Many people have no connections to a church. Answers may include: If you are a pastor of an established church, you can send workers to help with the services in the new church plant, raise funds in your church for a project for the new church plant, and help them with manpower at outreaches or provide supplies for them. Also, your church can adopt a church plant pastor and his or her family at Christmas and give them gifts and cards.

#### 12.2.2 — Explain the relationship of pioneers and settlers as it relates to church planting and how your church fits.

Christians understand the importance of the local church because they have experienced the spiritual and personal benefits of corporate worship, education, and fellowship. The unchurched are less likely to have shared those experiences or appreciation for the value of the church. But what both are likely overlooking is the irreplaceable value and positive influence the church has had on the community in indirect—but huge—ways. Increasing numbers of people believe that they can be spiritual without being religious—that they do not need the church to be (or do) good. But they likely are unaware that they are living in grace borrowed from the church. Have you ever seen videos from non-Christian nations where an accident victim lies injured in the middle of a busy street but absolutely no one stops to help? Recently in China, a student fell into a river, where she flailed for a while and finally stopped moving, drowning while hundreds of people watched passively. A newly arrived British diplomat saw the dire situation, dove in, and saved her (Landale 2020). Christianity teaches the value of all lives. The contrast with the worldview of other religions is stark.

The worldview that flows out of faith in Christ and obedience to the Bible is responsible for some of the best, most uplifting parts of our society.

The early church’s respect for life inspired them to raise strong voices against infanticide, slavery, the degradation of women, and the cruelty of the gladiatorial games. This was in stark contrast to the prevailing attitudes and disregard for human life that prevailed in Roman culture.

In AD 252, Christians in Corinth risked their lives to save those suffering from plague who had callously been dumped into the streets to die (Williams 2000).

Hospitals and universities are largely products of the Christian Church. In the Middle Ages, monasteries served as hospitals, places of refuge, education, knowledge preservation, agricultural advancement, and the furthering of art and literature.

The abolition of slavery, prison reform, labor reform, and the founding of organizations that cared for the poor and broken of society were largely driven by Christians and the church (Williams 2000).

It seems likely that the decay currently seen in our communities mirrors the decline of the church in America. Signs that the grace of the church age is fading, and our communities need revitalizing, are everywhere today—increasing crime and violence, a skyrocketing homeless population, urban decay, isolation, and increased fracturing of communities are just some of the major problems widely evident. To stop the decline, the church must step up.

“The Church is truly the hope of America,” General Superintendent Doug Clay wrote. “I’m such a fan of the local church because I am a product of the local church. I’ve seen firsthand in my life and the lives of so many others the lasting difference of an encounter with Jesus. That’s the heart of AGTrust—making sure there is a healthy church and healthy minister in every community, so that all may have an opportunity to meet Jesus” (Clay 2021).

“Churches are perceived to be an important element of a community, even among the unchurched. This positive view is partly due to the fact that most unchurched adults are de-churched, or former churchgoers. So, although they may be wary of personal involvement, they have an understanding of the service and assistance that churches can provide to their communities,” says David Kinnaman, President of the Barna Group (Barna Group 2011).

The Church Multiplication Network (CMN) was pioneered by Steve Pike, an Assemblies of God US missionary, in 2008 to meet communities’ needs for churches in direct response to Wood’s articulated core value of vigorously planting new churches. The vision of the Church Multiplication Network is to see a healthy, Spirit-empowered church in every community marked by spiritual and numerical growth. God has blessed the efforts. Since the beginning of CMN’s existence, it has facilitated the launch of more than 5,000 new AG churches and trained more than 8,000 leaders. Amazingly, 20 percent of all AG churches were established between 2008 and 2019. In conjunction with AGTrust, CMN distributed more than 20 million dollars in matching funds to nearly 700 churches (Church Multiplication Network 2021b).

In spite of these encouraging successes, the task requires much more of us. Two-thirds of US cities still do not have an Assemblies of God church. The need for churches is even more pressing as many cities continue to move from church to post-church to something former CMN Director Jeffrey Portman (starting in 2020) describes as pre-churched. This is due to a long-term lack of gospel penetration. “Many local residents don’t know anyone who goes to church,” Portman said (Kennedy 2020a). Church is not a part of many Americans’ lives or even part of their thinking at all. CMN is doing something to stop the slide into a post-Christian, churchless world lacking the positive, godly presence of the church.

“We are called to minister to a fractured world,” General Superintendent Doug Clay said. “This fracture is a result of being alienated from God. Only Jesus can heal that fracture” (Kennedy 2017).

“We believe that a generation of church planters and missions-minded pastors and leaders will change the face of this country by discipling their congregations and reaching out down their blocks, across their towns, throughout their communities, and into the world,” wrote CMN Director Chris Railey (2014–2020) and Director of Leadership Development John Davidson. Their goal was to see ten thousand AG churches planted from 2020 to 2030 (Railey and Davidson 2019).

Thanks to the Church Multiplication Network and AGTrust, church planters do not have to do it all on their own. Every AG church planting project can apply for up to $75,000 in matching funds, and another $25,000 for building-related expenses in the first year. Matching Fund Churches pay back 10 percent of their non-designated income until the entire amount of the initial investment has been paid back. This replenishes the fund so others can be blessed. Matching Fund Churches have an amazing planting success rate of 90 percent (Church Multiplication Network 2021a).

Every healthy, vibrant church that is planted represents another community impacted and revitalized through the power of the gospel. Every healthy, vibrant church and believer can impact their community—or others—by joining the church-planting mission. As in the Early Church, church multiplication should not be just what we do; it should be part of who we are. Even those who are not called to be church planters have a part to play in starting churches that will revitalize our communities. Everyone can give to CMN and AGTrust to help start churches. Every church can send workers to start a church. Church plants today include parent-affiliated churches, multi-site campuses, and collaborative networks, all of which make starting new churches faster and easier—and more effective.

### Revitalizing Churches: The Acts 2 Journey

#### 12.3.1 — Summarize five characteristics of a healthy church and the major reason churches plateau.

Unfortunately, not every church positively impacts its community; some barely manage to bless those within its own walls. That is why the Assemblies of God’s goal is not just to see churches in every community, but to ensure that those churches are healthy, vibrant, and reaching out. To this end, the Acts 2 Journey (A2J) was born from the vision of Alton Garrison, assistant general superintendent at the time.

In spite of the overall growth of the Assemblies of God, many churches desperately needed to be revitalized and strengthened so as to be part of God’s continuing mission into the future. Among Assemblies of God churches in America, 80 percent have plateaued or have declining attendance – a percentage that has been rising since the early 1990s. More than 50 percent of churches have declined by 10 percent in five years, while only 20 percent have grown by 10 percent or more during the same time (Railey and Davidson 2019).

Over the years of helping churches renew their vision and revitalize their church, several important truths have become clear:

Lost vision is the primary cause of the church plateau.

Inward focus is the leading cause of church decline.

It takes a team (not just a pastor) to turn a church in a new direction.

A new life requires a new vision and new relationships.

Any church—no matter the size or circumstances—can move toward greater effectiveness. Summarize five characteristics of a healthy church and the major reason churches plateau.

The Acts 2 Journey is biblical-based, stylistically neutral, and scalable to location. It effectively helps plateaued and declining churches regain their vision and the outward focus crucial for health and growth. A healthy Acts 2 church does five things:

Worships—pursuing and obeying God passionately

Connects—engaging and maintaining loving relationships

Grows—develops and mobilizes its people

Serves—acting with clear direction and outward focus

Goes—reproducing and multiplying Christ’s mission in other people and places (https://acts2journey.com/) (see figure 12.1).

The Acts 2 Journey is based on the template of Acts 2, in which the early Church had an empowering encounter with Pentecost (Acts 2:4), clearly communicated to others what was happening (Acts 2:14–18), and implemented a process so effective that it turned the world upside down (Acts 2:42–47).

A typical Acts 2 Journey involves a cohort of churches made up of pastors and their vision teams. Over the course of a year, each church in the cohort assesses its current reality, clarifies its mission, discerns God’s preferred future, identifies and commits to live out biblical core values, and creates an operating plan tailored to its context for evangelism, fellowship, discipleship, ministry, and worship.

More than 1,500 churches have taken the Acts 2 Journey, many of them with the help of scholarships from AGTrust (https://acts2journey.com/). Hundreds more have engaged the process globally. The Acts 2 Journey has proven effective at reversing long-term decline in churches. Since 2010, only 5 percent of churches that engaged in the Acts 2 Journey process have closed or moved to PAC (Parent Affiliated Church) status compared to nearly twenty-three percent of churches in the AG USA during that time (Clarensau, 2023).

The Acts 2 Journey can help almost any church, whether declining, plateaued, or even growing. Of the churches in the USA that have the Acts 2 Journey template, nearly one-third are already growing numerically but want to engage their leaders in a proven process to raise the church to the next level of effectiveness. (Acts 2 Journey 6).

**Q:** Acts 8:8 reports there was great joy in Samaria following the ministry of Philip. How would you describe the impact of your church in the local community?

**A:** Answers will vary.

### Revitalizing Christians: The Bible Engagement Project

#### 12.4.1

When Doug Clay became the new general superintendent in 2017, it was time for another transformation in the Assemblies of God. God opened his eyes and quickened his spirit to the need to revitalize AG believers through engagement with the Word of God. While wrestling with the problem of Bible illiteracy even within the church, he happened to read about Josiah’s rediscovering the Word of God in the house of God (2 Kings 22). “How do you lose the Word of God in the house of God?” Clay wondered. He was determined to do whatever he could to see that the same thing did not happen within the Assemblies of God. As a board member for several AG schools, he had observed that many students were entering without a strong biblical foundation. His heart longed for each one—for every person in every AG church—not only to know the Bible, but to have it transform their lives.

The Bible Engagement Project (BEP) , perhaps Doug Clay’s signature leadership vision for the AG, fulfills a focus of AGTrust’s initiative: to increase not just Bible literacy (knowledge) but Bible engagement (transformational internalization). The material is free for churches, small groups, and individuals and is downloadable from the BEP app.

“Our church members have a hunger for a focus on Bible study and a need for resources to help in that journey, but on the whole, we as leaders have been less likely to offer and focus on those tools when compared to non-AG churches,” said Rick DuBose, assistant general superintendent and executive over the Bible Engagement Project and its resources. “The statistics show clearly that Bible engagement changes the way people view the world and live in the world. With this in mind, we must return to a focus on a systematic approach to Bible study in our churches” ( AG News 2019).

In 2020, BEP released Listen curriculum. It was the culmination of many studies and surveys and of much planning, preparation, involvement, and prayer. Released through the Bible Engagement Project app, the Listen curriculum actively engages people with God and His Word. The highly interactive digital content is age-aligned, meaning that adults, youth, children, and preschoolers all deal with the same Bible passages and themes but on their own level. The curriculum is well suited to small groups, families, or individuals, making it a helpful tool for family discussion and discipleship. Beyond improving biblical literacy, the curriculum is transforming lives as individuals, families, and churches engage with the Bible in a new and powerful way.

The first phase, Listen , provides an overview of the entire Bible as one book and one story. The second, Learn , focuses on themes recurring throughout the Bible in a developmentally appropriate way, and the third, Live , helps all ages discover what it means to live out their faith by diving into the Gospels and Acts.

Greater Bible engagement is not just an educational goal; it is essential if the Pentecostal distinctive and powerful witness and outreach historically identifying the Assemblies of God are to persist. According to “Built on The Bible: Barna Report on Bible Engagement in the Assemblies of God”:

"The more Bible-engaged a person is, the more likely the individual is to have experienced the baptism in the Holy Spirit with the evidence of speaking in tongues." (AG News 2019)

A 2019 Barna survey of US adults showed only 5 percent as “Bible centered,” meaning that Scripture informs their lives and choices. Nearly half are “Bible disengaged,” meaning the Word of God has no impact on them (AG News 2019). People who engage with God’s Word four or more times a week are more likely to improve their own lives and share the life-changing message of Christ with others (Bible Engagement Project, Facebook post, April 18, 2021, https:// www.facebook.com/BibleEngagementProject).

People who engage with the Bible four or more times a week are:

228 percent more likely to share their faith with others,

407 percent more likely to memorize Scripture, and

231 percent more likely to disciple others ( AG News 2019).

“The AG is committed to stewarding the conversation within the church as it relates to Bible engagement,” DuBose said. “We feel like God is directing us to recalibrate our efforts and ministries to be singularly focused on Bible engagement. All ministries and resources will flow from that vision” (AG News 2019).

As the Assemblies of God look to the future, they are laser-focused on revitalizing communities through empowered churches, revitalizing churches by empowering believers, and revitalizing believers by helping them engage with God’s transforming Word.

General Superintendent Clay affirms that focus: “We want the AG to be known for being Bible engaged, Spirit engaged, missions engaged. We have a vision for seeing a healthy church in every community that’s marked by spiritual and numerical growth, and we believe that church planting, church revitalization, and Bible engagement intertwined together can help us achieve that vision” (Bible Engagement Project, Facebook video, March 22, 2021,).

**Q:** Describe the importance of Bible engagement.

**A:** People who engage with the Bible four or more times a week are much more likely to share their faith with others, memorize Scripture, and disciple others. Bible engagement, along with church planting and church revitalization, creates healthy churches.

**Q:** Summarize the various revitalization ministries in the Assemblies of God.

**A:** AGTrust—has initiatives to plant churches, strengthens existing churches, and increases Bible engagement by providing funding, expertise, connections, and resources to local churches, pastors, and believers. CMN—facilitates the launch of thousands of new churches and trains leaders; distributes matching funds to churches. Acts 2 Journey—strengthens existing churches that are struggling; helps them renew their visions and gain outward focus. BEP—uses curriculum they developed to increase Bible literacy (knowledge) and Bible engagement (transformational internalization). UNIT 4

## 13

### The Constitution’s Foundation

#### 13.1.1 — Explain why an organization needs legal documents like the Constitution and the Bylaws.

Why Does an Organization Need a Constitution and a Set of Bylaws?

Imagine belonging to an organization without any rules. Such an organization could not last long. No one could tell who was a member. Every person participating in the organization could make decisions he or she thought best. There would be almost no teamwork or accountability. Each participant could create his or her own goals for the group. The group’s meetings would be little more than chaos and conflict. Outsiders would be unable to determine the group’s purpose or values. Clearly, without rules and organization, chaos rules a group and its activities. Such an organization will never accomplish anything meaningful. In fact, it will soon cease to exist.

It is not legally necessary for an organization to have both a constitution and bylaws. When an organization has both, the Constitution is always superior to the bylaws. Our Constitution sets forth the official identity of the organization. It also defines the basic qualifications and conditions under which the organization operates. The bylaws contain the rules and procedures for the daily operation of the organization. This includes administrative details about offices, departments, and procedures required to accomplish the work of the organization. A simple way to compare these documents is to think of the Constitution as the official description of the Assemblies of God and the bylaws as the rules and procedures of everyday operation. Changing the contents of the Constitution is more difficult than changing the bylaws. (As noted in the unit introduction, both documents have changed some, but the basic organizational structure remains unchanged.) This arrangement shows the superiority of the Constitution to the bylaws.

The General Council Constitution

In the early days of the Assemblies of God many did not feel the need for a constitution. There was concern that too much organization would stifle the spontaneity of the church. It was not until 1927, after the fellowship grew and its ministries became more varied and complex, that the General Council agreed to adopt a constitution. These legal documents helped to ensure order, accountability, and continuity while providing protection for the integrity of the organization.

The Constitution Contains a Doctrinal Statement

Space in this study will not permit a thorough discussion of the entire Constitution and Bylaws. Our goal is to create an overview of these documents. We will emphasize key elements and summarize important content. After completing this unit, you may not be an expert in every detail of these documents. You should, however, have a general knowledge of their scope and contents. This is important to help you be an informed member of the organization and provide understanding when it comes to decision making and voting in business meetings. Just as members of a local church should understand how their church operates, each minister should have a basic understanding of how the larger Fellowship operates.

The first part of the Constitution is the Constitutional Declaration. It provides a summary statement of who we are and our purpose for being. You will immediately notice the frequency of biblical terms and references to Bible passages. The writers of the Constitution were determined to ground the organization in the Word of God. Remember, the reason the Assemblies of God exists is that God poured out His Spirit on hungry believers. The first sections of the Constitution resonate with reminders of this fact.

The next articles (Articles I–IV) state the name, purposes, identity, prerogatives (rights and privileges), and principles for fellowship of the General Council. Article V is our Statement of Fundamental Truths. This is a significant part of the Constitution. Notice that this statement of what we believe and teach is placed close to the beginning. This is not by chance. The placement of the doctrinal statement shows how essential sound teaching is to the Movement. Unity, order, wisdom, and maturity cannot thrive where there is confusion and conflict. A church body has little hope of pleasing God without agreement on the most central Bible teachings. Since the Bible teaches that unity is one of the single most definitive characteristics of the Church, agreement about doctrine is essential.

Review the lessons in Unit 2 that discussed the need in the early years for a doctrinal statement. It was clear that disagreement about Bible doctrine would destroy the spiritual health and effectiveness of the Fellowship. The founders responded to this threat by drafting a statement of those truths considered fundamental to sound biblical teaching. They were not trying to replace Bible teaching. Neither were they claiming to be inspired or have divine authority. Rather, these wise founders were creating a basis of fellowship that would preserve unity and promote accurate interpretation of Scripture.

This lesson introduced the need for a Constitution and for an official statement of key biblical teachings. Both the Constitution and its Statement of Fundamental Truths were effective in protecting the Fellowship from error and promoting unity and effectiveness. The Statement of Fundamental Truths proved to be a keystone ingredient in this document. The next lesson will consider these truths more fully.

**Q:** Briefly describe what would happen to an organization without rules.

**A:** Student’s answer could include that the organization would be in continual chaos. There would be no way to determine membership or who is in authority. Decisions could not be made that would be binding on the membership. Resources would be wasted because there would be no coordinated, consistent control. Conflict would be difficult to resolve without rules. The purpose of the organization may change often. The organization without rules would soon cease to exist.

**Q:** What is the function of an organization’s governing instruments?

**A:** The governing instruments are the documents that legally define an organization and its rules of government and operation.

**Q:** How does a constitution compare to a set of bylaws?

**A:** The Constitution is superior in authority to bylaws and is therefore more difficult to amend.

**Q:** Is it necessary for all members of an organization to share common beliefs in order to experience unity? Why or why not?

**A:** Yes; uncertainty about beliefs creates confusion and conflict. Without an agreed-upon statement of doctrinal tenets, influential members can introduce false teaching and generate schism.

**Q:** What is the purpose of the Statement of Fundamental Truths? How does this statement of truths compare to the authority of Scripture?

**A:** The Statement of Fundamental Truths is intended to be a basis of fellowship. It is not intended to replace Scripture, nor does it claim the authority of Scripture. The statement is not inspired, but Scripture is.

### The Fellowship’s Spiritual Foundation

#### 13.2.1 — List and summarize the Sixteen Fundamental Truths.

The Statement of Fundamental Truths is central to the Constitution and to the unity of the Fellowship. This focus on key teachings of the Bible helps maintain unity by providing accountability among ministers. It also helps protect believers in local Assemblies from false doctrine. Those who teach contrary to the fundamental truths are not allowed to pastor churches in the Fellowship or hold ministerial credentials. Believers can submit with a measure of confidence to the leadership of credentialed ministers in the Assemblies of God. Because of the importance of these sixteen doctrines, this lesson is dedicated to learning these truths and their Bible references.

Sixteen Truths Considered Fundamental to the Assemblies of God Fellowship

This section of our lesson will help you summarize and learn the Sixteen Fundamental Truths. It is not necessary to memorize the wording of the entire Article V of the Constitution. It is important to know the sixteen truths and be able to summarize their content. As you study each statement of truth, concentrate on learning principles rather than memorizing the words.

Sixteen Fundamental Truths summarized:

1. The Scriptures are inspired by God. Both Old and New Testaments are verbally inspired . This means that every word is significant and was intended by God as part of His revelation. Since the Bible is inspired by God, it is infallible (completely trustworthy) and has final authority over what we believe and how we live.

2. There is One True God , the self-existent. (He was not created.) “I AM.” He is the Creator of all that is and the Redeemer of humans. The One True God exists as a Triune Being, meaning He is one Being of three persons.

3. The Lord Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God .

4. Mankind fell by voluntary transgression . Although humans were made in God’s image and were created good and upright, their voluntary sin caused them to fall. This fall brought the experience of physical and spiritual death. Spiritual death is separation from God.

5. Humans can only be saved from this death through the shed blood of Jesus Christ . This salvation is achieved through repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ. The outward evidence of salvation is a life of righteousness and holiness.

6. God directed the church to practice two ceremonies , called ordinances . The two ordinances of the church are baptism in water and Holy Communion.

7. The baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience available to all believers . This was promised in the Bible and experienced by all in the early church. This experience is distinct from and subsequent to the experience of being born again. This means the baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience different from salvation and comes after salvation.

8. The initial physical evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit is speaking with other tongues (languages) as God’s Spirit makes it possible .

9. Sanctification is the necessary act of separation from that which is evil .

10. The church is the body of Christ . God lives in the church through the Spirit. Each believer is a vital part of the church. The church exists to fulfill God’s plans for her. This Fellowship exists for four reasons: to evangelize the world, to worship God together, to build a body of saints being perfected in the image of Christ, and to demonstrate God’s love and compassion for all the world.

11. The Bible teaches that the Lord calls and appoints some believers to ministry in the body . These ministers are specifically appointed to lead the church in the fulfillment of the fourfold purpose.

12. Divine healing is a key part of the gospel . Deliverance from sickness is provided for in the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

13. The Blessed Hope of the church is the resurrection of those who have died as believers in Christ along with the translation of those who are alive so that all may be with the Lord forever.

14. The millennial reign of Christ is promised in the Bible . This visible return of Christ to rule on earth with His saints for a thousand years follows the rapture of the church.

15. There will be a final judgment of the wicked . The wicked dead will be raised from death and judged according to their works. Those whose names are not found in God’s Book of Life will be thrown into the lake of fire forever.

16. The Bible promises a new heaven and a new earth .

Learn the Sixteen Fundamental Truths by reviewing the above summaries. In addition, read through Article V of the Constitution several times. You do not need to memorize the words of the above list or Article V. Your goal is to thoroughly understand the principles of these teachings. Pay close attention to the Bible references that support each truth. When you are confident of your knowledge of the Sixteen Fundamental Truths, complete exercise six. You should do so without looking back in this IST or at the Constitution.

Biblical Foundations Support the Fundamental Truths

The teachings considered basic to Assemblies of God Fellowship were not invented by early Pentecostal believers. These truths are taught in the Bible. They represent the Bible’s teaching about important Christian beliefs. Although the Bible teaches much more than what is represented in the Sixteen Fundamental Truths, these are considered basic to Christian living and church unity. The biblical teachings represented in the Sixteen Fundamental Truths of the Assemblies of God form the basic foundation of the Fellowship. Candidates for Assemblies of God ministerial credentials are required to: (1) know the Sixteen Fundamental Truths and Scripture references for each, (2) believe these biblical teachings as stated in the Constitution, and (3) teach these truths in public ministry.

While agreement to the Statement of Fundamental Truths form the basis for ministerial credentialing, there are also other things that the AG believes to be true about the way Christians interpret the Bible. These things may not rise to the level of importance for agreement as those in the sixteen fundamental truths, but they are important to learn about. These teachings are outlined in position papers and cover topics such as abortion and euthanasia, use of alcohol, divorce, creationism, sexual identity, racism, and several other topics. You can find these on the Assemblies of God website (https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers).

Fundamental Truth

1.

2. There is one true God, eternally self-existent, properly understood as one Being of three persons.

2.

3. Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God.

3.

4. Humankind voluntarily fell out of relationship with God through sin.

4.

5. Only the shed blood of Jesus can redeem individuals from sin and death.

5.

6. The ordinances of the church are water baptism and holy communion.

#### 13.2.2 — Associate two Bible passages with each of the Sixteen Fundamental Truths.

The Statement of Fundamental Truths is central to the Constitution and to the unity of the Fellowship. This focus on key teachings of the Bible helps maintain unity by providing accountability among ministers. It also helps protect believers in local Assemblies from false doctrine. Those who teach contrary to the fundamental truths are not allowed to pastor churches in the Fellowship or hold ministerial credentials. Believers can submit with a measure of confidence to the leadership of credentialed ministers in the Assemblies of God. Because of the importance of these sixteen doctrines, this lesson is dedicated to learning these truths and their Bible references.

Sixteen Truths Considered Fundamental to the Assemblies of God Fellowship

This section of our lesson will help you summarize and learn the Sixteen Fundamental Truths. It is not necessary to memorize the wording of the entire Article V of the Constitution. It is important to know the sixteen truths and be able to summarize their content. As you study each statement of truth, concentrate on learning principles rather than memorizing the words.

Sixteen Fundamental Truths summarized:

1. The Scriptures are inspired by God. Both Old and New Testaments are verbally inspired . This means that every word is significant and was intended by God as part of His revelation. Since the Bible is inspired by God, it is infallible (completely trustworthy) and has final authority over what we believe and how we live.

2. There is One True God , the self-existent. (He was not created.) “I AM.” He is the Creator of all that is and the Redeemer of humans. The One True God exists as a Triune Being, meaning He is one Being of three persons.

3. The Lord Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God .

4. Mankind fell by voluntary transgression . Although humans were made in God’s image and were created good and upright, their voluntary sin caused them to fall. This fall brought the experience of physical and spiritual death. Spiritual death is separation from God.

5. Humans can only be saved from this death through the shed blood of Jesus Christ . This salvation is achieved through repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ. The outward evidence of salvation is a life of righteousness and holiness.

6. God directed the church to practice two ceremonies , called ordinances . The two ordinances of the church are baptism in water and Holy Communion.

7. The baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience available to all believers . This was promised in the Bible and experienced by all in the early church. This experience is distinct from and subsequent to the experience of being born again. This means the baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience different from salvation and comes after salvation.

8. The initial physical evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit is speaking with other tongues (languages) as God’s Spirit makes it possible .

9. Sanctification is the necessary act of separation from that which is evil .

10. The church is the body of Christ . God lives in the church through the Spirit. Each believer is a vital part of the church. The church exists to fulfill God’s plans for her. This Fellowship exists for four reasons: to evangelize the world, to worship God together, to build a body of saints being perfected in the image of Christ, and to demonstrate God’s love and compassion for all the world.

11. The Bible teaches that the Lord calls and appoints some believers to ministry in the body . These ministers are specifically appointed to lead the church in the fulfillment of the fourfold purpose.

12. Divine healing is a key part of the gospel . Deliverance from sickness is provided for in the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

13. The Blessed Hope of the church is the resurrection of those who have died as believers in Christ along with the translation of those who are alive so that all may be with the Lord forever.

14. The millennial reign of Christ is promised in the Bible . This visible return of Christ to rule on earth with His saints for a thousand years follows the rapture of the church.

15. There will be a final judgment of the wicked . The wicked dead will be raised from death and judged according to their works. Those whose names are not found in God’s Book of Life will be thrown into the lake of fire forever.

16. The Bible promises a new heaven and a new earth .

Learn the Sixteen Fundamental Truths by reviewing the above summaries. In addition, read through Article V of the Constitution several times. You do not need to memorize the words of the above list or Article V. Your goal is to thoroughly understand the principles of these teachings. Pay close attention to the Bible references that support each truth. When you are confident of your knowledge of the Sixteen Fundamental Truths, complete exercise six. You should do so without looking back in this IST or at the Constitution.

Biblical Foundations Support the Fundamental Truths

The teachings considered basic to Assemblies of God Fellowship were not invented by early Pentecostal believers. These truths are taught in the Bible. They represent the Bible’s teaching about important Christian beliefs. Although the Bible teaches much more than what is represented in the Sixteen Fundamental Truths, these are considered basic to Christian living and church unity. The biblical teachings represented in the Sixteen Fundamental Truths of the Assemblies of God form the basic foundation of the Fellowship. Candidates for Assemblies of God ministerial credentials are required to: (1) know the Sixteen Fundamental Truths and Scripture references for each, (2) believe these biblical teachings as stated in the Constitution, and (3) teach these truths in public ministry.

While agreement to the Statement of Fundamental Truths form the basis for ministerial credentialing, there are also other things that the AG believes to be true about the way Christians interpret the Bible. These things may not rise to the level of importance for agreement as those in the sixteen fundamental truths, but they are important to learn about. These teachings are outlined in position papers and cover topics such as abortion and euthanasia, use of alcohol, divorce, creationism, sexual identity, racism, and several other topics. You can find these on the Assemblies of God website (https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers).

### The Structural Foundation

#### 13.3.1 — Define the term cooperative fellowship, and describe how this term reflects the intent of the founders of the Assemblies of God.

This lesson will examine what it means to be a voluntary cooperative fellowship. We will also review the basic governmental structure of the Assemblies of God. From the focus on the local assembly to the executive leadership structure, the Constitution strives to represent biblical principles and values. At the same time, it preserves effective order and sound administration.

Emphasis on the Local Church

Review the single statement of Article II of the Constitution. The term cooperative fellowship is taken from this statement. Notice that the title of Article II is Nature . What does this title say about the importance of the article’s content? It tells us that the identity of the organization is to be understood by what this article contains. We will also better understand the intent of the founders through understanding this article (See also Bylaws Article VII, Section 2, Paragraph g.).

Voluntary r efers to local assemblies participation in the activities and support of the interests of the larger organization as voluntary members. Each minister and local church chooses to be a part of the Assemblies of God.

Cooperative highlights the manner of the local assembly’s participation. This voluntary participation includes willing submission to the authority of the Constitution and Bylaws of the Assemblies of God. It also includes support of the Fellowship’s purposes and goals.

Fellowship places emphasis on the local church. The Fellowship depends on the cooperation of the individual member churches. In the Assemblies of God the term, “ voluntary cooperative fellowship ” supports a clear principle—the local church is sovereign and sets its own direction while cooperating with the larger body of believers with whom it has chosen to affiliate. The larger organization provides many functions, but with the highest regard for the interests, rights, and responsibilities of the local assembly.

The General Council of the Assemblies of God Membership

Organizations that are incorporated under state laws are required to define themselves and their affairs in certain ways. Incorporation is a legal process whereby an organization creates a legal identity. There are several good reasons why it is desirable for all religious organizations to incorporate (Hammar 2000, 278–282). The Assemblies of God is incorporated, meaning it has a legal identity recognized by state and federal governments. Therefore, the Fellowship has a corporate name, The General Council of the Assemblies of God (Constitution, Article I). The Constitution carefully defines what this name means and how it applies to the existence and activities of the Fellowship.

The Constitution also identifies the membership of the Assemblies of God. This is significant for both legal and practical reasons. Membership determines who is entitled to the privileges and subject to the responsibilities related to the Fellowship.

Read Articles I, VII, and IX of the Constitution carefully and answer questions 9–16.

Article IX—General Council Administrative Leadership

Article IX in the Constitution describes the administrative officers, presbyteries, and boards of the General Council. The General Council is the term used for the official sessions of the organization. This official meeting occurs once every two years. The Constitution provides for officers to carry out the policies and programs adopted by the General Council. It also provides for boards and presbyteries to make official business decisions while the General Council is not in session . These officers, boards, and presbyteries represent the authority of and are accountable to the General Council. The highest decision-making authority in the Fellowship is the General Council. The decisions of the General Council when it is in session govern the affairs of the Fellowship. However, the daily activities are administered by officers and boards under the governing authority of the General Council.

We will discuss the officers, boards, and councils more thoroughly in the next chapter. Our goal now is to understand the basic structure of the organization as outlined in the Constitution.

Districts and Local Assemblies

If the Constitution only provided for national organization and authority, the Fellowship’s emphasis on the local assembly would be diminished. This is wisely expressed in the Constitution’s recognition of districts and local assemblies. Article X defines district councils and describes the authority of these councils and their relationship to the General Council.

The Constitution creates the General Council to administer the affairs and interests that relate to the national and international Fellowship. It also creates district councils to administer the affairs and interests of individual churches and ministers.

Read Article X in the Constitution. More details about district council organization and function will be discussed in subsequent lessons. Our purpose here is to understand the Constitution’s provision for the function and authority of district councils. Two words in Article X, Section 2 are key to understanding the district councils’ responsibilities: ecclesial and sacerdotal . The Constitution states that the district council supervises all ecclesial and sacerdotal activities in its prescribed field. ( Ecclesial is a form of the word ecclesiastical .) Ecclesial activities involve the church, especially the local assembly. The word comes from the Greek word ekklesia , which means “assembly.” The word sacerdotal refers to the functions of ministers within the local church. The Constitution is simply stating that district councils have responsibility for the local assemblies and the ministers within their districts. A district can be either a defined geographic region or a language group, such as the Iowa District or the Korean District. In recent years, some districts have adopted the term “network,” but the function is the same.

The Constitution specifies the most important function of the district council—to oversee the process for credentialing ministers. Article X, Section 4 outlines the authority of the district council in this process. It is the responsibility of each district council to review the lives and qualifications of every individual who applies to be an Assemblies of God minister. The district councils do not determine the qualifications. The General Council sets the standards and qualifications. The district councils examine and present candidates who meet these requirements to the general secretary. They then undergo a final review by the General Council Credentials Committee.

The Bylaws have additional provisions for district councils. These will be discussed in the next chapter.

Local Churches Relate to the General Council and District Councils

This study has discussed at length the nature of the Assemblies of God as a cooperative fellowship. Each church participates in the Fellowship on a voluntary basis. The word affiliate means to “associate with an organization as a subordinate member.” Local assemblies that affiliate with the Assemblies of God organization are choosing to become subordinate members of the Fellowship.

There are two classifications of affiliation within the Assemblies of God: General Council affiliation and District affiliation. The primary status of association with the Fellowship is General Council affiliation. However, the Constitution allows district councils to establish a district affiliated status for churches that do not qualify for General Council affiliation. Since district affiliation requirements differ among districts, these will not be discussed here. You should be aware of the levels of affiliation available to local assemblies.

There is also a category called “parent-affiliated church” or PAC. A PAC is a distinct worshiping community stemming from an existing General Council Affiliated Church or duly authorized District Council Affiliated Church. A PAC operates under the supervision and authority of the Parent Church, following terms and conditions set by the Parent Church. Sometimes known as satellites, extension campuses, sites, and video venues, PACs accommodate a wide range of methodologies to expand ministry and bring the gospel to places the parent church might not be able to reach.

Holding membership as an Assemblies of God church implies certain responsibilities and privileges. These responsibilities and privileges are outlined in Article XI of the Constitution, which establishes the practical details of what is meant by voluntary cooperation. The rights and privileges outlined in this article define the Fellowship at its most basic level. This article balances the need for accountability in matters such as doctrine and holiness with the highest regard for the local assembly’s self-government.

Answer questions 19–21 from the information in Article XI of the Constitution.

**Q:** How does the term cooperative fellowship fulfill the goals of the founders of the Assemblies of God?

**A:** Student’s answer should include something like the following: the term focuses attention and priority on the local assembly rather than on the national organization. The interests and well-being of the local church are valued above a religious organization. This was intended to prevent the local church’s loss of self-determination under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. At the same time, the term recognizes the need for cooperation in fulfilling common purposes, which includes submission to doctrinal unity and moral purity.

**Q:** Compare and contrast a cooperative fellowship with a traditional denominational organization.

**A:** Student’s own answer, but could include a reference to the practices of some denominations to own church property at the national organizational level, appoint pastors to the local church without local consensus, and deny local parishioners the opportunity to be represented in the decision-making process at the national level. The General Council Constitution

**Q:** What is the General Council?

**A:** The legal entity of the Fellowship when it is in session (a meeting convened for the purpose of conducting official business).

**Q:** What does the term Assemblies of God refer to in the legal name?

**A:** It refers to the entire constituency (churches, members, and ministers) of the Fellowship.

**Q:** Define the membership of the General Council, and define membership of the Assemblies of God.

**A:** The General Council membership includes all licensed and ordained ministers and all churches holding a Certificate of Fellowship issued by the General Council of the Assemblies of God. The membership of the Assemblies of God includes all individual members of local assemblies affiliated with the General Council and the various district councils, including all credentialed ministers.

**Q:** Describe the difference between membership in the Assemblies of God and membership in The General Council of the Assemblies of God.

**A:** This is a legal difference since the latter term is the title of the legal entity of the corporation. Since the General Council is the sessions of the corporation, General Council membership entitles members to participate in the decision-making activities of the sessions. Membership in the Assemblies of God entitles members to be represented at the General Council through church delegates. The interests of the church are represented, not the individual members (unless the member is a licensed or ordained minister).

**Q:** How many corporate officers does the General Council have? What are their titles, and what are their terms of office?

**A:** Four are identified in the Constitution: general superintendent, assistant general superintendent, general secretary, general treasurer; four-year terms each.

**Q:** What officers make up the Executive Leadership Team?

**A:** Six executive officers make up the Executive Leadership Team: general superintendent, assistant general superintendent, general secretary, general treasurer, and the executive directors of Assemblies of God World Missions and Assemblies of God U. S. Missions.

**Q:** How many representatives does each district council have on the General Presbytery?

**A:** Three—the district superintendents and two individuals elected by each District Council. Additional members of the General Presbytery are listed in Article IX, Section 3, of the Constitution, with additional information given in Article II, Section 2 (d) and Article III, Section 9, of the Bylaws.

**Q:** What name does the Constitution give to the official policy-making body of the General Council (when the General Council is not in session)?

**A:** The General Presbytery.

**Q:** How many representatives does each district council have on the General Presbytery?

**A:** Three—the district superintendents and two individuals elected by each District Council. Additional members of the General Presbytery are listed in Article IX, Section 3, of the Constitution, with additional information given in Article II, Section 2 (d) and Article III, Section 9, of the Bylaws.

**Q:** List activities that you would consider ecclesial.

**A:** Answer could include planting a new church, helping resolve an internal congregational conflict, and reviewing the qualifications of an assembly for affiliation.

**Q:** List activities you would consider sacerdotal.

**A:** Answer could include installation of a new pastor in a local church, investigating complaints against a pastor, reviewing the qualifications of candidates for ministerial credentials, and establishing minimum requirements for the ordained minister credential.

**Q:** Summarize in your own words the seven requirements for a local church to qualify for General Council affiliated status.

**A:** Student’s answers could be similar to the following: (1) Accept the Sixteen Fundamental Truths. (2) Adopt a standard of membership. (3) Have at least twenty voting members [who qualify under the standards referenced in (2) above]. (4) Organize a governmental structure according to specific legal and accountability principles. (5) Have enough spiritually mature members to fill the offices of leadership. (6) Accept as lead pastor only Assemblies of God credentialed minsters. (7) Demonstrate a willingness to contribute to Assemblies of God missions.

**Q:** In what ways can the General Council intervene in local church government?

**A:** Student's answer should be similar to the following: In no way as long as its governance model conforms to guidelines specified in the Constitution.

**Q:** The Certificate of Affiliation can be withdrawn if a church practices or promotes unscriptural doctrine or polity. Does this conflict with the description of the Assemblies of God as a cooperative fellowship? Why or why not?

**A:** Student’s answer could be similar to the following: No. To be cooperative, a church agrees to submit to certain conditions for the sake of unity and scriptural propriety. If a church chooses to violate the agreed standards in doctrine or conduct, it is choosing not to cooperate with the Fellowship and has voided its affiliation. 14 CHAPTER
